[Proposition 5 of arXiv:2604.25470, 'A mathematical analysis of hierarchical Hopfield models'] Fix $\delta\in(0,1)$ and $\rho\in\mathbb N_0$, and let
	$m:=\lfloor \delta L\rfloor+1$.
	Under our assumptions let $\alpha$ be fixed.
	Then there exist constants $a=a(\kappa)>0$, $C=C(L)>0$, and $c=c(\kappa,L,C)>0$
	such that
	\[
	\mathbb P\bigl(\mathcal G_\alpha(\delta,\rho)^c\bigr)
	\le
	L\,N_f^{-a}
	+
	\mathbb P\bigl(\|\eta^{(\alpha)}\|_1>C\log N_f\bigr)
	+
	\frac{\bigl((M-L)e^{-c(\log N_f)^2}\bigr)^{\rho+1}}{(\rho+1)!}.
	\]
	In particular, if $M=M(N_f)$ grows at most polynomially in $N_f$, then
	\[
	\mathbb P\bigl(\mathcal G_\alpha(\delta,\rho)^c\bigr)\xrightarrow[N_f\to\infty]{}0.
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\emph{nested fractal} if the following conditions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(NF\arabic*)}]
\item There is a nonempty bounded open set \(\mathcal U\) such that
  \(\Psi_i(\mathcal U)\cap\Psi_j(\mathcal U)=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\) and
  \(\bigcup_i\Psi_i(\mathcal U)\subset\mathcal U\).
\item The set \(K\) is connected.
\item For every distinct \(x,y\in V_0\), the reflection
  \(\mathscr R_{x,y}\) preserves \(V_0\) and, for each \(r\ge1\),
  permutes the level-\(r\) fractal cells together with their boundaries.
\item For distinct \(i,j\in\cI\),
  \[
    \Psi_i(K)\cap\Psi_j(K)
    =
    \Psi_i(V_0)\cap\Psi_j(V_0).
  \]
\end{enumerate}

body: [Corollary 51 of arXiv:2609.03875, 'Measure theory without infinities'] Let $\mathcal{Q}$ be a $\sigma$-ring, $\K$ be a topological field, and $\mf A$ be a Hausdorff topological $\K$-vector space. Then $\ms M(\mathcal Q,\mf A)$ is a $\mathbb K$-vector space. If $k\in \mathbb{K}$ is nonzero, then $k\mu = k\cdot\mu$ for every $\mu\in \ms M(\mathcal Q,\mf A)$. If $\mf B$ is a sequentially closed topological vector subspace of $\mf A$, then $\ms M(\mathcal Q,\mf B)$ is a $\K$-vector subspace  of $\ms M(\mathcal Q,\mf A)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 51 of arXiv:2609.03875

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). If a real sequence (a_n)_{n>=1} is subadditive, meaning a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n for all m,n>=1, then lim_{n->infinity} a_n/n exists, possibly equal to -infinity, and equals inf_n a_n/n. This elementary but powerful lemma converts a one-directional combinatorial inequality into existence of a limit, and is the deterministic backbone behind results such as convergence of the free energy per site in statistical mechanics or the growth rate of a combinatorial quantity, for instance existence of the connective constant for self-avoiding walks, or existence of free energy limits in the Ising or Potts models under volume-doubling or concatenation subadditivity. An approximate or almost-subadditive version, a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n + e(m,n) with a controlled error term, such as e(m,n)=o(m+n) or a summable correction, still yields convergence of a_n/n to an infimum-type limit under mild additional conditions, a form often needed when exact subadditivity fails because of boundary effects. It does not give any rate of convergence, only existence of the limit, and it does not apply to sequences that are only superadditive or that fail monotonicity entirely without the appropriate sign flip; Kingman's theorem is the random, ergodic-theoretic generalization for stationary sequences and is not itself implied by Fekete's lemma. Typical failure: Verifying subadditivity only for a convenient special subsequence, such as powers of 2 or specific volume shapes like cubes, and then applying Fekete's lemma as though the inequality had been established for all m, n; the lemma genuinely requires the inequality for all pairs, or at least a cofinal family closed under addition, and skipping intermediate cases silently assumes exactly the regularity, such as shape-independence of the volume limit in statistical mechanics, that itself needs a separate van Hove or Fisher-type argument. Canonical reference: Fekete, 1923, Mathematische Zeitschrift; Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, 1997, SIAM, Chapter 1.
a real-valued sequence, or for the approximate version a sequence with a controlled, typically o(n) or summable, subadditivity defect
the subadditive inequality a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n holding for all, or eventually all, pairs m, n
boundedness of a_n/n from below, or explicit acceptance that the limit may be -infinity, for the limit to be meaningful in context
for statistical-mechanics applications: correct identification of the quantity, such as a log partition function, as subadditive under the relevant combination operation, such as concatenation or union of volumes
title: Technique: Fekete's Lemma and Approximate Subadditivity

[Lem 24 of arXiv:2607.21759, 'Marchenko--Pastur law for tensor powers of exchangeable unconditional vectors'] For fixed $d$, $\sup_n \E(X_1^4\dotsm X_d^4) < \infty$ is equivalent to \cref{thm:main} \cref{cond:2nd-4th-compare} for a constant $L$: for all $1 \leq r\leq d$, there exists some constant $L$ such that for all large enough $n$, \[
        \E(X_1^4\dotsm X_r^4 X_{r+1}^2\dotsm X_{2d - r}^2) \leq L^r.
    \]

[Lemma 103 (Random harmonic rearrangement) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge1}$ be independent copies of a nonnegative random variable
$Y$ with $0<\mathbb EY<\infty$ and $\mathbb EY^2<\infty$.  Fix $c>0$ and
$0\le\theta<1$, and let $D_\omega$ be the positive diagonal operator whose
unordered diagonal entries are
\[
 d_k(\omega)=\frac{cY_k(\omega)}{k-\theta}.
\]
Then $D_\omega$ is compact almost surely and
\begin{equation}
 uN_{D_\omega}(u)\longrightarrow c\mathbb EY,
 \qquad
 s_N(D_\omega)\sim\frac{c\mathbb EY}{N}
 \quad\text{almost surely}.
 
\end{equation}
If $Y$ has finite moments of every positive order, use the convention
$0^z=0$ for $\operatorname{Re}z>0$.  Then almost surely
$\zeta_{D_\omega}$ admits a meromorphic continuation to
$\operatorname{Re}z>1/2$ with a unique pole there at $z=1$, and
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname*{Res}_{z=1}\zeta_{D_\omega}(z)=c\mathbb EY.
 
\end{equation}

body: The symmetric group S_n is the group of all bijections (permutations) of {1, ..., n} under composition, of order n!. It is generated by transpositions (and by adjacent transpositions); the parity of the number of transpositions in any expression of a permutation is well-defined (even/odd), giving the sign homomorphism onto {+1, -1} whose kernel is the alternating group A_n. By Cayley's theorem every group embeds in some symmetric group.

[Lemma 62 of arXiv:2608.07239, 'Unified framework for asymptotically uniform iterative construction of generalised random '] Let $\lambda\geq4\log\alpha$. For $p\in[0,1]$, we define the functions
		\begin{align}
			\beta^{(a)}_p(\lambda)&:=\ell c_2\sqrt{\lambda(qM+2\lambda)(q^2\alpha M+3\lambda^2)},
			\\\beta^{(b)}_p(\lambda)&:=3\ell c_3\sqrt{\lambda(q^2M+7\lambda^2)(q^3\alpha M+8\lambda^3)},
			\\\beta_p(\lambda)&:=4\beta^{(a)}_p(\lambda)+\min\{\beta^{(b)}_p(\lambda),2q^2\alpha M\}.
		\end{align}
		Then the events
		\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
			\item $\begin{aligned}[t]
				|\Delta_p(F^{(2)})-\Lambda_p(F^{(2)})-\mathbb{E}(\Delta_p(F^{(2)})-\Lambda_p(F^{(2)}))|\geq\beta^{(a)}_p(\lambda),
			\end{aligned}$
			\item $\begin{aligned}[t]
				&|\Delta_p(R_p^{(2)})-\Lambda_p(R_p^{(2)})-\mathbb{E}(\Delta_p(R_p^{(2)})-\Lambda_p(R_p^{(2)}))|\\&\geq\beta^{(a)}_p(\lambda)+\min\{\beta^{(b)}_p(\lambda),2q^2\alpha M\},
			\end{aligned}$
			\item $\begin{aligned}[t]
				|\Lambda_p(V^{(2)})-\mathbb{E}(\Lambda_p(V^{(2)}))|\geq\beta^{(a)}_p(\lambda),
			\end{aligned}$
			\item $\begin{aligned}[t]
				|\Lambda_p(S)-\mathbb{E}(\Lambda_p(S))|\geq\beta^{(a)}_p(\lambda)
			\end{aligned}$
		\end{enumerate}
		have probability $O(e^{-\frac14\lambda})$ each. For $r=0,\ldots,\alpha-k-1$, it follows that
		\begin{align}
			\mathbb{P}(|\Psi_p^{(2)}-\psi_p^{(2)}|\geq\beta_p(\lambda))&=O(e^{-\frac14\lambda}),
			\\\mathbb{P}(|\Psi_r^{(2)}-\psi_{p_r}^{(2)}|\geq\beta_{p_r}(\lambda))&=O(\alpha^{\sfrac12}e^{-\frac14\lambda}).
		\end{align}

[Proposition prop:effective.degrees.freedom of arXiv:2606.04859, 'Stein's method for the Wishart distribution'] Let $d\in \mathbb{N}$ be fixed and let $N = N_n$ depend on some positive integer parameter $n$ (e.g., a sample size). Assume that $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_N > 0$ and that there exist constants $0 < c < C < \infty$, independent of $n$ and $j$, such that
\[
c \, n \leq \sum_{j = 1}^N \alpha_j \leq C n, \qquad  rac{c}{n}I_d \preceq \Sigma_j \preceq  rac{C}{n}I_d, \qquad j\in [N],
\]
where $\preceq$ denotes the Loewner order. Let $
u_0 > 3d-3$ be fixed, and let $
u_{\mathrm{UB}}$ be any minimizer of $G$ over $[
u_0, \infty)$. Then, as $n	o \infty$,
\[

u_{\mathrm{TG}}\asymp n, \qquad 
u_{\mathrm{K}}\asymp n, \qquad 
u_{\mathrm{LS}}\asymp n, \qquad 
u_{\mathrm{US}}\asymp n, \qquad 
u_{\mathrm{UB}}\asymp n.
\]
In particular, each of the above choices satisfies $
u = \mathcal{O}(n)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: On a bounded domain, sup over the domain of |f| equals sup over the boundary. On an unbounded domain this is false without a growth restriction, and the Phragmén–Lindelöf principle is exactly the repair: the conclusion |f| ≤ M inside holds only under a subcritical growth bound, and the critical rate is attained by explicit functions. Load-bearing hypothesis and its failures: (1) Strip of width π, S = {|Im z| < π/2}. The function f(z) = exp(exp(z)) is entire, satisfies |f| = exp(e^x cos y), so |f| = 1 on both boundary lines Im z = ±π/2, yet |f(x)| = exp(e^x) → ∞ along the real axis. Its growth is exp(exp(|Re z|)), i.e. exactly the critical rate α = 1, so the hypothesis 'α < 1' cannot be relaxed to 'α ≤ 1'. (2) Sector of opening π/2, S = {|arg z| < π/4}. The function f(z) = exp(z^2) has |f| = 1 on both boundary rays (there z^2 is purely imaginary) and |f(x)| = exp(x^2) → ∞ on the axis of the sector; its growth exp(|z|^2) matches the critical exponent β = α = 2, so again the strict inequality β < α is needed. (3) Three-lines theorem without boundedness on the closed strip: f(z) = exp(-i exp(iπ z)) is entire, |f(x + iy)| = exp(e^{-πy} sin(πx)), so |f| = 1 on both lines Re z = 0 and Re z = 1, while on the middle line Re z = 1/2 it equals exp(e^{-πy}), which is unbounded as y → -∞. Hence M(0) = M(1) = 1 but M(1/2) = ∞: log-convexity of M fails without the boundedness hypothesis. Practical rule when auditing: whenever a bound 'on the boundary' is promoted to a bound 'inside' on a strip, sector, half-plane or any unbounded region, find the explicit growth estimate in the argument and check that its exponent is strictly below the critical one for that region's opening angle.
title: Pitfall: the maximum principle on an unbounded domain needs a growth hypothesis

[Proposition 3 of arXiv:2608.29713, '\textbf{A Cartan geometry from a correspondence space in Riemannian geometry}'] Let $(p:\mathcal P\to N,\omega)$ be a Cartan geometry of type
$(G,H)$. Then $\dim N=2n-1$, and $N$ carries canonically the following objects:
\[
(\bar{g},U,\alpha,\mathcal E,\mathcal B,\Psi),
\]
where
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\bar{g}$ is a Riemannian metric;
\item $U\in\mathfrak X(N)$ is a unit vector field;
\item $\alpha:=\bar{g}(U,\cdot)$;
\item $\mathcal E$ and $\mathcal B$ are distributions such that $TN$ splits orthogonally as
$$
TN= \mathbb R U\oplus\mathcal E\oplus \mathcal B,
\qquad
\operatorname{rank}\mathcal E=\operatorname{rank}\mathcal B=n-1;
$$
\item $\Psi\in\mathcal T_{(1,1)}(N)$ satisfying
\[
\Psi^2=-\operatorname{Id}+\alpha\otimes U,
\qquad
 \bar{g}\big(\Psi(V),\Psi (W)\big)=\bar{g}(V,W)-\alpha(V)\alpha(W),
\]
where $V,W\in\mathfrak{X}(N)$, and
\[
\Psi(U)=0,
\qquad
\Psi(\mathcal E)=\mathcal B,
\qquad
\Psi(\mathcal B)=\mathcal E.
\]
\end{enumerate}
In particular, $(\bar{g},U,\alpha,\Psi)$ is an almost contact metric structure.

[Proposition 12 (Distinct-speed wave/Klein--Gordon diagonals) of arXiv:2606.16662, '2606.16662'] Let \(\tau=(i;j,j)\) and work in the standard high-frequency wave/Klein--Gordon normalization: the outer Duhamel factor has gain \(\lambda_i=1\), the stochastic convolution leg has gain \(\alpha_j=1\), and hence \(\Gamma_{i;j,j}=3\) in Assumption~\ref{ass:coeff}.  Assume that, at high frequency,
\[
        \omega_a(n)=(m_a^2+c_a^2|n|^2)^{1/2},
        \qquad m_a>0,
        \qquad c_i\ne c_j .
\]
Suppose that
\[
        K_i(t,n)=\frac{\sin(t\omega_i(n))}{\omega_i(n)}
\]
and that \(\Psi_j\) is the corresponding stochastic convolution.  Assume
\(d<4\) and choose \(\eps>0\) so that \(20\eps<4-d\).  Then the same-color
diagonal kernel satisfies Assumption~\ref{ass:diag} on a sufficiently small
proportional aperture \(|q|\le c_{\rm ap}N\), with phase gain \(\vartheta=1\)
and any retained gain \(\Delta\) satisfying
\[
        20\eps<\Delta<4-d.
\]
More precisely, after the trigonometric expansion the principal phases are
\begin{equation}
        \Phi_{\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2}(q,\ell)
        =\epsilon_1\omega_i(q+\ell)+\epsilon_2\omega_j(\ell),
        \qquad \epsilon_1,\epsilon_2\in\{+1,-1\},
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
        |\Phi_{\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2}(q,\ell)|\gtrsim N,
        \qquad |\ell|\sim N,
        \qquad |q|\le c_{\rm ap}N .
\end{equation}
Consequently, in this normalization, a retained same-color diagonal has loop gain
\begin{equation}
        0<\Delta<1+\Gamma_{i;j,j}-d=4-d.
\end{equation}
In dimension three, every fixed \(0<\Delta<1\) is available after choosing
\(\eps\) sufficiently small.
title: Distinct-speed wave/Klein--Gordon diagonals

[Lemma LemmaKeyFacts of arXiv:2605.16244, 'Analysis of a twisted Bose--Einstein Markov chain with applications to sampling Catalan st'] Let $n,k\ge1$ and $x,y \in [k]^n$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item For all $\sigma\in S_n$,
\bal
|([k]^n)_\sigma|=k^{\ell(\sigma)}.
\eal
When $k=n+1$, the restriction to parking functions satisfies
\bal
|(\mathrm{PF}_n)_\sigma|=(n+1)^{\ell(\sigma)-1}.
\eal
\item We have
\bal
G_x \cong S_{i_1(x)}\times\cdots\times S_{i_k(x)} \quad \text{and} \quad |G_x|=\prod_{a=1}^{k} i_a(x)!.
\eal
\item We have that
\bal
|[k]^n/S_n|=|\mathrm{Comp}_{n,k}|=\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}.
\eal
When $k=n+1$, the parking-function restriction satisfies
\bal
|\mathrm{PF}_n/S_n|=|\mathrm{IPF}_n|=C_n.
\eal
\item We have
\bal
G_x\cap G_y\cong\prod_{a,b=1}^k S_{m_{a,b}(x,y)} \quad \text{and} \quad
|G_x\cap G_y|=\prod_{a,b=1}^k m_{a,b}(x,y)!
\eal
\item For \(g\in G_x\cap G_y\), each nonempty \(B_{a,b}(x,y)\) is \(g\)-invariant, so
\[
g|_{B_{a,b}(x,y)}:B_{a,b}(x,y)\to B_{a,b}(x,y)
\]
is a permutation, and
\[
\ell(g)
=
\sum_{\substack{1\le a,b\le k\\ B_{a,b}(x,y)\neq\emptyset}}
\ell\!\left(g|_{B_{a,b}(x,y)}\right).
\]
\end{enumerate}

Attributed source theorem, not independently audited here. Fix delta in [0,1). There are c_delta>0 and finite kappa_delta, independent of dimension, such that for every d>=2 and kappa>=kappa_delta, any common-randomness simulator with at most Q transcript bits that samples every N(0,Sigma) satisfying kappa^-1 I<=Sigma<=I within TV error delta must have Q>=c_delta*d*log2(kappa). The inequalities on Sigma are Loewner inequalities. This is a total-bit bound and supplies no bound on information in one real-valued score query.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a centered, almost surely bounded Gaussian process (X_t)_{t in T}, let M = sup_t X_t and sigma^2 = sup_t Var(X_t). The Borell-TIS inequality states P(|M - E[M]| >= u) <= 2 exp(-u^2/(2 sigma^2)) for all u >= 0, giving Gaussian concentration of the supremum around its mean at the scale of the process's maximal pointwise variance, regardless of the cardinality or geometry of the index set. Separately, Slepian's inequality compares two centered Gaussian processes on the same index set with equal marginal variances: if E[(X_s-X_t)^2] <= E[(Y_s-Y_t)^2] for all s,t, then E[sup X] <= E[sup Y], and with the equal marginal variances the same condition, equivalently E[X_s X_t] >= E[Y_s Y_t] for all s,t, also gives the tail comparison P(sup X > u) <= P(sup Y > u) for every u; no condition on the sign of the correlations is needed, and none can replace the equal variances. The Sudakov-Fernique inequality removes the equal-variance requirement, needing only the pointwise increment domination, but concludes only the expectation comparison E[sup X] <= E[sup Y], not the stronger distributional comparison. Together these tools reduce bounding E[sup] of a complicated Gaussian field to bounding it for a simpler, dominating comparison field. Borell-TIS does not give the value of E[M] itself, which requires a separate chaining or Dudley-integral bound, and Sudakov-Fernique is strictly weaker in conclusion than the classical Slepian inequality even when both sets of hypotheses happen to hold. Typical failure: Invoking the classical Slepian inequality's tail or distributional comparison after only verifying the weaker Sudakov-Fernique hypotheses, namely increment domination without equal variances; Sudakov-Fernique licenses comparing E[sup X] to E[sup Y] only, and treating the two comparison theorems as interchangeable overstates what has actually been proven. Canonical reference: Borell, 1975, Inventiones Mathematicae; Tsirelson, Ibragimov and Sudakov, 1976, in Proceedings of the School-Seminar on Random Processes; Slepian, 1962, Bell System Technical Journal; Fernique, 1975, Ecole d'Ete de Probabilites de Saint-Flour, Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics.
a centered Gaussian process, almost surely bounded on the index set, for Borell-TIS
for Slepian/Sudakov-Fernique: two Gaussian processes on the same index set with pointwise increment-variance domination E[(X_s-X_t)^2]<=E[(Y_s-Y_t)^2]
for the classical Slepian tail comparison specifically: equal marginal variances (then increment domination is equivalent to E[X_sX_t]>=E[Y_sY_t]); no correlation-sign condition replaces them
measurability and separability of the process so the supremum is well defined

[Lemma 16 (Stochastic normalization of a weakly flat profile) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Suppose that \(S\) is symmetric, \(S_{ii}=0\), and
\[
 \frac{c}{N}\le S_{ij}\le\frac{C}{N}\quad(i\ne j),
 \qquad \max_i|q_i(S)|=o(1).
\]
For all sufficiently large \(N\), there is a positive diagonal matrix
\(D=\diag(d_1,\ldots,d_N)\) such that
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde S:=DSD,
 \qquad
 \sum_j\widetilde S_{ij}=1\quad(1\le i\le N).
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{align}
 \norm{D-I}_{\infty}
 &\le C\max_i|q_i(S)|=o(1),\\
 \sum_i|d_i-1|^2
 &\le C\sum_i|q_i(S)|^2,\\
 \norm{\widetilde S-S}_{\HS}
 &\le C N^{-1/2}\norm{q(S)}_2=o(1).
 
\end{align}
If \(H_{ij}\) has variance \(S_{ij}\), then
\(\widetilde H_{ij}:=\sqrt{d_id_j}\,H_{ij}\) has variance
\(\widetilde S_{ij}\).  Uniform boundedness of \(\sqrt N H_{ij}\) and
uniform convergence of its fourth cumulants are preserved by this rescaling.

For the spike-generated profile \eqref{eq:R3-variance-matrix}--
\eqref{eq:R3-rem-bound}, the following stronger estimates hold:
\begin{align}
 \max_i|q_i(S_N)|&=o(N^{-1/2}),
 \\
 \norm{D-I}_\infty&=o(N^{-1/2}),
 \\
 \norm{D-I}_{\HS}^2&=o(1),
 \\
 \norm{S_N-DS_ND}_{\HS}&=o(N^{-1/2}),
 \\
 \max_{i\ne j}\frac{|S_{ij}-d_id_jS_{ij}|}{S_{ij}}
 &=o(N^{-1/2}).
 
\end{align}

[Lemma lem:almost-splitting of arXiv:2609.01464, 'Removability of non-isolated singularities for Einstein metrics and RCD spaces'] For each $n\geqslant2$, set $\rho:=1/(100n)$.  There is a function
$\Psi(\kappa)\to 0$ as $\kappa\to 0$ with the following
property.  Let $(Y,\mathrm{d}_Y,\mathfrak m_Y,y)$ be $\operatorname{RCD}(-\kappa,n)$,
$0<\kappa<1$, and let $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$. Let $I$ denote the $n\times n$ identity matrix.  Assume
\begin{align}
 &u\text{ is harmonic on }B_6(y),\qquad
 \max_i\|\nabla u_i\|_{L^\infty(B_{6}(y))}\leqslant C(n),\\
 &\fint_{B_{6}(y)}|G_u-I|\,\mathrm{d}\mathfrak m_Y
 +\fint_{B_{6}(y)}\sum_i|\operatorname{Hess} u_i|^2\,\mathrm{d}\mathfrak m_Y\leqslant \kappa.
 
\end{align}
Then
\begin{equation}
 d_{GH}\left((\overline B_{2\rho}(y),y),
 (\overline B_{2\rho}(0^n),0^n)\right)\leqslant\Psi(\kappa).
\end{equation}

body:
Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system and $A: X \to M_d(\mathbb{R})$ a measurable cocycle with $\log^+ \|A\| \in L^1(\mu)$; write $A^n(x) = A(T^{n-1}x)\cdots A(x)$.

ONE-SIDED (FILTRATION) VERSION - no invertibility of $T$ or of $A$ needed. For $\mu$-a.e. $x$: (a) the limit $\Lambda(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \big(A^n(x)^{\mathsf T} A^n(x)\big)^{1/2n}$ exists (a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix); (b) there are an integer $1 \le k(x) \le d$, exponents $\infty > \lambda_1(x) > \lambda_2(x) > \dots > \lambda_{k(x)}(x) \ge -\infty$ (only the smallest may be $-\infty$; this happens at every $x$ whose orbit meets the set where $A$ is singular, hence almost everywhere when $T$ is ergodic and $A$ is singular with positive probability, and can also happen for a.e.-invertible $A$ when $\log^+\|A^{-1}\|$ is not integrable), and a filtration of linear subspaces $\mathbb{R}^d = V_1(x) \supsetneq V_2(x) \supsetneq \dots \supsetneq V_{k(x)}(x) \supsetneq V_{k(x)+1}(x) = \{0\}$, measurable in $x$, such that $A(x) V_i(x) \subset V_i(Tx)$ and
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x) \quad\text{for every } v \in V_i(x) \setminus V_{i+1}(x);$$
(c) $k$, the $\lambda_i$ and the multiplicities $m_i = \dim V_i - \dim V_{i+1}$ are $T$-invariant functions of $x$ (constants when $T$ is ergodic); (d) $\lim \frac1n \log |\det A^n(x)| = \sum_i m_i \lambda_i(x)$, and more generally $\lim \frac1n \log \|\Lambda^p A^n(x)\|$ (norm on the $p$-th exterior power) equals the sum of the $p$ largest exponents counted with multiplicity; (e) the $\lambda_i$ with multiplicities are exactly the limits $\lim \frac1n \log \sigma_j(A^n(x))$ of the singular values, i.e. the logarithms of the eigenvalues of $\Lambda(x)$.

TWO-SIDED (SPLITTING) VERSION. If moreover $T$ is invertible, $A(x) \in GL_d(\mathbb{R})$ a.e. and $\log^+ \|A^{-1}\| \in L^1(\mu)$, then for a.e. $x$ all exponents are finite and there is a measurable $A$-equivariant splitting $\mathbb{R}^d = E_1(x) \oplus \dots \oplus E_{k(x)}(x)$, $A(x)E_i(x) = E_i(Tx)$, $\dim E_i = m_i$, with $\lim_{n \to \pm\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x)$ for all $v \in E_i(x) \setminus \{0\}$ (the SAME exponent forwards and backwards), $V_i(x) = \bigoplus_{j \ge i} E_j(x)$, and the angles between the Oseledets subspaces decay subexponentially along orbits: $\lim_{n\to\pm\infty} \frac1n \log \sin\angle\big(E_i(T^n x), \bigoplus_{j\ne i} E_j(T^n x)\big) = 0$.

WHERE IT FAILS. (1) Without $\log^+\|A\| \in L^1$ the limits need not exist: for $d = 1$ the theorem IS Birkhoff's theorem for $\log|a|$, which fails when $\log^+|a| \notin L^1$. (2) Without $\log^+\|A^{-1}\| \in L^1$ (or with $T$ non-invertible) there is in general NO equivariant splitting, only the forward filtration: the subspaces of vectors with exponent exactly $\lambda_i$, $i \ge 2$, are not canonically defined and the 'slow' directions are not invariant under $A$. (3) The exponents depend on the measure $\mu$: different ergodic measures for the same $T$ and $A$ generally have different exponents, and a point outside the full-measure set need not have exponents at all. (4) Convergence is not uniform in $x$, and the Oseledets subspaces are only measurable, in general not continuous, in $x$. (5) The theorem is about $\|A^n(x)v\|$ along ONE orbit; it says nothing about eigenvalues of $A^n(x)$ or about $\|A^n\|$ averaged over $x$.
T is measure-preserving on a probability space; for the one-sided version T need not be invertible
A is measurable with log^+ ||A|| integrable
the splitting version additionally needs T invertible, A(x) invertible a.e., and log^+ ||A^{-1}|| integrable
all statements hold for mu-a.e. x; exponents depend on mu

body:
In Ganguly, Hegde and Zhang, 'van den Berg-Kesten-type correlation inequalities for disjoint polymers in the KPZ universality class' (arXiv:2512.17823), P(. | X = K), for a random element X and a deterministic point K of the same space, is defined through a regular conditional distribution: a probability kernel mu from the space of X to the space of the conditioned random element Y such that P(Y in B | X) = mu(X, B) almost surely for every measurable B, evaluated at K, so P(Y in B | X = K) = mu(K, B). Such a kernel exists whenever Y takes values in a Borel space; this is the existence theorem the paper cites as Theorem 8.5 of Kallenberg's Foundations of Modern Probability (third edition). The kernel is unique only up to a null set of the law of X, so its value mu(K, .) at a single point K depends on the version chosen unless P(X = K) > 0, where it is the elementary conditional probability. In the discrete settings of the paper's Section 2 these are ordinary conditional probabilities. The paper has no Theorem 8.5 of its own.
X is a random element of a measurable space and K a point of that space
the conditioned random element Y takes values in a Borel (standard Borel) space

body:
Own-work route diagnostic T387-C005 v1; unaudited sketch, no novelty claimed. Consider f=m^(-1)sum_r a_r ReLU(w_r dot x+b_r), no output bias, exact shared-example joint SGD with a common schedule, identical deterministic derivative conventions, and no neuron-specific randomness. Initialize every neuron identically at a=b=1/4,w=0. Equality of all neuron parameter triples is invariant at every finite step, even after gates change, so f=a ReLU(w dot x+b). With a fixed binary sign-at-zero convention its classifier is constant or a halfspace and hence unate. For any unate H:{-1,1}^d->{-1,+1} and a parity support S of size k>=2, |Hhat(S)|<=|Hhat({i})| for each i in S, by the fixed sign of the discrete derivative. Parseval on these k+1 distinct coefficients gives |Hhat(S)|<=1/sqrt(k+1). Under a mixture with uniform signs of weight 1-rho and independent signs of mean mu of weight rho, this synchronized predictor therefore has error at least (1-rho)(1-1/sqrt(k+1))/2 at every step. In particular, k=8,d>=9,0<rho<1/4,0<mu<1 rules out error<=1/4, although the same initialization may encode the support with high probability in its weights during the first phase. At rho=1/8 the error lower bound is 7/24. This rules out only the all-identical continuation route, not diverse or mixed-sign initialization, arbitrary bounded neuron-specific errors, or the k=3 experiment. Finite exact checks covered all 194 coordinatewise increasing truth tables on 2,3,4 variables; the all-dimensional argument has no independent or formal certificate.
Exact gradients, simultaneous common-rate updates, identical neuron initialization and deterministic conventions.
Fixed binary zero-prediction convention and no additional output bias.
k>=2: singleton coefficients and the full-support coefficient must be distinct.
Unateness is essential; parity itself is a counterexample without it.

  Then for any $x, x' \in W$, $x \Vdash^{\text{c}}_\mathfrak{M} \varphi$ and $x \leq x'$ implies $x' \Vdash^{\text{c}}_\mathfrak{M} \varphi$.

    Suppose that $x' \in W_\bot$, then it trivially holds since $x' \Vdash^{\text{c}}_\mathfrak{M} \varphi$ by Proposition (prop:all-is-fair of the paper).
    Now suppose that $x' \notin W_\bot$, then $x \notin W_\bot$ by $W_\bot$ being upward closed with respect to $\leq$.

body:
[Ppn 80 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] On the time interval $[q_0,\gamma(1)]$,
for $\tilde{w}_t$ as defined by Lemma~\ref{l:time.change}, we have
    \[
        \int_{q_0}^{\gamma(1)}
        \Big(
            \bbE w_{\lambda(s)} - \bbE \tilde w_s
        \Big)_+ \,ds
        \le 2\epsilon^{1/4}
    \]
for all $\epsilon>0$ small enough.

\begin{proof} By Lemma~\ref{l:generalized.inverse.fn}, for bounding the integral we can ignore the measure-zero set of times $s$ for which $\gamma'(\lambda(s))=0$. Therefore, without loss, we restrict our attention to times $s$ for which
$\gamma'(\lambda(s))>0$. In this case, we have $\gamma'(\lambda(s)) \lambda'(s) = 1$, so the definition of $\tilde w_s$ for $s\in[q_0,\gamma(1)]$ 
can be written as $\tilde w_s = \lambda'(s)^{1/2} w_{\lambda(s)} \ind\{\lambda(s) \le \tau\}$. We therefore have
    \begin{align*}
        \int_{q_0}^{\gamma(1)}\lt(
            \bbE w_{\lambda(s)} - \bbE\tilde w_s
        \rt)_+ \,ds
        &\le
        \int_{q_0}^{\gamma(1)}
        \bbE\Big[
        w_{\lambda(s)} - \lambda'(s)^{1/2}
            w_{\lambda(s)} \ind\{ \lambda(s) \le \tau\}
    \Big]_+\,ds\\
        &\le
        \int_{q_0}^{\gamma(1)}
        \bbE\Big[ \lambda'(s)^{1/2} w_{\lambda(s)} \ind\{
        \lambda(s) > \tau\}\Big]\,ds\,,
    \end{align*}
    where the last inequality uses $\lambda' \ge 1$, as a consequence of \eqref{e:gamma.prime}. We then apply the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality to bound the above by
    \begin{align*}
      &  \bigg(
            \int_{q_0}^{\gamma(1)}
            \bbP(\lambda(s) > \tau)\,ds\bigg)^{1/2}
            \cdot\bigg(
            \int_{q_0}^{\gamma(1)}
            \lambda'(s)
            \bbE\Big[
            (w_{\lambda(s)})^2 \ind\{ \lambda(s) > \tau\}\Big]
            \,ds
        \bigg)^{1/2}\\
  &\quad      \le \bigg(
            \int_{q_0}^{\gamma(1)}
            \lambda'(s)
            \bbE\Big[
            (w_{\lambda(s)})^2 \ind\{
             \lambda(s) > \tau\}\Big]
            \,ds
        \bigg)^{1/2}.
    \end{align*}
Changing variables to $u = \lambda(s)$, we bound the last integral above by
    \begin{align*}
        \int_{q_0}^1
        \bbE[(w_u)^2 \ind\{u > \tau\}]\,du
        &= \bbE
            \int_\tau^1 (w_u)^2 \,du
       = \bbE[Y(1)^2 -\hat Y(1)^2]
        = 1 - \gamma(1)
        \le 4\epsilon^{1/2}\,,    \end{align*}
where the last step again uses
Proposition~\ref{p:gamma-1}. This proves the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let $t_0 \ge 4$ and $\eta_t = 2/(\mu(t+1))$ for every $t \ge t_0$, and let $R_0$ be an $\mathcal{F}_{t_0 - 1}$-measurable quantity satisfying $R_0 \ge Z_{t_0}$ almost surely. Then, for every $\alpha \in (0,1)$, the process $\{\widehat U_t^{\mathrm{sub,EB}}(\alpha)\}_{t \ge t_0}$ is well defined and fully observable from $R_0$ and the SGD trajectory. Moreover,
\[

        f(\bar x_t) - f(x^\star)
        \le
        \widehat U_t^{\mathrm{sub,EB}}(\alpha)
    \right)
    \ge
    1-\alpha.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 7 (Global convergence in the strictly subcritical regime) of arXiv:2608.20638, 'Provable Edge-of-Stability for Adam on a One-Dimensional Quadratic'] Assume
\[
    0<\beta_1<1,
    \qquad
    0\le \beta_2<1,
    \qquad
    \sqrt{\beta_2}>\beta_1^2,
    \qquad
    w_{\max}<2.
\]
Then every trajectory of Adam on $f(x)=\tfrac12x^2$ converges to the
origin.  More precisely, for every initial state
$(x_0,m_0,v_0)\in\R^2\times[0,\infty)$, there exist constants $C>0$ and
$\gamma_0\in(0,1)$, possibly depending on the initial state, such that
\[
    \abs{x_t}+\abs{m_t}+v_t
    \le C\gamma_0^t,
    \qquad t\ge0.
\]
In particular, $(x_t,m_t,v_t)\to(0,0,0)$ and $w_t\to w_{\max}$.

[Theorem thm:dgt4-diffusive-membrane of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] Let $d\geq5$. Suppose that $(\zeta(x))_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$ are i.i.d.\ and
	atomless, with mean
	zero and finite positive variance. Assume either that
	\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
		\item the $\zeta(x)$ are Gaussian; or
		\item the $\zeta(x)$ are bounded above and, for some $\alpha>2$,
		\[
			\frac{\mathbb{P}(\zeta(0)<-\lambda r)}{\mathbb{P}(\zeta(0)<-r)}
			\longrightarrow\lambda^{-\alpha}
			\qquad(r\to\infty)\, ,
		\]
		for every $\lambda>0$.
	\end{enumerate}
	Then, for every $T>0$ and every $s>(d-4)/2$, as $R\to\infty$,
	\[
		R^{(d-4)/2}\bigl(u_{\lfloor R^2T\rfloor}-\mathbb{E} u_{\lfloor R^2T\rfloor}(0)\bigr)^{(R)}\Longrightarrow\mathcal H_{\kappa,T}\qquad\text{in }H^{-s}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^d)\, ,
	\]
	where $\kappa=1$ in case \textup{(a)} and $\kappa=1-1/\alpha$ in case
	\textup{(b)}. Moreover, as $n\to\infty$,
	\[
		\mathbb{P}(u_n(0)=0)\sim\frac{G(0,0)\kappa}{n}\, .
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 8 (Last-occurrence scale comparison) of arXiv:2604.26298, 'The Expiring Coupon Collector\\ Sliding-Window Surjection Flux and Rare-Entry Laws'] Let \(N=n-1\), \(m=M-1\), and assume
\[
        n\le M\le n\log n,
        \qquad
        M>n.
\]
Let \(\tau>0\) be defined by
\[
        \frac{\tau}{1-e^{-\tau}}=\frac mN=:\rho .
\]
For \(1\le u\le m-1\), put
\[
        q_u:=\left(1-\frac1N\right)^{u-1},
        \qquad
        y_u:=1-e^{-u/n},
\]
and
\[
        \Lambda_u
        :=N\frac{e^{-\tau(m-u)/m}(1-e^{-\tau u/m})}{1-e^{-\tau}}.
\]
Then, uniformly for \(1\le u\le m-1\),
\[
        q_u\Lambda_u\asymp
        \lambda_{n,M}y_u,
        \qquad
        \lambda_{n,M}:=n\left(1-\frac1n\right)^M.
\]
title: Last-occurrence scale comparison

[Proposition 30 of arXiv:2608.19065, 'Boundedly exchangeable graphs'] For $k\in\nbb_0$, write
\[
    \widehat p_n(k)
    \coloneqq
    \frac{1}{\nu(E_n)}
    \sum_{x\in v(G)\cap E_n}
    \mathbf{1}{\{\deg(x)=k\}}
\]
on the event $\{\nu(E_n)>0\}$, and set $\widehat p_n(k) \coloneqq 0$
otherwise. Then
\[
    \widehat p_n(k)
    \overset{\pbb}{\longrightarrow}
    e^{-\delta V_t}\frac{(\delta V_t)^k}{k!}.
\]
If \eqref{CondSummable} holds, then this convergence holds almost surely.

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.04139, 'The conformally invariant metric on CLE$_4$ II:\\ existence of geodesics'] We continue our study of the conformal loop ensemble (CLE) with parameter $\kappa=4$, the critical threshold at or below which the loops are simple and disjoint, touching neither each other nor the domain boundary. This paper is the second in a series of three establishing that the loops of a CLE$_4$ uniquely determine a conformally invariant, local, and geodesic metric such that the metric ball growth from the domain boundary coincides with the uniform exploration of Werner and Wu. In this second paper, we prove the existence of geodesics, showing that any geodesic between two loops is supported on the CLE$_4$ loops (off a set of Hausdorff dimension zero) and does not intersect the domain boundary. Along the way, we establish sharp quantitative estimates for the CLE$_4$ metric geometry, including exponential tail bounds for rectangle distances and multi-scale four-arm SLE$_4$ non-intersection bounds for metric balls.
title: Abstract of arXiv:2609.04139: The conformally invariant metric on CLE$_4$ II:\\ existence of geodesics

body:
STATUS: proof (unaudited); own-work draft; no novelty assertion. An explicit two-parameter family of balanced, opposite-head period-two orbits in joint-head factored logistic attention has complete three-dimensional linear stability spectrum: transverse multiplier zero, one positive multiplier >25/12, and another positive multiplier crossing 1 at a unique explicit quadratic threshold tau_c in (0,1/4). The cycles are never attracting, despite normal contraction. Both strict regimes for the second balanced multiplier occur.
ASSUMPTIONS: b,kappa>0; unique T in (1/2,1) solves cosh(T)^2=2cosh(T/4)^2; h(s)=a+b tanh(kappa s), a=b(tanh T+tanh(T/4))/2, H=b(tanh T-tanh(T/4))/2, d=b kappa sech(T)^2, V=sqrt(H/(4d)), w=sqrt(T/kappa), g=1/(1+exp(-VH)), eta=2V/(gH). Simultaneous Euclidean GD for log(1+exp(-v h(kq))); orbit (V,w,-w)<->(-V,w/2,-w/2). Repeated identical signed links are permitted; distinct-link and arbitrary opposite-cycle classification not asserted.
SCOPE/GAP: Independent review pending. Classifies this exact family only; asymmetric-head cycles, other balanced cycles and general factored-GD almost-everywhere convergence remain unresolved. Numerical and exact polynomial checks are not an independent proof audit.

# Opposite-head balanced two-cycles: exact family and full linear stability

Claim T328-W698-016, v1. Target 1. PROOF, UNAUDITED.
This is a family classification, not a classification of all balanced cycles or a global GD theorem. No novelty claim is made.

## Exact family

Let b,kappa>0. There is a unique T in (1/2,1) with

    cosh(T)^2 = 2 cosh(T/4)^2.

Put a=b(tanh T+tanh(T/4))/2, H=b(tanh T-tanh(T/4))/2,
d=b*kappa*sech(T)^2, V=sqrt(H/(4d)), w=sqrt(T/kappa),
g=(1+exp(-VH))^(-1), eta=2V/(gH).
For logistic loss log(1+exp(-v*h(kq))) and h(s)=a+b*tanh(kappa*s),
simultaneous Euclidean GD has the exact two-cycle

    (V,w,-w) -> (-V,w/2,-w/2) -> (V,w,-w).

Both states have margin -VH and loss log(1+exp(VH))>log 2.
Since 0<a<b this is a legitimate separable two-token link. Repeating the same signed link permits any number of examples and either raw label, but this theorem makes no claim about distinct links.

Indeed, h(-w^2)=-H, h(-w^2/4)=H, and h'(-w^2/4)=2d.
The head increments are -2V and 2V. Writing delta=eta*v*g*h',
the factor multipliers are delta_0=1/2 and delta_1=-1; on k=-q the
k multipliers are 1-delta, namely 1/2 and 2. All cycle identities follow.

## Full spectrum

Set tau=(1-g)VH, R=2T(tanh T+tanh(T/4)),
D0=1/2+2T*tanh T, D1=2-T*tanh(T/4).
On balanced coordinates (v,k), the two Jacobians are

    Jj = [[1-2tau, B], [B/2, Dj-R*tau]],
    B=-w(1+tau)/V,  B^2/2=2R(1+tau)^2.

The full two-step Jacobian has spectrum {0, eigenvalues(J1*J0)}.
The zero multiplier is the normal coordinate k+q. The larger balanced
multiplier is >25/12 throughout the family, so these cycles are never attracting.
Here and below a multiplier is an eigenvalue of the two-step derivative,
not a one-step derivative between the two different points.

Let S=D0+D1, P=D0*D1 and define

    Q(tau) = q0 + q1*tau + q2*tau^2,
    q0 = 2R(2R-S-2),
    q1 = 20R^2-8R-4P+4,
    q2 = 4(P-1)+10RS+24R^2-4R.

There is a unique positive root tau_c of Q. The other balanced multiplier
lambda_minus is positive and is <1, =1, or >1 exactly when tau is <tau_c,
=tau_c, or >tau_c, respectively. Thus the full linear spectrum consists of
one contracting zero multiplier, an always expanding positive multiplier,
and a positive multiplier with this exact threshold. At equality no nonlinear
classification along the unit eigendirection is asserted. Both strict regimes
are realized as b/sqrt(kappa) varies. The cycle always has an unstable direction.

## Root and elementary bounds

The function cosh T/cosh(T/4) has positive logarithmic derivative
tanh T-(1/4)tanh(T/4) for T>0. At T=1/2 its value is <sqrt 2:
cosh(1/2)<=8/7, since (2n)!>=2^n bounds the cosh series geometrically.
At T=1 its value is >sqrt 2, because cosh 1>37/24 and
cosh(1/4)<=32/31, and (1147/768)^2>2.
The intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity prove uniqueness.

For the cosh series at 1, the terms beginning at 1/24 have consecutive
ratios at most 1/30. Consequently

    cosh 1 <= 3/2 + (1/24)/(1-1/30) = 179/116 < 31/20 < 8/5.

Also 7/3<e<3 (the lower bound follows from 1+1+1/2; the upper follows
from 1/n!<=1/2^(n-1) for n>=2, strictly for n>=3). Hence
tanh(1/2)>2/5 and tanh 1<4/5.

Write A=tanh T, B0=tanh(T/4). The root equation gives

    A^2=(1+B0^2)/2,
    R = 2T*sech(T)^2/(A-B0) = 2T(A+B0).

Since A-B0 is the integral of sech(u)^2 from T/4 to T,

    (8/3)*sech(T)^2 < R < 8/3.

In particular R>3200/2883>11/10, and also R>25/24. Further,

    9/10 < D0 < 21/10,    1 < D1 < 2.

For y=VH>0, tau=y/(1+exp y) satisfies 0<tau<1/3: the Taylor lower bound
exp y>1+y+y^2/2 implies 1+exp y>3y since (y-2)^2/2>=0.
Thus alpha=1-2tau>1/3. Both diagonal terms of the balanced Jacobians
are positive, since

    D0-R*tau > 9/10-8/9 = 1/90,
    D1-R*tau > 2-T*tanh(T/4)-8/9 > 1/9.

Put C=B^2/2=2R(1+tau)^2>25/12. The monodromy trace is

    tr(J1 J0)=alpha^2+2C+(D0-R*tau)(D1-R*tau)>25/6.

Its two off-diagonal entries are B*(alpha+D0-R*tau) and
(B/2)*(alpha+D1-R*tau), both negative. Its eigenvalues are distinct and
real, since their discriminant is the squared diagonal difference plus
four times a strictly positive off-diagonal product. The larger eigenvalue
is therefore greater than half the trace, hence >25/12.

Moreover

    det Jj = (1-2tau)*Dj - R*(2+5tau) < Dj-2R < 0.

For j=0 use Dj<21/10<2R, and for j=1 use Dj<2<2R. Thus
det(J1 J0)>0 and, its trace being positive, both balanced multipliers are
positive. Direct expansion gives

    det(J1 J0-I) = Q(tau).

Since lambda_plus>1, the sign of Q is exactly the sign of lambda_minus-1.
Finally q0<0: using R=2T(A+B0),

    2R-S-2 = 2T*A+5T*B0-9/2
             < 8/5+5/4-9/2 < 0.

Also q1>13/5, since P<21/5 and the function 20R^2-8R is increasing for
R>11/10, with value 77/5 at 11/10. The coefficient q2>0 follows from
P>0, S>0 and 24R^2-4R>4. These signs give the unique positive root and
all the asserted eigenvalue comparisons.

## Both strict regimes occur

For completeness we verify tau_c<1/4 without floating point. The same
geometric tail bound gives, at x=9/10,

    cosh x <= 1+x^2/2 + (x^4/24)/(1-x^2/30).

The square of this rational upper bound is strictly less than
2*(1+(x/4)^2/2)^2. Thus T>9/10. The exponential Taylor bounds
exp(9/5)>17/3 and exp(9/20)>3/2 imply A>7/10 and B0>1/5, so
R>81/50>8/5. These finite rational comparisons are reproduced in
scripts/verify_opposite_cycle_exact.py.

At tau=1/4, expansion yields

    8Q(1/4)=84R^2-11RS-50R-6P+6.

Using S<41/10, P<21/5, R>8/5, and monotonicity of
84R^2-(951/10)R on R>=8/5, the right side exceeds

    84*(8/5)^2-(951/10)*(8/5)-6*(21/5)+6 = 1092/25 > 0.

Hence 0<tau_c<1/4. The quantity y=VH is a positive constant times
b/sqrt(kappa), so it ranges over all positive numbers. Since tau(y)->0
as y->0 or y->infinity, while tau(1)=1/(1+e)>1/4, both strict regimes
occur. This is a full linear stability classification for this family,
including the unit-multiplier threshold, not a proof about other cycles.

## Differentiation and ambient-coordinate check

At a balanced point (v,k,-k), let s=-k^2, h=h(s), d=h'(s), e2=h''(s),
g=(1+exp(vh))^(-1), delta=eta*v*g*d. The balanced Jacobian is

    J11 = 1-eta*g*(1-g)*h^2,
    J12 = -2*eta*k*g*d*(1-(1-g)*v*h),
    J21 = J12/2,
    J22 = 1-delta+2*k^2*eta*v*(g*e2-g*(1-g)*v*d^2).

Substitution gives the displayed J0,J1. In full coordinates U=k+q obeys
U_+=(1+delta)U. Along U=0 its derivative has no dependence on the
balanced perturbations, since the term U*d(delta) vanishes. Its two-step
multiplier is (1+1/2)*(1-1)=0. The derivative is block triangular with
balanced block J1 J0, so this accounts for its complete three-dimensional
spectrum even without assuming an imbalance invariant for GD.

The independent ambient numerical check differentiates the loss as
Lvv=g(1-g)h^2, Lvs=g(1-g)vhd-gd,
Lss=g(1-g)v^2d^2-gv*e2, Ls=-gvd, and uses

    Hessian L = [[Lvv, q Lvs, k Lvs],
                 [q Lvs, q^2 Lss, kq Lss+Ls],
                 [k Lvs, kq Lss+Ls, k^2 Lss]].

This numerical comparison is evidence only. The proof above uses exact
real identities and explicit rational inequalities, with every series tail
bounded geometrically or used as a nonnegative Taylor remainder.

## Scope and unresolved obstruction

The normal multiplier alone would falsely suggest attraction: the balanced
block always has an expanding eigenvalue. This family therefore supplies
no positive-volume attracting third fate. The remaining route is to classify
asymmetric opposite-head cycles (unequal head magnitudes), factor-sign-flip
cycles, longer periods, or nonperiodic bounded orbits. Nothing here proves
almost-everywhere convergence for factored GD or excludes those alternatives.
b,kappa>0; unique T in (1/2,1) solves cosh(T)^2=2cosh(T/4)^2; h(s)=a+b tanh(kappa s), a=b(tanh T+tanh(T/4))/2, H=b(tanh T-tanh(T/4))/2, d=b kappa sech(T)^2, V=sqrt(H/(4d)), w=sqrt(T/kappa), g=1/(1+exp(-VH)), eta=2V/(gH). Simultaneous Euclidean GD for log(1+exp(-v h(kq))); orbit (V,w,-w)<->(-V,w/2,-w/2). Repeated identical signed links are permitted; distinct-link and arbitrary opposite-cycle classification not asserted.

Let b,kappa>0. There is a unique T in (1/2,1) with

    cosh(T)^2 = 2 cosh(T/4)^2.

Put a=b(tanh T+tanh(T/4))/2, H=b(tanh T-tanh(T/4))/2,
d=b*kappa*sech(T)^2, V=sqrt(H/(4d)), w=sqrt(T/kappa),
g=(1+exp(-VH))^(-1), eta=2V/(gH).
For logistic loss log(1+exp(-v*h(kq))) and h(s)=a+b*tanh(kappa*s),
simultaneous Euclidean GD has the exact two-cycle

    (V,w,-w) -> (-V,w/2,-w/2) -> (V,w,-w).

Both states have margin -VH and loss log(1+exp(VH))>log 2.
Since 0<a<b this is a legitimate separable two-token link. Repeating the same signed link permits any number of examples and either raw label, but this theorem makes no claim about distinct links.

Indeed, h(-w^2)=-H, h(-w^2/4)=H, and h'(-w^2/4)=2d.
The head increments are -2V and 2V. Writing delta=eta*v*g*h',
the factor multipliers are delta_0=1/2 and delta_1=-1; on k=-q the
k multipliers are 1-delta, namely 1/2 and 2. All cycle identities follow.

## Full spectrum

Set tau=(1-g)VH, R=2T(tanh T+tanh(T/4)),
D0=1/2+2T*tanh T, D1=2-T*tanh(T/4).
On balanced coordinates (v,k), the two Jacobians are

    Jj = [[1-2tau, B], [B/2, Dj-R*tau]],
    B=-w(1+tau)/V,  B^2/2=2R(1+tau)^2.

The full two-step Jacobian has spectrum {0, eigenvalues(J1*J0)}.
The zero multiplier is the normal coordinate k+q. The larger balanced
multiplier is >25/12 throughout the family, so these cycles are never attracting.
Here and below a multiplier is an eigenvalue of the two-step derivative,
not a one-step derivative between the two different points.

Let S=D0+D1, P=D0*D1 and define

    Q(tau) = q0 + q1*tau + q2*tau^2,
    q0 = 2R(2R-S-2),
    q1 = 20R^2-8R-4P+4,
    q2 = 4(P-1)+10RS+24R^2-4R.

There is a unique positive root tau_c of Q. The other balanced multiplier
lambda_minus is positive and is <1, =1, or >1 exactly when tau is <tau_c,
=tau_c, or >tau_c, respectively. Thus the full linear spectrum consists of
one contracting zero multiplier, an always expanding positive multiplier,
and a positive multiplier with this exact threshold. At equality no nonlinear
classification along the unit eigendirection is asserted. Both strict regimes
are realized as b/sqrt(kappa) varies. The cycle always has an unstable direction.

## Root and elementary bounds

The function cosh T/cosh(T/4) has positive logarithmic derivative
tanh T-(1/4)tanh(T/4) for T>0. At T=1/2 its value is <sqrt 2:
cosh(1/2)<=8/7, since (2n)!>=2^n bounds the cosh series geometrically.
At T=1 its value is >sqrt 2, because cosh 1>37/24 and
cosh(1/4)<=32/31, and (1147/768)^2>2.
The intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity prove uniqueness.

For the cosh series at 1, the terms beginning at 1/24 have consecutive
ratios at most 1/30. Consequently

    cosh 1 <= 3/2 + (1/24)/(1-1/30) = 179/116 < 31/20 < 8/5.

Also 7/3<e<3 (the lower bound follows from 1+1+1/2; the upper follows
from 1/n!<=1/2^(n-1) for n>=2, strictly for n>=3). Hence
tanh(1/2)>2/5 and tanh 1<4/5.

Write A=tanh T, B0=tanh(T/4). The root equation gives

    A^2=(1+B0^2)/2,
    R = 2T*sech(T)^2/(A-B0) = 2T(A+B0).

Since A-B0 is the integral of sech(u)^2 from T/4 to T,

    (8/3)*sech(T)^2 < R < 8/3.

In particular R>3200/2883>11/10, and also R>25/24. Further,

    9/10 < D0 < 21/10,    1 < D1 < 2.

For y=VH>0, tau=y/(1+exp y) satisfies 0<tau<1/3: the Taylor lower bound
exp y>1+y+y^2/2 implies 1+exp y>3y since (y-2)^2/2>=0.
Thus alpha=1-2tau>1/3. Both diagonal terms of the balanced Jacobians
are positive, since

    D0-R*tau > 9/10-8/9 = 1/90,
    D1-R*tau > 2-T*tanh(T/4)-8/9 > 1/9.

Put C=B^2/2=2R(1+tau)^2>25/12. The monodromy trace is

    tr(J1 J0)=alpha^2+2C+(D0-R*tau)(D1-R*tau)>25/6.

Its two off-diagonal entries are B*(alpha+D0-R*tau) and
(B/2)*(alpha+D1-R*tau), both negative. Its eigenvalues are distinct and
real, since their discriminant is the squared diagonal difference plus
four times a strictly positive off-diagonal product. The larger eigenvalue
is therefore greater than half the trace, hence >25/12.

Moreover

    det Jj = (1-2tau)*Dj - R*(2+5tau) < Dj-2R < 0.

For j=0 use Dj<21/10<2R, and for j=1 use Dj<2<2R. Thus
det(J1 J0)>0 and, its trace being positive, both balanced multipliers are
positive. Direct expansion gives

    det(J1 J0-I) = Q(tau).

Since lambda_plus>1, the sign of Q is exactly the sign of lambda_minus-1.
Finally q0<0: using R=2T(A+B0),

    2R-S-2 = 2T*A+5T*B0-9/2
             < 8/5+5/4-9/2 < 0.

Also q1>13/5, since P<21/5 and the function 20R^2-8R is increasing for
R>11/10, with value 77/5 at 11/10. The coefficient q2>0 follows from
P>0, S>0 and 24R^2-4R>4. These signs give the unique positive root and
all the asserted eigenvalue comparisons.

## Both strict regimes occur

For completeness we verify tau_c<1/4 without floating point. The same
geometric tail bound gives, at x=9/10,

    cosh x <= 1+x^2/2 + (x^4/24)/(1-x^2/30).

The square of this rational upper bound is strictly less than
2*(1+(x/4)^2/2)^2. Thus T>9/10. The exponential Taylor bounds
exp(9/5)>17/3 and exp(9/20)>3/2 imply A>7/10 and B0>1/5, so
R>81/50>8/5. These finite rational comparisons are reproduced in
scripts/verify_opposite_cycle_exact.py.

At tau=1/4, expansion yields

    8Q(1/4)=84R^2-11RS-50R-6P+6.

Using S<41/10, P<21/5, R>8/5, and monotonicity of
84R^2-(951/10)R on R>=8/5, the right side exceeds

    84*(8/5)^2-(951/10)*(8/5)-6*(21/5)+6 = 1092/25 > 0.

Hence 0<tau_c<1/4. The quantity y=VH is a positive constant times
b/sqrt(kappa), so it ranges over all positive numbers. Since tau(y)->0
as y->0 or y->infinity, while tau(1)=1/(1+e)>1/4, both strict regimes
occur. This is a full linear stability classification for this family,
including the unit-multiplier threshold, not a proof about other cycles.

## Differentiation and ambient-coordinate check

At a balanced point (v,k,-k), let s=-k^2, h=h(s), d=h'(s), e2=h''(s),
g=(1+exp(vh))^(-1), delta=eta*v*g*d. The balanced Jacobian is

    J11 = 1-eta*g*(1-g)*h^2,
    J12 = -2*eta*k*g*d*(1-(1-g)*v*h),
    J21 = J12/2,
    J22 = 1-delta+2*k^2*eta*v*(g*e2-g*(1-g)*v*d^2).

Substitution gives the displayed J0,J1. In full coordinates U=k+q obeys
U_+=(1+delta)U. Along U=0 its derivative has no dependence on the
balanced perturbations, since the term U*d(delta) vanishes. Its two-step
multiplier is (1+1/2)*(1-1)=0. The derivative is block triangular with
balanced block J1 J0, so this accounts for its complete three-dimensional
spectrum even without assuming an imbalance invariant for GD.

The independent ambient numerical check differentiates the loss as
Lvv=g(1-g)h^2, Lvs=g(1-g)vhd-gd,
Lss=g(1-g)v^2d^2-gv*e2, Ls=-gvd, and uses

    Hessian L = [[Lvv, q Lvs, k Lvs],
                 [q Lvs, q^2 Lss, kq Lss+Ls],
                 [k Lvs, kq Lss+Ls, k^2 Lss]].

This numerical comparison is evidence only. The proof above uses exact
real identities and explicit rational inequalities, with every series tail
bounded geometrically or used as a nonnegative Taylor remainder.

## Scope and unresolved obstruction

The normal multiplier alone would falsely suggest attraction: the balanced
block always has an expanding eigenvalue. This family therefore supplies
no positive-volume attracting third fate. The remaining route is to classify
asymmetric opposite-head cycles (unequal head magnitudes), factor-sign-flip
cycles, longer periods, or nonperiodic bounded orbits. Nothing here proves
almost-everywhere convergence for factored GD or excludes those alternatives.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:e8427878f76b3f5d0b1a029354eb91f7c571a940d2076ac46475e69a4011f9e2","revision_digest":"sha256:e86713f93b04c61543fa9e37661cce7ca2aba40eec388324c29e7d3d34360175","source_id":"owner:T328:w698:claim-016:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20; independent review pending","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Theorem 86 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Let $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ be the equilibrium measure of a variational datum obeying Assumptions~\ref{Assumption_A} and \ref{Assumption_B}. Then the following properties hold for any $h \in [H]$.
 \begin{enumerate}
 \item[(i)] The density $\mu_h(x)$ is an $\frac{1}{2}$-H\"older continuous function of $x$ everywhere except, possibly, at $x \in \{\hat{a}_h',\hat{b}_h'\}$.
 \item[(ii)] For any $x\in\amsmathbb R\setminus \{\hat{a}_h',\hat{b}_h'\}$, the limits
 \[
 \Gm_{\mu_h}(x^{\pm}) = \lim_{\epsilon \rightarrow 0^+} \Gm_{\mu_h}(x \pm {\ii}\epsilon)
 \]
 exist. Furthermore, we have $\textnormal{Im}(\Gm_{\mu_h}(x^{\pm}))=\mp \pi \mu_h(x)$.
 \item[(iii)] The function $q_h^+(z)$ from Definition~\ref{GQdef} is meromorphic for $z \in \amsmathbb M_h$. Its only possible singularities are simple poles at $\hat a'_h$ (respectively $\hat b'_h$), which can appear only if $\iota^-_h=0$ (respectively $\iota^+_h=0$).
 \item[(iv)] The function $ (q_h^-(z))^2$ is meromorphic in $\amsmathbb M_h$. Its only possible singularities in $\amsmathbb{M}_h$ are simple or double poles at $\hat a'_h$ (respectively $\hat b'_h$), which can appear only if $\iota^-_h=0$ (respectively $\iota^+_h=0$). Besides, the endpoints of a band of $\mu_h$ in $(\hat a'_h,\hat b'_h)$ is necessarily a zero of $(q_h^-(z))^2$.
 \item[(v)] The function $s_h(z)$ from Definition~\ref{GQdef2} is meromorphic for $z \in \amsmathbb M_h$. Its only possible singularities in $\amsmathbb{M}_h$ are simple poles at $\hat a'_h$ (respectively $\hat b'_h$), which can appear only if $\iota^-_h=0$ (respectively $\iota^+_h=0$).
 \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Any matrix $U\in M_N(\mathbb C)$ which is unitary, $U^*=U^{-1}$, is diagonalizable, with the eigenvalues on the unit circle $\mathbb T$. More precisely we have
$$U=VDV^*$$
with $V\in U_N$, and with $D\in M_N(\mathbb T)$ diagonal. The converse holds too.

[Lem non-uniform-Antal-Pisztora of arXiv:2606.01627, 'The geometry of the giant component of random geometric graphs'] For each $\lambda_0 > \lambda_c(d)$ there is $c(d,\lambda_0) > 0, \rho(d,\lambda_0) < \infty$
    such that the following holds.

    Let $\sigma$ be a metric on $\mathbb{R}^d$
    which satisfies
    \[
        \sigma(x,y) \le \|x - y\| \le 2\sigma(x,y)
    \]
    for all $x,y \in \mathbb{R}^d$.
    Let $\nu$ be a positive measure on
    $\mathbb{R}^d$ which satisfies 
    $\frac{d\nu}{d\mathcal{L}} \ge \lambda_0$.
    Let $G$ be the random geometric
    graph
    whose vertices are the
    points of a Poisson process on $\mathbb{R}^d$
    with intensity measure $\nu$
    and whose edge set consists
    of pairs of vertices with
    $\sigma$-distance at most 1.

    Then for any $x,y \in \mathbb{R}^d$
    and any $t \ge \rho\|x-y\|$ we have
    \[
        \mathbb{P}_{x,y}( x \stackrel{G}{\longleftrightarrow} y, d_G(x,y) \ge t)
        \le \exp(-ct).
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:balance of arXiv:2608.16915, 'Exact mean--covariance dynamics of the Weber field in the stochastic Lagrangian representa'] Testing (equation eq:Req of the paper) against $\mathcal R$ and integrating over $\mathbb{T}^3$, using
$\diver u=0$, gives
\begin{equation}
  \tfrac12\tfrac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d} t}\left\lVert \mathcal R\right\rVert_{L^2}^2
  +\nu\left\lVert \nabla\mathcal R\right\rVert_{L^2}^2
  +\int_{\mathbb{T}^3}\mathcal R^\top S\,\mathcal R
  =2\nu\int_{\mathbb{T}^3}\mathcal R\cdot\sum_k(\partial_kM)^\top(\partial_kN).
\end{equation}
The antisymmetric part of $G$ makes no contribution, since
$r^\top(G-G^\top)r=0$ for every vector $r$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition of arXiv:2609.00233, 'A survey on mapping class groups of 3-manifolds'] We define \emph{flips of $S^1 \times S^2$ factors}. Remove $S_j \times I$ from $M$, fill in the boundary component $F_{n+2j-1}$ with a 3-ball $E_1$, and $F_{n+2j}$ with another 3-ball $E_2$.  Consider an ambient isotopy of $S^3$ that switches the positions of $E_1$ and $E_2$. This results in a diffeomorphism of $\varphi\colon B \to B$ that fixes all boundary components apart from $F_{n+2j-1}$ and $F_{n+2j}$, which are switched. Extend by the identity everywhere apart from on $S_j \times I$. We may assume that $\varphi$ determines the map $(x,t) \mapsto (-x,1-t)$ on $S_j \times \{0,1\}$. This is because the two 2-spheres are switched, and because they are glued to $B$ with maps of degree $(-1)^t$, in order to have an oriented manifold. We can therefore extend using the formula $(x,t) \mapsto (-x,1-t)$ on all of $S_j \times I$.
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2609.00233, 'A survey on mapping class groups of 3-manifolds'

body:
[Lem 73 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\epsilon \in (0,1)$ and any function $p \in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ with $p(q_0)=0$ (i.e., satisfying condition~\ref{it:3.5withzero}), there exists sufficiently large $L$
 (depending on $p,\epsilon$) and $\tilde p \in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ satisfying $1/L \le \tilde{p}(q_0) \le \epsilon$ and $\|\tilde{p}\|_{C^2([q_0,1])} \le L$ (i.e., satisfying condition~\ref{it:3.1}) 
 such that $\|p' - \tilde p'\|_1 \le \epsilon$. 
If $p$ is furthermore concave (i.e., satisfying condition~\ref{it:3.3}), then the same conclusion holds with $\tilde p$ also concave (i.e., satisfying condition~\ref{it:3.1concave}). 
\begin{proof}
Since $p\in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ is absolutely continuous, we have $p' \in L^1([q_0,1];[0,+\infty))$. Since $p(q_0) = 0$ and $p(1) = 1$, we have $\|p'\|_1 = 1$. 

Throughout this proof, we use the term ``step function'' to refer to a function on $[q_0,1]$ that is piecewise constant with finitely many discontinuities. Since step functions are dense in $L^1([q_0,1];[0,+\infty))$, there exists a step function $g_1 : [q_0,1] \to [0,+\infty)$ such that
	\[\|p' - g_1\|_1 \le \epsilon / 6\,.\]
For sufficiently large $L$, there exists a smooth function $g_2 : [q_0,1] \to [0,L]$ with $\|g_2\|_{C^2([q_0,1])} \le L/10$, such that $\|g_1 - g_2\|_1 \le \epsilon / 6$, which implies
	\[\|p' - g_2\|_1 \le \epsilon / 3\,.\]
Since $\|p'\|_1 = 1$, we have $\|g_2\|_1 \le 1 + \epsilon/3$. 
We then define
	\[\tilde p(t) = 1 
		- \bigg(1-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\bigg)
		\int_t^1 g_2(s)\,ds\,,\]
and we note that $\tilde{p}$ is smooth and nondecreasing with
$\|\tilde{p}\|_{C^2([q_0,1])} \le L$. For $\epsilon < 1$, we can bound
	\[
    \|p' - \tilde p'\|_1
    = \bigg\|p' - \bigg(1-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\bigg) g_2\bigg\|_1
    \le \|p' - g_2\|_1 + \frac{\epsilon}{2} \|g_2\|_1
    \le \frac{\epsilon}{3} + \bigg(1+\frac{\epsilon}{3}\bigg) \frac{\epsilon}{2}
    \le \epsilon\,.
\]
Since $p(1) = \tilde p(1) = 1$, it follows that
\[
    \tilde p(q_0) \le p(q_0) + \|p' - \tilde p'\|_1
    =\|p' - \tilde p'\|_1
     \le \epsilon\,.
\]
For sufficiently large $L$, we also have
\[
    \tilde p(q_0) = 1 - \bigg(1-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\bigg) \|g_2\|_1 
    \ge 1 - \bigg(1-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\bigg)
    	\bigg(1+\frac{\epsilon}{3}\bigg)
	\ge \frac{\epsilon}{6} 
    \ge \frac{1}{L}\,.
\]
Thus $\tilde p$ satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.1}, as desired.
If $p$ is concave, then $p'$ is nonincreasing, and we can further arrange for the approximations $g_1$ and $g_2$ to be nonincreasing: in this case the resulting $\tilde{p}$ is concave, and so it satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.1concave}. This concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 73 of arXiv:2608.29416

body:
[Lemma lem:saturation of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] Let $L \supseteq \textbf{FIK}$ and let $(\Gamma, \Delta)$ be a maximal $L$-consistent theory.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
    \item $\varphi \in \Gamma$ if there is a finite $\Gamma_0 \subseteq \Gamma$ such that $L \vdash \bigwedge \Gamma_0 \to \varphi$.
    \item If $\varphi \lor \psi \in \Gamma$, then either $\varphi \in \Gamma$ or $\psi \in \Gamma$.
  \end{enumerate}
  \begin{proof}
    (1) Suppose towards a contradiction that there is such $\Gamma_0 \subseteq \Gamma$ but $\varphi \notin \Gamma$, then $\varphi \in \Delta$ by maximality, so $(\Gamma, \Delta)$ is $L$-inconsistent.
    (2) Suppose $\varphi \lor \psi \in \Gamma$, then $L \vdash (\varphi \lor \psi) \to (\varphi \lor \psi)$ implies either $\varphi \notin \Delta$ or $\psi \notin \Delta$ by $L$-consistency. By maximality, this means either $\varphi \in \Gamma$ or $\psi \in \Gamma$.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Saturation

An extra completion can only remove work earlier, and an extra never consumes primary capacity, so each primary workload is no larger than its baseline counterpart. Under iid uniform primary routing, the ordinary M/G/1 load condition lambda*E B_primary<1 supplies a baseline stability benchmark. Check: At primary arrivals add the same work in both coupled systems; between arrivals the proposed primary workload has at least the baseline service opportunity; cancellation subtracts nonnegative work. The comparison requires zero preemption/cancellation overhead and no hidden primary slowdown. Obstruction: This comparison does not prove maximality or quantify response gains, and is not claimed as a new policy. body:
[Theorem 3 (Cutoff-window profiles for colored top-\texorpdfstring{$m$}{m}-to-random and reversed-chain optimal strong stationary times) of arXiv:2604.09933, 'Explicit cutoff profiles for colored top-\texorpdfstring{$m$}{m}-to-random shuffles'] Fix \(c\in\R\) and integers \(p\ge1\) and \(m\ge1\), with \(m\) independent of \(n\). Let \(k=k_n(c)\). Then
\[
\sep\bigl((Q^{(m)})^{*k},U\bigr)=s_p(c)+o(1),
\]
\[
\left\|\frac{(Q^{(m)})^{*k}(\cdot)}{U(\cdot)}-1\right\|_{L^q(U)}^q
=
H_{q,p}(c)+o(1)
\qquad(1\le q<\infty),
\]
\[
D\bigl((Q^{(m)})^{*k}\|U\bigr)=h_p(c)+o(1),
\]
and, with convergence in the extended interval \([0,\infty]\),
\[
\left\|\frac{(Q^{(m)})^{*k}(\cdot)}{U(\cdot)}-1\right\|_{L^\infty(U)}
\longrightarrow H_{\infty,p}(c).
\]
In particular,
\[
\bigl\|(Q^{(m)})^{*k}-U\bigr\|_{\TV}
=
f_p(c)+o(1),
\qquad
\chi^2\bigl((Q^{(m)})^{*k},U\bigr)
=
g_p(c)+o(1).
\]
Hence the total-variation cutoff is at \(\frac{n}{m}\log n\) with window \(\frac{n}{m}\).

Furthermore, with the reversed-chain notation above, if \(p\ge2\), then \(\tau_{\mathrm{cov}}\) is an optimal strong stationary time and
\[
\Prob(\tau_{\mathrm{cov}}>j)
=
1-P_j^{(m)}(0)
=
\sep\bigl((Q^{(m)})^{*j},U\bigr)
\qquad(j\ge0).
\]
If \(p=1\), then \(\tau_{n-1}\) is an optimal strong stationary time and
\[
\Prob(\tau_{n-1}>j)
=
1-P_j^{(m)}(0)-P_j^{(m)}(1)
=
\sep\bigl((Q^{(m)})^{*j},U\bigr)
\qquad(j\ge0).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Cutoff-window profiles for colored top-\texorpdfstring{$m$}{m}-to-random and reversed-chain optimal strong stationary times

A random measure \[\eta\colon \Omega \to M_{\overline{\mathbb{N}}}(\mathbb{R}_+ \times Y)\] is of (QL) class if and only if
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] it is $\sigma$-finite i.e. there exists a sequence  $(U_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ of elements of the family  $\Gamma_\eta$ defined by 
 \begin{equation}
\Gamma_\eta := \{ A \in \mathscr{E} : \mathbb{E} \,\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{\eta([0,t] \times A)} < \infty \mbox{ for all } t \geq 0 \},
\end{equation}
such that   $U_n \nearrow E$,
\item[(ii)]
there exists a $\sigma$-finite random measure 
\[\widehat{\eta}: \Omega \times \bigl( \mathscr{B}(\mathbb{R}_+) \otimes \mathscr{Y}\bigr) \to \mathbb{R},
\]
such that $\tilde{\eta} = \eta - \widehat{\eta}$ is a martingale random measure,
\item[(iii)] for any $A \in \Gamma_\eta$  the process 
the process 
\[ \mathbb{R}_+ \times \Omega  \ni (t,\omega) \mapsto \widehat{\eta}(\omega;[0,t]\times A)
\]
is continuous.
\end{enumerate}

body:
[Corollary nonamentran of arXiv:2604.07227, 'Transition probabilities of step-reinforced random walks'] Suppose $G$ is a group generated by a finite symmetric set $\Gamma$ such that $G_{\Gamma}$ is nonamenable. \\
   (i) Let $S$ be an irreducible generalized SRRW on $G$ with parameter $\alpha \in [0,1)$ and step distribution $\mu$ whose support is $\Gamma$. Then, there exists a constant $\kappa=\kappa(G,\mu,\alpha) \in (0,1)$ such that 
    \begin{equation}
        
         \sup_{x\in G} \mathbb{P}(S_n=x) \leq \kappa^n, \quad \forall n\geq 1.
    \end{equation}
    In particular, $\liminf_n d(e_G,S_n)/n >0$ a.s. where $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ denotes the graph distance in $G_{\Gamma}$. \\
    (ii). Assume $G_{\Gamma}$ is the infinite d-regular tree $\mathbb{T}_d$ with $d\geq 3$. Let $S$ be an ERW on $G_{\Gamma}$ with memory parameter $p \in [0,1]$. Then for any $p \in [0,1)$ and $d\geq 3$, there exists a positive constant $\rho = \rho(G,p,d) \in (0,1)$ such that
    $$
\sup_{x\in G} \mathbb{P}(S_n=x) \leq \rho^n, \quad \forall n\geq 1.
    $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary nonamentran of arXiv:2604.07227

Then X is isotropic log-concave in dimension one, E|Cov(f(X),X|Y)|^2=E A^2, and (E||Cov(X|Y)||_op)(E Var(f(X)|Y))=(E A)^2. Bayes' posterior is N((Y-1)/s,1/s) truncated below -1. Its variance is bounded, continuous and nonconstant, so E A^2>(E A)^2. Consequently the unweighted expectation-factorization shortcut is false in this class. [Proposition 24 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] Let $\Omega_0=(\alpha_0,\beta_0)\Subset\R$, $\kappa>0$, and
$w_\kappa(x)=e^{\kappa(\beta_0-x)}-1$. Assume
\[
B_{\Omega_0,\kappa}
=d\int_{\Omega_0}J(\beta_0-y)w_\kappa(y)\,dy-q(\beta_0)\kappa>0
\]
and put
\[
\mathfrak C_{\Omega_0,\kappa}
:=\sup_{x\in\Omega_0}
\left[
-\frac{d\{\int_{\Omega_0}J(x-y)w_\kappa(y)\,dy-w_\kappa(x)\}
+q(x)w_\kappa'(x)}{w_\kappa(x)}
\right].
\]
Suppose $a(x)\ge a_*$ on $\Omega_0$. Set
$\Lambda_0=\max\{\|a\|_\infty,|\mathfrak C_{\Omega_0,\kappa}-a_*|\}$,
and let $\gamma_0$ be a Harnack growth exponent corresponding to
$d,J,q_0,q_1,\|a\|_\infty,\Lambda_0$. If there exist
$\beta_+,\beta_->\gamma_0$ such that
\[
\mathfrak C_{\Omega_0,\kappa}-a_*+
\limsup_{x\to+\infty}\{a(x)+d(M(\beta_+)-1)+q(x)\beta_+\}<0
\]
and
\[
\mathfrak C_{\Omega_0,\kappa}-a_*+
\limsup_{x\to-\infty}\{a(x)+d(M(\beta_-)-1)-q(x)\beta_-\}<0,
\]
then $\Lp(\cA_\R)$ is simple in the positive cone.

Let (Omega_1, mu) and (Omega_2, nu) be sigma-finite measure spaces such that L^2(mu) and L^2(nu) are separable. (a) If k is in L^2(nu ⊗ mu), then for nu-almost every y the function x -> k(y,x) f(x) is mu-integrable for each f in L^2(mu), and (T_k f)(y) = integral of k(y,x) f(x) dmu(x) defines a Hilbert-Schmidt operator T_k: L^2(mu) -> L^2(nu) with ||T_k||_2 = ||k||_{L^2(nu ⊗ mu)}; in particular T_k is bounded and compact, with ||T_k|| <= ||k||_{L^2}. (b) Conversely, every Hilbert-Schmidt operator T: L^2(mu) -> L^2(nu) is of the form T_k for a kernel k in L^2(nu ⊗ mu) that is unique up to a null set. Thus k -> T_k is an isometric isomorphism of L^2(nu ⊗ mu) onto the Hilbert-Schmidt class S_2(L^2(mu), L^2(nu)). (c) The adjoint of T_k is the integral operator with kernel (x,y) -> conjugate of k(y,x). Note that an L^2 kernel is defined only almost everywhere, so its values on the diagonal (a null set when the diagonal is null) carry no information.

[Theo 3 of arXiv:2512.02766, 'Fine-Graining and Continuous Space Scaling Limit of the $H^{2|2}$ Model on the Hierarchica'] Consider a finite weighted graph $\mathcal{G}$ and let $\mathcal{G}'$ be its reduced graph obtained via a subset $U\subset V$ that is indistinguishable from outside. Consider the $H^{2|2}$-model (with boundary condition $\eta'$) on the reduced graph $\mathcal{G}'$ given by its random $\beta'$-field $(\beta'_k)_{k\in V'}$. Conditionally on $(\beta'_{k})_{k\in V'}$, one can sample the random vector $(\beta_k)_{k\in V}$ by introducing additional randomness and reconstruct the $H^{2|2}$-model (with boundary condition $\eta$ s.t. $\eta_{i}=\eta'_{i}$ for $i\notin U$ and $\eta_{i}= \frac{1}{|U|} \eta'_{u}$ for $i\in U$) on the original graph $\mathcal{G}$ explicitly.

Especially, the random vector $(\beta_i)_{i\in U}$ has an explicit conditional density as a function of $\{\beta'_k\}_{k\in V}$.

body: [Example 1 (summarizing Theorems 4.3 and 4.4 of Li and Li, 2024) of arXiv:2511.18562, 'Ensuring Calibration Robustness in Split Conformal Prediction Under Adversarial Attacks'] For sufficiently large $d$, consider training a two-layer neural network of the form $\displaystyle F(X)$ $\displaystyle=\big(F_{1}(X),F_{2}(X),\ldots,F_{k}(X)\big),$ $\displaystyle F_{i}(X):$ $\displaystyle=\sum_{r\in[m]}\sum_{p\in[P]}\widetilde{\mathrm{ReLU}}\!\big(\langle w_{i,r},x_{p}\rangle\big),$ where $X=(x_{p})_{p\in[P]}\in(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{P}$, $w_{i,r}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ are trainable weights, and $m=\mathrm{polylog}(d)$ denotes the network width. Suppose the model is initialized randomly and trained for $T=\Theta(\mathrm{poly}(d)/\eta)$ iterations on a sampled training dataset $\mathcal{Z}$ using a learning rate $\eta$. Under these conditions, the following properties hold with high probability: 1. Standard Training: The model at T iteration $F^{(T)}$ converges to a non-robust global minimum. Let $F_{i}^{T}$ be the $F_{i}(X)$ at T-th iteration. In particular, there exists a perturbation $\Delta(X,y)$ independent of $F^{(T)}$ such that the robust test accuracy is poor: $\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{(X,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}$ $\displaystyle\Big[\arg\max_{i\in[k]}F^{(T)}_{i}(X+\Delta(X,y))\neq y\Big]$ $\displaystyle=1-o(1).$ 2. Adversarial Training: The model $F^{(T)}$ converges to a robust global minimum. Consequently, for perturbations $\|\Delta\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon$, the robust test accuracy is high: $\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{(X,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}\Big[\exists\Delta\in(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{P},\ \|\Delta\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon\ \text{s.t.}\$ $\displaystyle\arg\max_{i\in[k]}F^{(T)}_{i}(X+\Delta)\neq y\Big]$ $\displaystyle=o(1).$

body: An integral domain R (not a field) is a Dedekind domain if it is Noetherian, integrally closed in its field of fractions, and every nonzero prime ideal is maximal (Krull dimension 1). Equivalent characterisations: every nonzero proper ideal factors uniquely as a product of prime ideals; every nonzero ideal is invertible (the fractional ideals form a group under multiplication); the localisation at every nonzero prime is a discrete valuation ring and R is Noetherian; R is Noetherian, integrally closed, of dimension 1. Examples: every principal ideal domain (Z, k[x]); the ring of integers O_K of any algebraic number field K; the integral closure of a Dedekind domain in a finite separable extension of its fraction field (which is how O_K is proved Dedekind); the coordinate ring of a smooth affine curve over a field. Non-examples: Z[sqrt(-3)] (not integrally closed; its normalisation Z[(1 + sqrt(-3))/2] is Dedekind), k[x, y] (dimension 2). Facts: a Dedekind domain is a unique factorisation domain if and only if it is a principal ideal domain, if and only if its ideal class group (fractional ideals modulo principal ones) is trivial; for O_K the class group is finite (Minkowski) and its order is the class number; every ideal in a Dedekind domain is generated by at most two elements, and every fractional ideal is projective of rank 1; a nonzero prime p of Z factors in O_K as p O_K = P_1^{e_1} ... P_g^{e_g} with sum e_i f_i = [K : Q], f_i the residue degrees, and p ramifies (some e_i > 1) exactly when p divides the discriminant of K. Dedekind domains are exactly the one-dimensional regular Noetherian domains, so 'Dedekind' is 'smooth curve' in arithmetic.

[Theorem FCLT of arXiv:2607.02742, 'Gaussian fluctuations for the parabolic Anderson model with L\'evy white noise'] Under the hypotheses of Theorem~(QCLT of the paper), for every $R>0$, the process
$\{F_R(t)\}_{t\geq0}$ has a c\`adl\`ag modification (denoted also $F_R$).
Moreover, for any $T>0$,
\[
\frac{1}{\sqrt R}F_R(\cdot)
\xrightarrow{d}
\mathcal{G}(\cdot) \quad \mbox{in $(D[0,T],J_1)$ as $R \to \infty$},
\]
where $\{\mathcal{G}(t)\}_{t\geq 0}$ is a zero-mean (continuous) Gaussian process with covariance 
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{G}(t) \mathcal{G}(s)]=\Sigma_{t,s} \quad \mbox{(given by (equation limit-cov of the paper))},
\]
Moreover, the convergence also holds in $(D[0,T],U)$, where $U$ denotes the topology of uniform convergence. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Own-work diagnostic, T387-C004 v1; status sketch, not independently checked, and no novelty claimed. Let x in {-1,1}^d have mixture law (1-rho)Uniform+rho ProductMean(mu), y=product over a support S of size 2<=k<d, and z=(x,1). In a two-layer model f=m^(-1)sum_r a_r ReLU(w_r dot x+b_r), suppose every gate and every hinge loss are active before the next independent online example. Put u_r=(w_r,b_r), h=eta/m, v=E[yz], M=E[zz^T], C=M-vv^T. Both layers and biases update simultaneously. Then Cov(Delta a_r,Delta a_s|past)=h^2 u_r^T C u_s and Cov(Delta u_r,Delta u_s|past)=h^2 a_r a_s C. Here v_i=rho mu^(k-1) for i in S, rho mu^(k+1) for i outside S, v_bias=rho mu^k; M has unit diagonal, input off-diagonals rho mu^2 and input-bias entries rho mu. At w_r=0,b_r=b for every neuron, the centered output increments are identical h b(y-rho mu^k), so averaging m coefficients gives no additional 1/m variance reduction beyond h=eta/m. For a relevant/irrelevant input pair its increment variance is h^2 a_r^2[2(1-rho mu^2)-g^2], g=rho mu^(k-1)(1-mu^2). These are conditional shared-sample covariance identities, not a lower bound or a theorem about general width scaling. Thirty-six small distribution cases passed exact rational checks; no formal or independent proof certificate exists.
Fresh online sample independent of past.
All ReLU gates and hinge losses active.
Exact gradients, both layers updated using the same example.
Statements about no extra width averaging concern identical-bias zero-input-weight initialization only.

For x1=(1,1/4), x2=(-1,1/4), both labels+1, train hidden and output weights of f_theta(x)=sum_j v_j ReLU(w_j.x), without biases, by continuous gradient flow of summed exponential or logistic losses. Suppose every neuron is A+ (w.x1>0,w.x2<0,v>0), B+ (w.x1<0,w.x2>0,v>0), or D (both inner products negative, v arbitrary), with at least one A+ and one B+. At every finite time the activation sets remain fixed. Both predictions diverge, each as log(t), and theta/||theta|| converges to a direction with global normalized margin min_i f_theta(x_i)/||theta||^2=sqrt(17)/16. More precisely let a=sqrt(17)/4, e_i=x_i/a, s_j=v_j(0)+w_j(0).e_i>0 for neurons in sector i, and S_i=sum_{j in sector i}s_j^2. The limit has v_j=s_j/(2 sqrt(S_i)) and w_j=v_j e_i in that sector; all D components vanish. This holds for every finite width m>=2 and any initialization scale. With iid coordinates N(0,sigma^2), sigma>0, the exact probability of this sufficient global family is G_m=2^(-m)-2*(1/4+p/2)^m+p^m, p=atan(1/4)/pi. It consists of choose(m+1,3) signed count-orbits modulo neuron permutations (1,4,10,20,35 at widths2..6). C neurons and initially negative-output live neurons are excluded; G_m is not the full global-basin probability and the full bad-KKT basin remains unresolved.

Summed exponential or logistic loss and continuous gradient flow
Only A+,B+,D neurons initially, with both A+ and B+ nonempty; all inequalities strict

[Lemma le:aux-W-l-1 of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] \mbox{}\\
  Let the graph $G$ be finite and $l\in\{0,\ldots,r\}$. 
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item 
    Given $(W^{(l)}_e)_{e\in E_l}$, the random vector $\beta^{(l)\neq}$ has the
  conditional distribution $\nu_{\Lambda_l}^{W^{(l)\neq}}$. 
  \item 
    Assuming $l\ge 1$, take an arbitrary edge $\bar e=e_{j,l-1}\in E_{l-1}$ with
      $e\in E$ and $1\le j\le 2^{l-1}$; see Figure (fig:splitting-an-edge of the paper).
      Call $v=v_{e,2^{-l}(2j-1)}\in \Lambda_l\setminus\Lambda_{l-1}\subseteq\Lambda_l\setminus\Lambda_0$
      its midpoint.
      It splits $\bar e$ into the two edges $e'=e_{2j-1,l}$ and $e''=e_{2j,l}$ in $E_l$. 
      Then, one has 
      \begin{align}
        
   W^{(l-1)}_{\bar e}=\frac{W_{e'}^{(l)}W_{e''}^{(l)}}{2\beta_v^{(l)\neq}}.
 \end{align}
\item 
  Assume $l\ge 2$, which implies that $\Lambda_{l-1}\setminus\Lambda_0\neq\emptyset$. 
  Take an arbitrary vertex
      $\bar v=v_{e,2^{-(l-1)}j}\in\Lambda_{l-1}\setminus\Lambda_0$ with $e\in E$ and
      $1\le j\le 2^{l-1}-1$. In particular, $\bar v$ belongs also to
      $\Lambda_l\setminus\Lambda_0$; see Figure (fig:splitting-an-edge of the paper).
      Call $e^1=e_{2j,l}\in E_l$ and $e^2=e_{2j+1,l}\in E_l$ the
      two edges adjacent to $\bar v$ in $G_l$. Call
      $v^1=v_{e,2^{-l}(2j-1)},v^2=v_{e,2^{-l}(2j+1)}\in\Lambda_l\setminus\Lambda_{l-1}\subseteq\Lambda_l\setminus\Lambda_0$
      the two neighboring vertices
      of $\bar v$ in $G_l$. Then, one has 
      \begin{align}
        
        2\beta_{\bar v}^{(l-1)\neq}=2\beta_{\bar v}^{(l)\neq}-\frac{(W_{e^1}^{(l)})^2}{\beta_{v^1}^{(l)\neq}}
      -\frac{(W_{e^2}^{(l)})^2}{\beta_{v^2}^{(l)\neq}}.
    \end{align}
  \item
     Assume $l\ge 1$ again. 
    Given $(W^{(l)}_e)_{e\in E_l}$, the random variables $\beta^{(l)\neq}_v$,
    $v=v_{e,2^{-l}(2j-1)}\in\Lambda_l\setminus\Lambda_{l-1}$, are conditionally independent with
    conditional law $(2\beta^{(l)\neq}_v)^{-1}\sim \operatorname{IG}((W_{e'}^{(l)}+W_{e''}^{(l)})^{-1},1)$, where
    we use the notation $e'=e_{2j-1,l}$ and $e''=e_{2j,l}$ from item (item1 of the paper).
  \item 
    If the family of weights $(W_e)_{e\in E}$ is independent or even i.i.d.,
    then so is the family of weights $(W^{(l)}_e)_{e\in E_l}$.
  \end{enumerate}

body:
[Proposition 23 (Weak reparametrisation and reduced uniqueness) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space, and let $\xi:[0,A]\to E$ and $\widetilde\xi:[0,B]\to E$ be continuous bounded-variation paths with $\xi\sim_{\mathrm{rep}}\widetilde\xi$, witnessed by continuous nondecreasing surjections $\sigma:[0,1]\to[0,A]$ and $\widetilde\sigma:[0,1]\to[0,B]$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item If $0\leq u\leq w\leq1$, $s=\sigma(u)$, $t=\sigma(w)$, $\widetilde s=\widetilde\sigma(u)$, and $\widetilde t=\widetilde\sigma(w)$, then
\[
\xi|_{[s,t]}\sim_{\mathrm{rep}}
\widetilde\xi|_{[\widetilde s,\widetilde t]}.
\]
The two subpaths have equal signatures and are constant simultaneously.
\item The equivalent reducedness conditions in \cref{prop:reducedness} are invariant under $\sim_{\mathrm{rep}}$.
\item If neither path has a nontrivial constant subinterval, then there is an increasing homeomorphism $h:[0,A]\to[0,B]$ such that
\[
\xi=\widetilde\xi\circ h.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, two tree-reduced bounded-variation paths with the same initial point and the same signature are weakly reparametrisation-equivalent.

body: Lemma (campaign status: proved): With equations $\sum_i\eta_i=0$ and $\sum_i b_i\eta_i+\sum_j\xi_j=u$: if some $\Delta=b_i-b_j\notin\{0,\pm1,\pm2,\pm3\}$, conditioning on the other ten balanced signs gives at most $252\cdot3+420\cdot3=2016<2592$.
