body:
Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT stacking pool (23 members, 285 outputs, the per-sample relative metric; PLACEHOLDER_CELLS). The error covariance of the members is rank-deficient in practice: $\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}$ of $10^{6}$ to $10^{17}$, three to five eigenvalues below $0.05\,\sigma^2$ (members that are near-linear combinations of one another). Inside the long-only minimum-variance stack, eight cleaners of that covariance were compared on the same cells, the same split and the same small-calibration draws: the raw sample covariance, the $\eta$-regularised rotationally invariant estimator with floors $0, 0.05, 0.2, 1.0\,\sigma^2$, Ledoit-Wolf 2004 linear shrinkage, Ledoit-Wolf 2020 analytical nonlinear shrinkage and Lam's NERCOME. Result: raw, RIE without floor, LW2020 and NERCOME tie - PLACEHOLDER_TIE - at full calibration ($n = 932$) and in the $n = 60/120/240$ arms; the floor $0.05\,\sigma^2$ is marginally negative, floors $0.2$ and $1.0$ lose PLACEHOLDER_FLOORS, linear shrinkage loses PLACEHOLDER_LW2004, and the sum-to-one (unconstrained-sign) forms of the same cleaners lose PLACEHOLDER_S1. Mechanism (seed 101, medians over outputs): the constraint keeps 7-11 of 23 members; the condition number falls from $10^{6}$-$10^{17}$ on the full covariance to $4\times10^{2}$-$3\times10^{4}$ on the active principal submatrix; eigenvalues under the floor fall from 3-5 to 0-1; the active sets of raw, RIE and LW2020 overlap at Jaccard 0.86-0.90 (0.80-0.83 at $n = 60$). By the active-set lemma the weights depend on the covariance only through $S_{AA}$, which is well conditioned, and there every consistent cleaner is close to the identity; a floor or a linear shrinkage lifts the small eigenvalues of the full matrix before the constraint acts and distorts $w_A$. The reading of the whole program: random-matrix theory identifies what to clean (the error covariance, in the reported metric, with an intercept) and why the plug-in fails (the near-null directions of a collinear ensemble); the fix that survives the population is the long-only constraint, itself a data-determined covariance shrinkage, and the spectral cleaners are interchangeable inside it. The pre-registered contrary hypothesis - that the floor was a kernel-bandwidth artefact which LW2020's theory-fixed bandwidth would remove - was refuted on its first cell: consistent estimators correctly keep the tiny eigenvalues, because in the population they are tiny.
the pool protocol: members fitted on training data, the test rows split 40/60 into calibration and evaluation with a fixed permutation, metric = mean per-sample relative L2
the small-calibration arms subsample the calibration rows only; evaluation rows are never touched

[Theorem thm:main-p-spin of arXiv:2411.09075, 'Weak Poincar{\'e} Inequalities, Simulated Annealing, and Sampling from Spherical Spin Glas'] Let $H_N$ be a mixed $p$-spin Hamiltonian whose mixture function $\xi$ satisfies (equation eq:SL-condition of the paper), which we recall below: 
    \[
        \xi''(q) < \frac{1}{(1-q)^2} \text{ for all } q \in [0,1). 
    \]
    Let $\mu$ be the associated Gibbs measure over the scaled sphere $\ScS_N$, with
    \[ \dif \mu(\sigma) \propto \exp(H_N(\sigma)) \dif\rho(\sigma). \]
    With probability $1-e^{-cN^{1/5}}$ over the randomness of $H_N$, the following holds.
    For some parameters $\delta_N = O(N^{-4/5})$, $T_N = \Omega(N^{1/5})$, the output measure $\nu$ of the the annealed Langevin diffusion scheme with these parameters satisfies
    \[ \dtv{\nu}{\mu} \le e^{-cN^{1/5}}. \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\begin{enumerate}[1)]
\item
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item
For any fixed $\lambda>0$ and $\alpha\in(-1/2,1/2)$, the processes
$U^{(4)}$ and $U^{(5)}$ are local
$(\alpha+\frac12,0,T)$-quasihelices for any $T>0$.

\item
Let $\alpha=1/2$. Then, for any fixed $\lambda>0$, the processes
$U^{(4)}$ and $U^{(5)}$ are local
$(1,1-\varepsilon,0,T)$-generalized quasihelices for any $T>0$ and any

Let $\alpha>1/2$. Then, for any fixed $\lambda>0$, the processes
$U^{(4)}$ and $U^{(5)}$ are local $(1,0,T)$-quasihelices for any $T>0$.
\end{enumerate}

\item
Let $0\le\gamma<1$, $-1/2<\alpha<1/2+\gamma/2$, and $\alpha\ne0$. Then, for any $0<T_1<T_2$, the process $V$ is a local $(1,T_1,T_2)$-quasihelix.
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2609.01540, '2609.01540'] Let \(g_j\) be smooth metrics on \(B_2\subset\mathbb R^n\) such that
\(g_j\to\delta\) in \(C^2(B_2)\), where \(\delta\) is the Euclidean
metric. Let \(f_j\in C^\infty(B_2)\) satisfy \(f_j(0)=0\), and let
\(\Gamma_j:=\operatorname{graph}f_j\) with upward unit normal \(N_j\).
Suppose that the \(\Gamma_j\) are locally area minimizing in
\((B_2\times\mathbb R,g_j+dt^2)\) and have locally uniformly bounded
area. Denote by \(dA_{\Gamma_j}\) the area measure induced on \(\Gamma_j\).
If \(N_0\in S^n\) satisfies \(N_0\cdot e_{n+1}>0\) and
\begin{equation}
    \int_{\Gamma_j\cap B_2^{n+1}}
    |N_j-N_0|^2\,dA_{\Gamma_j}
    \longrightarrow0,

\end{equation}
then \(N_j(0,0)\to N_0\).

Let $f$ be a proper convex function on $\mathbb{R}^d$, and let $D$ be the set of points where $f$ is differentiable. [Proposition Kraitchik 1942 of arXiv:2507.10294, 'Guessing Strategies for Shelf-Shuffling Machines'] Monge shuffles are deterministic. Let $n$ be even. If a deck of $n$ cards is Monge-shuffled $s$ times, the ending position $x_s$ and starting position $x_0$ of a card are given by 
\[2^{s+1}x_s=(2n+1)[2^{s-1}+(-1)^{s-1}(2^{s-2}+\ldots+2+1)]+2(-1)^{s-1}x_0+2^s+(-1)^{s-1}.\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let f be 2pi-periodic and let sigma_N(f) denote the Cesaro mean (1/(N+1)) sum_{n=0}^{N} S_n(f) of the partial sums of its Fourier series. (i) If f is continuous then sigma_N(f) converges to f UNIFORMLY. (ii) If f is in L^p for some p in [1, infinity) then sigma_N(f) converges to f in L^p norm. (iii) (Fejer-Lebesgue) If f is in L^1 then sigma_N(f)(x) converges to f(x) at every Lebesgue point of f, hence almost everywhere. This is the classical repair of the fact that the partial sums S_N themselves need NOT converge pointwise for a merely continuous f.
Periodicity;
the Cesaro means, not the partial sums.
Nonnegativity of the Fejer kernel is the property the Dirichlet kernel lacks and is exactly what makes all three conclusions work.

[Corollary 12 of arXiv:2605.30616, 'Brownian motion: the hyperbolic number setting'] Let $\left(X,\sigma\left(X\right),\mu\right)$ be a $\mathbb{H}$-valued
probability space with its $\mathbb{H}$-valued probability $\mu=\mu_{+}e_{+}+\mu_{-}e_{-}$,
where $\mu_{e}$ are bounded non-negative $\mathbb{R}$-valued measures
for all $e\in\left\{ \pm\right\} $, and let $L^{2}\left(X,\sigma\left(X\right),\mu\right)$
be the corresponding $\mathbb{R}$-Banach space equipped with its
$\mathbb{H}$-indefinite inner product $\left[,\right]$. Suppose
either 
\[
\mu_{+}\textrm{ is a classical probability, and }\mu_{-}=O,
\]
or 
\[
\mu_{+}=O,\;\textrm{and }\mu_{-}\textrm{ is a classical probability,}
\]
and hence, 
\[
\mu=\mu_{+}e_{+}+Oe_{-},\;\;\mathrm{respectively,\;\;}\mu=Oe_{+}+\mu_{-}e_{-}.
\]
Then
\[
L^{2}\left(X,\sigma\left(X\right),\mu\right)=L^{2}\left(X,\sigma\left(X\right),\mu_{+}\right)e_{+}\oplus L^{2}\left(X,\sigma\left(X\right),O\right)e_{-},
\]
respectively,
\[
L^{2}\left(X,\sigma\left(X\right),\mu\right)=L^{2}\left(X,\sigma\left(X\right),O\right)e_{+}\oplus L^{2}\left(X,\sigma\left(X\right),\mu_{-}\right)e_{-}.
\]
and hence, if $f=f_{+}e_{+}+f_{-}e_{-}$ and $g=g_{+}e_{+}+g_{-}e_{-}$
in $L^{2}\left(X,\sigma\left(X\right),\mu\right)$, then 
\[
\left[f,g\right]=\left\langle f_{+},g_{+}\right\rangle _{2}e_{+}+0e_{-}=\left(\int_{X}f_{+}g_{+}d\mu_{+}\right)e_{+}\in\mathbb{H},
\]
respectively,
\[
\left[f,g\right]=0e_{+}+\left\langle f_{-},g_{-}\right\rangle _{2}e_{-}=\left(\int_{X}f_{-}g_{-}d\mu_{-}\right)e_{-}\in\mathbb{H}.
\]

[Lemma 2 of arXiv:2608.26996, 'A note on shifting distributions via Poisson races'] Let $P,Q$ be two distributions over a finite set $\cX$
such that $D(Q||P) < \infty$.

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d.\ from $P$.
Let $T_1 < T_2 < \ldots$
be a rate-$1$ Poisson process on $(0,\infty)$ that is
independent of $X_1,X_2,\ldots$.
For each $i$, define
\[S_i = \frac{T_i}{R(X_i)}\]
where
\[R(x) := \frac{Q(x)}{P(x)}>0\]
(when $Q(X_i)=0$, define $S_i=\infty$).
Let
\[I = \mathsf{argmin} \ S_i.\]
Then,
\[X_I \sim Q.\]

[Lemma lem:annulus-transfer of arXiv:2608.28330, 'Realising atomless laws as distance distributions on metric measure spaces'] Let $\zeta$ and $\eta$ be finite Borel measures on $\mathbb R_+$ such that
		$\Theta=\zeta+\eta$ is an atomless probability measure and
		\[
		\operatorname{supp}\zeta\subseteq[0,R],\qquad
		0\in\operatorname{supp}\zeta,\qquad
		\operatorname{supp}\eta\subseteq[R,2R]
		\]
		for some $R>0$.  Then there are an integer $N\ge0$, compact metric
		probability spaces $(X_i,d_i,\mu_i)$, $i=1,\ldots,N$, positive
		numbers $p_1,\ldots,p_N,p_\ast$, and $1$-Lipschitz maps
		$\phi_i:X_i\to[R,2R]$ such that $\operatorname{diam} X_i<R$, $i=1,\ldots,N$ and $p_\ast+\sum_{i=1}^N p_i=1$.
		For independent $U_i,V_i\sim\mu_i$, let
		$\nu_i=\operatorname{Law}(d_i(U_i,V_i))$ and set $\tau=\sum_{i=1}^N p_i^2\nu_i$.
		Then $\tau\le\frac12\zeta$.  Moreover, the atomless measure
		$\zeta'=\zeta-\tau$ satisfies
		\[
		\operatorname{supp}\zeta'\subseteq[0,R],\qquad
		\zeta'(\mathbb R_+)=p_\ast^2,\qquad
		\zeta'\ge\frac12\zeta,\qquad
		0\in\operatorname{supp}\zeta'.
		\]
		Finally,
		\[
		\eta=\sum_{i=1}^N c_i\eta_i,\qquad

		\Big).
		\]

		$R$, then $\Theta$ has a compact realisation. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a family of sequences of complex Gaussian matrices, 
$$Z^i_N\in M_N(L^\infty(X))\quad,\quad i\in I$$
with pairwise independent entries, each following the complex normal law $G_t$, with $t>0$, the rescaled sequences of matrices
$$\frac{Z^i_N}{\sqrt{N}}\in M_N(L^\infty(X))\quad,\quad i\in I$$
become with $N\to\infty$ circular, each following the Voiculescu law $\Gamma_t$, and free.

body: [Theorem 3 of arXiv:2511.18562, 'Ensuring Calibration Robustness in Split Conformal Prediction Under Adversarial Attacks'] Assume that the predictive distribution $f$ assigns probability mass uniformly across all incorrect classes, while allocating the remaining probability to the true class. Let $P_{y,\text{true}}$ be the predictive probability for the true label. Split CP gives the prediction set by $C(x_{n+1})=\{y\in\{1,2,\dots,K\}:f_{y}(x_{n+1})\geq Q\}$ as mentioned in Section 3.1. The event stands for the number of classes contained in the prediction set given by the cardinality of $C(x_{n+1})$ given by: $\displaystyle|C(x_{test})|=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbbm{1}\left(f_{y}(x_{test})\geq 1-Q\right).$ The expectation of the prediction set size can be bounded by: $\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(|C(x_{test})|)\leq 1-\alpha\pm h(\epsilon_{cal},\epsilon_{test})$ $\displaystyle+(K-1)\left(1-\frac{1-Q}{1-P_{y,true}}\right)^{K-2}.$ As in the supporting evidence in Example 1, when adversarial training increases the prediction accuracy in the presence of $\ell_{\infty}$ test-time attacks, the following holds $\frac{1-Q^{\mathrm{adv}}}{\,1-P_{y,\mathrm{true}}^{\mathrm{adv}}\,}\;<\;\frac{1-Q^{\mathrm{clean}}}{\,1-P_{y,\mathrm{true}}^{\mathrm{clean}}\,},$ where $Q^{\mathrm{adv}}$ and $Q^{\mathrm{clean}}$ are the $(1-\alpha)$ -quantiles of the HPS score on the calibration set for adversarially trained and cleanly trained models, respectively, and $P_{y,\mathrm{true}}^{\mathrm{adv}}$ and $P_{y,\mathrm{true}}^{\mathrm{clean}}$ denote the corresponding true-label probabilities. Since the upper bound on the expected set size, $(K-1)\!\left(1-\frac{1-Q}{1-P_{y,\mathrm{true}}}\right)^{K-2}$, is increasing in $\frac{1-Q}{1-P_{y,\mathrm{true}}}$, the adversarially trained model yields a smaller expected prediction-set size than the cleanly trained model.

body:
[Theorem 22 (Toric Rees--Jacobi lattice and radial connection) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] Assume \eqref{eq:principal-isolated}.  For every fixed
\(\boldsymbol\lambda\) of support \(S\), the following assertions hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item The Jacobian algebra of \(G_{K\mid S}\) has dimension
\begin{equation}
 \dim_\C\mathcal J(G_{K\mid S})
 =\mu^{|S|}.
 
\end{equation}

\item The cohomology of
\((\Omega^\bullet_{\mathrm{pol}}[[\rho]],
\mathfrak D_{K\mid S})\) is concentrated in degree \(N_K\), and
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal L_{K\mid S}
 :=
 H^{N_K}\!\left(
  \Omega^\bullet_{\mathrm{pol}}[[\rho]],
  \mathfrak D_{K\mid S}
 \right)
 \simeq
 \mathcal J(G_{K\mid S})[[\rho]]
 
\end{equation}
is free of rank \(\mu^{|S|}\) over \(\C[[\rho]]\).  On every
standard-monomial parameter stratum the construction is algebraic in
\(\boldsymbol\lambda\) and these lattices form a locally free family.

\item On \(\rho\neq0\), the radial Gauss--Manin connection in the
Gaussian-normalised volume gauge is
\begin{equation}
 \nabla_{\rho,K}^{\mathrm{phys}}
 =
 \partial_\rho+
 \partial_\rho\!\left(\rho^{-2}\Psi_{K\mid S}\right)
 -\frac{N_K}{\rho}.
 
\end{equation}
It has pole order at most three and
\begin{equation}
 \rho^3\nabla_{\rho,K}^{\mathrm{phys}}
 \mathcal L_{K\mid S}
 \subset
 \mathcal L_{K\mid S}.
 
\end{equation}
Modulo \(\rho\), the induced endomorphism is
\begin{equation}
 \rho^3\nabla_{\rho,K}^{\mathrm{phys}}\bmod\rho
 =
 -2m_{G_{K\mid S}}
 \quad\text{on }\mathcal J(G_{K\mid S}),
 
\end{equation}
where \(m_G\) denotes multiplication by \(G\).

\item Suppose in addition that \(G_{K\mid S}\) is Morse.  The formal
cohomological radial connection, and likewise its dual period system, admit
a block decomposition indexed by the distinct critical values \(\gamma\) of
\(G_{K\mid S}\).  The block with leading action \(\gamma\) has rank
\[
 \#\{c\in\operatorname{Crit}(G_{K\mid S}):G_{K\mid S}(c)=\gamma\}.
\]
If \(G_{K\mid S}\) satisfies the central nonresonance condition
\eqref{eq:central-nonresonance}, then the zero-action block is a canonical
rank-one direct factor attached to \(c=0\).  Since
\[
 G_{K\mid S}(0)=H_{S,1}(0)=0,
\]
its normalised horizontal period has no negative exponential power.  We call
it the central Gaussian level.

If, more strongly, all critical values are pairwise distinct, every block is
rank one and the horizontal period solution indexed by a critical point
\(c\) has exponential factor
\begin{equation}
 \exp\!\left(
  \frac{G_{K\mid S}(c)}{\rho^2}
  +\frac{H_{S,1}(c)}{\rho}
  +O(1)
 \right).
 
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma lem:unif_par_comp_strat of arXiv:2607.04514, 'Boundary-layer asymptotics for Gaussian-smoothed singular measures'] Assume (ass:standing of the paper)~(ass:standing:chart of the paper). There are an open set \(\Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}}\subset\mathbb
  R^{m-c}\) and numbers \(R>0\), \(\delta_0>0\) such that
  \begin{equation*}
    \Theta_{\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}}\subset \Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}} \Subset\Theta_{\mathrm{out}},
    \qquad \Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}} + \mathbb B_{4R}^{m-c} \subset \Theta_{\rm out}
  \end{equation*}
  and the mapping
  \begin{equation*}
    M: \Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}} \times (\mathbb H_c^m\cap \mathbb B_{4R}^m)
    \to \mathcal{M},\qquad (\theta,\xi)\mapsto \Phi(\theta+\xi_{\mathcal S},\xi_{\mathcal C})
  \end{equation*}
  is well defined and of class \(C^{r+1}\). In addition, if we set
  \begin{equation*}
    \varphi(\theta)=\Phi(\theta,0), \qquad \mathbf{Q}(\theta)=\mathbf{Q}(\varphi(\theta)),
    \qquad \mathbf{L}(\theta)=\mathbf{L}(\varphi(\theta)),
  \end{equation*}
  and define \(\Delta: \Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}} \times (\mathbb H_c^m\cap \mathbb B_{4R}^m) \to
  \mathbb R^d = \mathbb R^{m-c}\times\mathbb R^c\times\mathbb R^k\) by
  \begin{equation}
    \Delta(\theta,\xi) = \mathbf{Q}(\theta)^\top\bigl(M(\theta,\xi)-\varphi(\theta) \bigr)
  \end{equation}
  then the following properties hold.

  \begin{enumerate}
    \item 
    The map
    \[
      \Delta:\Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}}\times
      (\mathbb H_c^m\cap\mathbb B_{4R}^m)\to\mathbb R^d
    \]
    is \(C^r\). Moreover, all mixed derivatives
    \[
      \partial_\theta^\beta\partial_\xi^\gamma M(\theta,\xi)
    \]
    with \(|\beta|+|\gamma|\leqslant r+1\), and all mixed derivatives
    \[
      \partial_\theta^\beta\partial_\xi^\gamma \Delta(\theta,\xi)
    \]
    with \(|\beta|+|\gamma|\leqslant r\), are uniformly bounded on
    \[
      \Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}}\times
      (\mathbb H_c^m\cap\mathbb B_{4R}^m).
    \]
    In addition, \(\Delta\) has the following anisotropic regularity: whenever
    \(|\gamma|\geqslant1\) and \(|\beta|+|\gamma|\leqslant r+1\), the derivative
    \[
      \partial_\theta^\beta\partial_\xi^\gamma\Delta(\theta,\xi)
    \]
    exists and is uniformly bounded on the same set.

    \item  At \(\xi=0\), one has
    \begin{equation*}
      M(\theta,0_m)=\varphi(\theta), \qquad \Delta(\theta,0_m) = 0_d,
      \qquad \mathrm{D}_\xi \Delta(\theta, 0)=[\,\mathbf{L}(\theta);\ \mathbf 0_{k\times m}\,].
    \end{equation*}

    \item  For each \(\theta\in\Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}}\), the map \( M(\theta,\cdot): \mathbb
    H_c^m\cap\mathbb B_{4R}^m \to\mathcal{M}\) is a \(C^{r+1}\) corner chart onto a relatively open
    neighborhood of \(\varphi(\theta)\) in \(\mathcal{M}\).

    \item  For \(\theta\in\Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}}\), define \(J(\theta,\xi) = \det
    \bigl(\mathrm{D}_\xi \Delta (\theta,\xi)^\top \mathrm{D}_\xi\Delta(\theta,\xi) \bigr)^{1/2}\). Then \(J\)
    is jointly \(C^{r}\) in \((\theta,\xi)\), all mixed derivatives
    \begin{equation*}
      \partial_\theta^\beta\partial_\xi^\gamma J(\theta,\xi), \qquad |\beta|+|\gamma|\leqslant r,
    \end{equation*}
    are uniformly bounded on \( \Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}} \times (\mathbb H_c^m\cap\mathbb
    B_{4R}^m)\), and \( J(\theta, 0)=|\det\mathbf{L}(\theta)|\).

    \item  For every \(x=\varphi(\theta)\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}\), \(\mathcal{M}\cap \mathbb
    B_{2\delta_0}(x)\subset M\bigl(\theta, \mathbb H_c^m\cap \mathbb B_{R}^m\bigr)\).
  \end{enumerate}

body:
[Proposition 9 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The language $G$ admits a well-defined decomposition into primitive languages:
\begin{align*}
  G = \Big[\Big(\C_1^{\geqslant 0} \circ \D_1^{\geqslant 1}\Big).\C_1
    \cup \C_1^{\geqslant0} \Big]
  \circ \cdots \circ
  \Big[
    \Big(\C_m^{\geqslant 0} \circ \D_m^{\geqslant 1}\Big).\C_m
    \cup \C_m^{\geqslant0} \Big].
\end{align*}
Its exponential generating function is hence
\[
  \hat\phi_G(z) = \left[ (1-p) \left( e^{z/m} - 1 \right) + 1 \right]^m.
\]
\begin{proof}
  It holds for all $i$ that
  \begin{align*}
    \hat\phi_{{\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant1}}}(z)
    
    &= e^{z/m} - e^{(1-p)z/m}\\
    &= \sum_{n=0}^\infty
        \frac{(z/m)^n - ((1-p)z/m)^n}{n!},\\
    \phi_{{\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant1}}}(z)
    &= \sum_{n=0}^\infty 
        (z/m)^n - ((1-p)z/m)^n.
  \end{align*}
  Then we multiply by $\phi_{\C_i}(z) = \left(1-p\right)z\,m^{-1}$,
  \begin{align*}
    \phi_{\left({\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant1}}\right).\C_i}(z)
    &= \frac{\left(1-p\right)z}{m} \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left[
      \left(\frac{z}{m}\right)^n - \left(\frac{\left(1-p\right)z}{m}\right)^n
      \right]\\
    &= (1-p)\sum_{n=1}^\infty
        (z/m)^{n}
      - \sum_{n=1}^\infty
      ((1-p)\,z/m)^{n},\\
    \hat\phi_{\left({\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant1}}\right).\C_i}(z)
    &= (1-p)\sum_{n=1}^\infty
        \frac{(z/m)^{n}}{n!}
      - \sum_{n=1}^\infty
        \frac{((1-p)z/m)^{n}}{n!}\\
    &= (1-p)\left(e^{z/m} - 1\right)
    - e^{(1-p)z/m} + 1.
  \end{align*}
  Finally add $\hat\phi_{\C_i^{\geqslant 0}}(z)
  = e^{(1-p)z/m}$ to achieve
  \begin{align*}
    \hat\phi_{
      {\left({\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant1}}\right).\C_i}
      \cup {\C_i}
    }(z)
    &= (1-p) \left( e^{z/m} - 1 \right) + 1,\\
    \hat\phi_G(z)
    &= \left[(1-p) \left( e^{z/m} - 1 \right) + 1\right]^m. \qedhere
  \end{align*}
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition of arXiv:2605.02226, 'Finitely Dependent Processes on Subshifts'] Let $ G$ be a finitely generated group with a finite generating set $S$. Then $ G$ is $ \delta$-\textbf{hyperbolic} with respect to $S$, if for any geodesic triangle in the Cayley graph of $G$, any side is contained in the union of the $ \delta$-neighborhoods of the other two sides. We say that $ G$ is \textbf{hyperbolic} if $G$ is $\delta$-hyperbolic with respect to a finite generating set $S$, for some $ \delta\geq 0$.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:ccbef96bfb7a85e6c317e46ffd3c62de6d3b2616fb7a25e8aa9f192a62260b43","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/cc/ccbef96bfb7a85e6c317e46ffd3c62de6d3b2616fb7a25e8aa9f192a62260b43.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:91acd56335975a932539f4073e0edfa8458a1eb6dee249a431112ed253e3e53b","bundle_entry_key":"antisymmetric-variance-trace","bundle_id":"population.probability-critical-moments-two-end-kernels-and-dependence-006","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"codex-probability-1000-20h-20260906/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.markov:known-antisymmetric-perturbation-reversibilization-trace-monotonicity","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# P0249: reversibilization trace inequality ? known-result consequence

Status: author-checked complete argument for a historical conjecture. A later primary theorem implies the result, so this entry is excluded from the current-open target and original-solution count. The direct matrix proof is not independently reviewed here.

Source question: Aldous?Fill, Conjecture 9.22, PDF pages 327?329, asks whether $\operatorname{tr}[Z^2(P^*-P)]\ge0$. Here $P$ is an irreducible finite-state transition matrix, $P^*$ its adjoint in $L^2(\pi)$, and $Z$ the centered fundamental matrix. The centered convention is $Z1=0$ and $Z=(I-P)^{-1}$ on $L^2_0(\pi)$. Adding the constant projection to $Z$ would not change the displayed product.

## Direct matrix proof

Restrict all operators to the finite-dimensional real Hilbert space $L^2_0(\pi)$. Put

$$A=I-P=H+K,\quad H=\frac{A+A^*}{2},\quad K=\frac{A-A^*}{2}.$$

The reversible Dirichlet form shows $H$ is positive definite: its only zero-energy functions on the full space are constants, because the underlying undirected chain is connected. Also $K^*=-K$ and $P^*-P=2K$.

Let $Q=H^{-1/2}KH^{-1/2}$, $B=-Q^2=Q^*Q\succeq0$, and define $F(t)=\operatorname{tr}(H+tK)^{-1}$ for real $t$. All these inverses exist since their symmetric part is positive definite. Using transpose invariance of trace and averaging the inverses with $t$ and $-t$ gives

$$F(t)=\operatorname{tr}\!\left[H^{-1}(I+t^2B)^{-1}\right].$$

Indeed $(I+tQ)^{-1}+(I-tQ)^{-1}=2(I-t^2Q^2)^{-1}$. Differentiate the last trace formula:

$$F'(t)=-2t\operatorname{tr}\!\left[H^{-1}B(I+t^2B)^{-2}\right]\le0\qquad(t\ge0).$$

The product inside the trace need not be symmetric. Its trace is nonnegative because $C=B(I+t^2B)^{-2}$ is positive semidefinite and $\operatorname{tr}(H^{-1}C)=\operatorname{tr}(C^{1/2}H^{-1}C^{1/2})\ge0$. This explicitly avoids an invalid commuting assumption.

Differentiating the original inverse instead gives $F'(1)=-\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}KA^{-1})=-\operatorname{tr}(A^{-2}K)$. Consequently

$$\operatorname{tr}[Z^2(P^*-P)]=-2F'(1)=4\operatorname{tr}\!\left[H^{-1}B(I+B)^{-2}\right]\ge0.$$

In fact equality holds if and only if $B=0$, equivalently $K=0$, equivalently the original chain is reversible. This follows from positive definiteness of $H^{-1}$ and the fact that the positive eigenvalues of $B$ remain positive under $b\mapsto b/(1+b)^2$.

## Independent route through established literature

Huang and Mao, *Variational formulas of asymptotic variance for general discrete-time Markov chains*, arXiv:2012.13895 (December 27, 2020), Theorem 4.3 on PDF page 14, proves that the asymptotic variance for a reversible kernel plus an antisymmetric perturbation is even in the perturbation parameter and decreases with its absolute value. Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.13895 . This is a stronger observable-by-observable statement than the required trace monotonicity.

For finite irreducible chains, first add one-half holding: $R=(I+P)/2$. Every convex mixture of $R$ and $R^*$ is irreducible and aperiodic, so the theorem's spectral-radius assumption on the mean-zero space is satisfied. Apply it to $R_t=(R+R^*)/2+t(R-R^*)/2$, for $-1\le t\le1$.

For an orthonormal basis $(e_j)$ of $L^2_0(\pi)$, the Poisson-equation formula reads

$$\sum_j\widetilde\sigma^2(R_t,e_j)=2\operatorname{tr}(I-R_t)^{-1}-(n-1).$$

Theorem 4.3 therefore gives the same trace monotonicity. Differentiate from the left at $t=1$; analyticity identifies this with the full derivative and yields the conjectured inequality for $R$. Since $Z_R=2Z_P$ and $R^*-R=(P^*-P)/2$, its trace expression is twice that for $P$. The conclusion follows even if $P$ is periodic. The original series definition of $Z$ in the periodic case is interpreted through the centered inverse or Abel limit.

The source does not explicitly name Aldous?Fill Conjecture 9.22 in the checked passage. The implication just proved is the reason for exclusion; no claim of a new resolution is made. body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, The conjectured dominating pair for DP-SGD with shuffled batches is not dominating (2026), gives a counterexample to Conjecture 3.2 of Chua, Ghazi, Kamath, Kumar, Manurangsi, Sinha and Zhang, How private are DP-SGD implementations? (ICML 2024, arXiv:2403.17673), which says that the Gaussian mixtures P_S = (1/T) sum_t N(2 e_t, sigma^2 I) and Q_S = (1/T) sum_t N(e_t, sigma^2 I) tightly dominate the adaptive batch linear query mechanism with shuffled batches for every adaptive query method. The conjecture fails for every number of steps T >= 2 and every batch size: a query method that answers like the conjectured worst case at every step but the last, and changes the last query when the earlier outputs suggest that the differing record sat in an early batch, has a larger hockey-stick divergence. At T = 2, sigma = 1, eps = 1/2 it reaches 0.22323 against 0.22127 for the pair, and an Arb interval certificate bounds the excess below by 1.04e-4; the same switch also beats the pair in KL divergence and in Renyi divergence of every order tested, from 1/4 to 5. Exact accounting for shuffled batches remains open. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/shuffled-ablq-dominating-pair (commit 7ac96a5055fb). Not refereed.
title: The conjectured dominating pair for DP-SGD with shuffled batches is not dominating, refuting Conjecture 3.2 of Chua et al. (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/shuffled-ablq-dominating-pair)

[Definition of arXiv:2609.01776, 'On the Cuspidal Cohomology of Iwahori Congruence Subgroups of $\mathrm{SL}(3, \mathbb{Z})$'] Let $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ be the standard basis of column vectors in $n$-space.  For any ring $R$, we will consider $\sigma_1, \sigma_2, h$ as matrices in $\mathrm{SL}(n, R)$ such that 
    \[\sigma_1 e_1 = e_2, \quad \sigma_1 e_2 = -e_1, \quad \sigma_1 e_i = e_i \quad \text{if } i \geq 3;\]
    \[\sigma_2 e_n = (-1)^{n + 1} e_1, \quad \sigma_2 e_i = e_{i+1} \quad \text{if } 1 \leq i < n;\]
    \[he_1 = e_2, \quad h e_2 = -e_1 - e_2, \quad he_i = e_i \quad \text{if } i \geq 3.\]
    In our setting, where $n = 3$ and $R = \mathbb{Z}$, we have the matrices
    \[\sigma_1 = 
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0 & -1 & 0 \\
        1 & 0 & 0 \\
        0 & 0 & 1
    \end{pmatrix}, 
    \quad \sigma_2 = 
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0 & 0 & 1 \\
        1 & 0 & 0 \\
        0 & 1 & 0
    \end{pmatrix}, 
    \quad h = 
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0 & -1 & 0 \\
        1 & -1 & 0 \\
        0 & 0 & 1
    \end{pmatrix}.
    \]

[Theorem Calderon's theorem of arXiv:2606.01683, 'Singular-value gap of nonreversible Markov processes'] [Calderón's interpolation theorem c.f. [Calderon1964]] 
    Let $(E_0, E_1)$ and $(F_0, F_1)$ be Banach couples. Consider a linear map
    $T: E_0 + E_1 \to F_0 + F_1$ such that
    \[
    \|T\|_{E_0 \to F_0} \leq M_0, \qquad \|T\|_{E_1 \to F_1} \leq M_1.
    \]
    Then for every $0 \leq \theta \leq 1$, $T:[E_0, E_1]_\theta \to [F_0, F_1]_\theta$ is bounded with
    \[
    \|T\|_{[E_0, E_1]_\theta \to [F_0, F_1]_\theta} \leq M_0^{1-\theta} M_1^\theta.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let L>=1 be an integer, A a real d_L by d_0 matrix of rank r, and let the prescribed intermediate dimensions d_1,...,d_(L-1) all be at least r. Among real compatible factors A=W_L ... W_1, the minimum of sum_(ell=1)^L ||W_ell||_F^2 equals L sum_(i=1)^r s_i(A)^(2/L). Empty sums are zero. If an intermediate dimension is smaller than r, no such factorization exists. In particular, for every compatible collection of real matrices, L sum_i s_i(W_L ... W_1)^(2/L)<=sum_ell ||W_ell||_F^2. For L>2 the exponent 2/L is below one: this is a Schatten quasi-norm power, not an application restricted to norm exponents >=1. Biases and nonlinear activations are absent from this matrix identity.

body: [Proposition 3.5 (The de Finetti Limit) of arXiv:2603.10190, 'Hoeffding-Type Concentration Bounds for Exchangeable Random Variables'] Under the assumptions of Lemma 3.1, there exists an $[0,1]$ -valued random variable $L$ such that $\bar{X}_{M}\longrightarrow L\qquad\text{almost surely}.$ Moreover, $\mathcal{L}(L)=\mu_{\#}\rho,$ where $\mu_{\#}\rho$ denotes the pushforward of $\rho$ under the map $q\longmapsto\mu(q)=\int_{[0,1]}xq(\mathrm{d}x).$ Consequently, $\operatorname{supp}\mathcal{L}(L)=\mathcal{M}_{\rho}.$

Let A be a positive self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space H, with form domain Q(A) = D(A^{1/2}) and form q_A(x, y) = ⟨A^{1/2}x, A^{1/2}y⟩. Let β be a Hermitian sesquilinear form with D(β) ⊃ Q(A) satisfying |β(x, x)| ≤ a q_A(x, x) + b‖x‖² for all x ∈ Q(A), with 0 ≤ a < 1 and b ≥ 0. Then there is a unique self-adjoint operator C, written C = A ∔ β (the form sum), with form domain Q(C) = Q(A) and ⟨Cx, y⟩ = q_A(x, y) + β(x, y) for x ∈ D(C), y ∈ Q(A). C is bounded below by −b, and any subspace that is a form core for A (dense in Q(A) in the form norm) is a form core for C. The same holds with A bounded below instead of positive, after shifting. Typical use: −Δ + V on ℝ³ with V = V_+ − V_- where V_- is only form-bounded (e.g. V ∈ L^{3/2}(ℝ³) + L^∞(ℝ³) is −Δ-form-bounded with bound 0 by the Sobolev inequality), defining a self-adjoint Hamiltonian although V need not be operator-bounded and D(C) need not contain or be contained in D(−Δ).
H is a complex Hilbert space
A is self-adjoint and bounded below (positive after a shift)
β is Hermitian, defined at least on Q(A)
form bound a < 1: |β(x,x)| ≤ a q_A(x,x) + b‖x‖² on Q(A)

body: [Definition 1 (Function-preserving transform) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] An invertible $T\in GL(d_{\mathrm{in}})$ is \emph{function-preserving} for the layer $Y=XW^\top$ if replacing $(W,X)\mapsto(WT^{-1},\,XT^\top)$ leaves the output unchanged: $(XT^\top)(WT^{-1})^\top=XW^\top$. The weight side $WT^{-1}$ is computed offline; the activation side $XT^\top$ must be produced at inference unless it can be \emph{absorbed} (\Cref{sec:live}).  More generally we call a map function-preserving when its action on one operand is undone exactly by a compensating offline change to the adjacent static weights or bias, by an invariance of the following operation, or by an inverse applied downstream; the linear input-axis case above is the one \Cref{sec:inversion} is stated for, and the other variants are named as such where they appear.

[Definition 28 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Given a configuration $\boldsymbol{\ell} \in \W_\N$ in a discrete ensemble of Section~\ref{Section_general_model}, the \emph{empirical measure} is the $H$-tuple of nonnegative atomic measures $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\N} = (\mu_{\N,h})_{h = 1}^{H}$ given by
\[
\forall h \in [H] \qquad \mu_{\N,h} = \frac{1}{\N} \sum_{i = 1}^{N_h} \delta_{\N^{-1}\ell_i^h}.
\]
This tuple $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\N}$ is equivalently specified by the measure $\mu_{\N} = \sum_{h = 1}^{H} \mu_{\N,h} = \frac{1}{\N} \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \delta_{\N^{-1}\ell_i}$. The empirical resolvent is the tuple $\boldsymbol{G}(z) = (G_h(z))_{h = 1}^{H}$ defined for any $h \in [H]$ and $z \in\amsmathbb{C} \setminus [\hat{a}_h,\hat{b}_h]$ by
\begin{equation}
 G_h(z) = \sum_{i = 1}^{N_h} \frac{1}{z - \frac{\ell_i^h}{\N}} = \N \int_{\hat{a}_h}^{\hat{b}_h} \frac{\dd \mu_{\N,h}(x)}{z - x} = \N \Gm_{\mu_{\N,h}}(z).
\end{equation}
It is a holomorphic function of $z$ in this domain, such that for any $h \in [H]$, we have $G_h(z) \sim \frac{N_h}{z}$ as $z \rightarrow \infty$.

We sometimes recenter the empirical measure by subtracting the equilibrium measure $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and introduce $\Delta \boldsymbol{G}(z) = \boldsymbol{G}(z) - \N \Gm_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}(z)$. In other words, for any $h \in [H]$ and $z \in \amsmathbb{C} \setminus \amsmathbb{A}_h^{\mathfrak{m}}]$ we have
\[
\Delta G_h(z) = G_h(z) - \N\Gm_{\mu_h}(z).
\]

[Mainthm Thm:A of arXiv:2609.01501, 'Singularities of star cluster algebras'] Let $ X := \phi^{-1} (\eta) 
	\subseteq \ensuremath{\mathbb{A}}_\kappa^{\ell_1+\cdots + \ell_m+m+2} $ 
	be as defined above. 
	The singularities of $ X $ have the following classification:
	\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
		\item 
		Either $ X $ has an isolated singularity locally at which $ X $ is isomorphic to a hypersurface singularity of type $ A_1 $, 
		
		\item 
		or $ Sing(X) \cong  \bigcup_{i=1}^s  C_i  $ has $ s $ disjoint components (where $ C_i $ is not necessarily irreducible)
		and for each $ i \in \{ 1, \ldots, s \} $,
		$ X $ is locally at $ C_{i} $ isomorphic to a cylinder over an intersection of compatible $ A_1 $-hypersurface singularities, 
		
		\item 
		or $ X $ is regular.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Lemma lem:alpha-Gp of arXiv:2609.03184, 'On uniquely colorable Cayley graphs'] Let $p \ge 5$ be a prime. The independence number of the graph $G_p$ is $4p$. An independent set attains this maximum size if and only if it is entirely contained within a single principal class. Furthermore, any independent set that mixes vertices from multiple classes has a strictly smaller size: it is bounded by $3p$ if it intersects exactly two classes, and by $3p+1$ if it intersects all three classes. Both bounds are sharp.

[Proposition prop:comparison of arXiv:2503.21737, 'High-intensity Voronoi percolation on manifolds'] Assume that all sectional curvatures of \(M\) lie in \([-K,K]\) for some \(K>0\) and that \(r_\text{inj}(M) > 0\).
    Then for all $\delta>0$, there exists an $r_0=r_0(\delta)$ such that for all $r\geq r_0$ there exists a $\lambda_0 = \lambda_0(r,\delta)$ such that for all $\lambda\geq \lambda_0$ and $x_0\in M$ we can find a coupling \((\xi, \eta)\) of Poisson point processes
    \begin{equation}
        \xi\sim \mathrm{PPP}(\lambda\cdot dx, \mathbb R^d) \quad \text{and} \quad \eta \sim \mathrm{PPP}(\lambda\cdot \mu_M, M),
    \end{equation}
    and a chart \(\varphi \in \pazocal{E} (x_0,r\lambda^{-1/d})\) so that the following holds with probability at least \(1-\delta\):
    \begin{enumerate}[(1)]
        \item  $ \pazocal G_{\mathbb R^d}(\xi)|_S = \varphi_*\pazocal G_{M}(\eta), \quad \text{where } S=B_{\mathbb R^d}\big(0, r\lambda^{-1/d}\big)$,
        \item  if a cell \(C(x;\xi)\), \(x\in\xi\), intersects \(S\), then \(\diam_{\mathbb R^d}(C(x;\xi)) \leq r\lambda^{-1/d}/100\),
        \item  if a cell \(C(x;\eta)\), \(x\in\eta\), intersects \(\varphi^{-1}(S) = B_M\big(x_0,r\lambda^{-1/d}\big)\), then \(\diam_{M}(C(x;\eta)) \leq r\lambda^{-1/d}/100\).
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Owner draft: independently checked proof (C012 v1). Let S be a nondegenerate d-simplex, d>=1, m=d+1. Unif(S) is n-CM exactly for every n>=d+1. For n>=m, vectors v_i in C^m with components m^(-1/2)exp(2*pi*i*k*i_index/n), k=0,...,m-1 and i_index=0,...,n-1, satisfy sum_i v_i v_i^*=(n/m)I. For one Haar unitary U, Haar-unitary squared moduli are Dirichlet(1,...,1). The barycentric vectors lambda_(i,j)=|(Uv_i)_j|^2 are therefore uniform on the simplex and obey sum_i lambda_(i,j)=n/m exactly. Mapping to the simplex vertices gives identical uniform marginals and sum n*centroid. For n<=d, a barycentric coordinate near one exceeds the required sum n/(d+1), proving impossibility. This handles nonmultiple orders missed by ordinary cyclic barycentric coupling. Novelty UNKNOWN.

[Lemma 162 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Consider a uniformly random tiling of $A\times B\times C$ hexagon. Using the notations \eqref{eq_N_hexagon} and \eqref{eq_L_hexagon}, the $N$ horizontal lozenges on the vertical section at distance $\mathfrak{t}$ from the left border with coordinates $1\leq \ell_1<\ell_2<\dots<\ell_N\leq L$ have probability distribution
\begin{equation}

 \amsmathbb P_N(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_N)=\frac{1}{\mathscr{Z}_N} \cdot \prod_{1 \leq i<j \leq N} (\ell_j-\ell_i)^2 \cdot \prod_{i=1}^N w(\ell_i),
\end{equation}
with the weight
\begin{equation}

w(\ell)=
 \left\{\begin{array}{lll}
  (\ell)_{C-\mathfrak{t}}\cdot (A+\mathfrak{t}+1-\ell)_{B-\mathfrak{t}}&& \textnormal{if}\,\,0 < \mathfrak{t}\leq \min(B,C),\\
  (\ell)_{C-\mathfrak{t}}\cdot (A+B+1-\ell)_{\mathfrak{t}-B} && \textnormal{if}\,\,B\leq \mathfrak{t}\leq C,\\
  (\ell)_{\mathfrak{t}-C}\cdot (A+C+1-\ell)_{B-\mathfrak{t}}&& \textnormal{if}\,\,C\leq \mathfrak{t}\leq B,\\
  (\ell)_{t-C}\cdot (A+B+C+1-\mathfrak{t}-\ell)_{\mathfrak{t}-B} && \textnormal{if}\,\, \max(B,C)\leq \mathfrak{t} < B+C,\end{array}\right.
\end{equation}
where $(a)_n$ is the Pochhammer symbol,
\[

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The mean and variance of the negative beta binomial law are
$$E=\frac{rb}{a-1}\quad,\quad V=\frac{rb(r+a-1)(a+b-1)}{(a-1)^2(a-2)}$$
and the corresponding skewness is given by the following formula,
$$\gamma=\frac{(2r+a-1)(2b+a-1)}{(a-3)\sqrt{\frac{rb(r+a-1)(a+b-1)}{a-2}}}$$
assuming $a>1,2,3$ respectively. As for $\kappa$, this is given by a more complicated formula.

body:
Let X and Y be normed spaces over R or C. A linear map T: X -> Y is compact if the image T(B_X) of the closed unit ball B_X = {x : ||x|| <= 1} is relatively compact in Y, i.e. its closure in Y is compact. Equivalent forms: (i) for every bounded sequence (x_n) in X the sequence (T x_n) has a subsequence that converges in Y; (ii) when Y is a Banach space, T(B_X) is totally bounded. Every compact operator is bounded, and every bounded operator of finite rank is compact. The set of compact operators X -> Y is written K(X,Y), and K(X) = K(X,X). The identity operator of X is compact if and only if X is finite-dimensional (Riesz's lemma). Terminology warning: older texts say 'completely continuous' for compact; in current usage 'completely continuous' means 'maps weakly convergent sequences to norm convergent sequences', which is implied by compactness but is weaker in general (it is equivalent to compactness when X is reflexive).

body: For coprime integers a and q there are infinitely many primes congruent to a mod q; the primes are equidistributed among the phi(q) admissible residue classes in the sense of Dirichlet density and, by the Siegel-Walfisz refinement, in natural density. The proof works with log L(s, chi) for all characters mod q, using orthogonality of characters to isolate the progression and nonvanishing of L(1, chi) to force divergence.

body:
[Lemma lem:PTASEP-kernel of arXiv:2608.02772, 'Non-Abelian Hirota-Miwa Equations for the KPZ Universality Class'] We have
\[
\mathbb{P}_y\Bigl(\bigcap_{i=1}^m
\{Y_{n_i}(t) > a_i\}\Bigr)
= \det(I - K_{t, \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{n}})_{\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})},
\]
where
\[
K_{t, \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{n}}(x, x')
= \sum_{1 \le j \le i \le m}
  \sum_{r \le a_i} \sum_{r' \le a_j}
   \psi_{t, r, n_i}(x)
  \bigl[\delta_{ij}\delta_{r,r'}
  + [B_{\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{n}}]_{ij}(r, r')\bigr]
  \phi_{t, r', n_j}(x').
\]
This identifies $K_{t, \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{n}}$ with the
kernel~(equation eq:K-def of the paper) on the product graph
$\mathcal{G}^m$, with $\psi, \phi$ as the seed data and
$B_{\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{n}}$ as the propagator.

body:
[Theorem 21 of arXiv:2608.19976, 'Random valuations'] Let $\nu$ be a measure on $\sC\times(0,\infty)$ which satisfies
  \eqref{eq:nu-levy} and such that
  $\nu(\{\emptyset\}\times(0,\infty))=0$. Then $\nu$ is invariant
  under translations on $\sC$ if and only if, for each 
  compact set $L\subset\R^d$ and Borel $A\subset(0,\infty)$, we have
  \begin{equation}
    
    \nu(\sC_L\times A)
    =\sum_{k=0}^{d} \int_A \int_{G(d,k)}
      \E(V_{d-k}(Y_{E,r}+\Pi_{E^\perp}L))G_{k,r}(dE) \mu(dr),
  \end{equation}
  where, for each $k=0,\dots,d$, $r\mapsto
  G_{k,r}$ is a measurable map from
  $(0,\infty)$ to the space of finite measures on
  $G(d,k)$ with the weak topology, and $\mu$ is a $\sigma$-finite measure on
  $(0,\infty)$. Furthermore, for each $E\in G(d,k)$ and $r>0$,
  $Y_{E,r}$ is a non-empty random compact convex set in $E^\perp$ such
  that
  \begin{equation}
    
    \int_{(0,\infty)}\min(1,r)
    \int_{G(d,k)}\E(V_{d-k}(Y_{E,r}+\Pi_{E^\perp}B)) G_{k,r}(dE)\mu(dr)<\infty
  \end{equation}
  for all $k=0,\dots,d$, where $B$ is the unit Euclidean ball in
  $\R^d$, and, for every compact set $L$ in $\R^d$, the map
  \begin{equation}
    
    (E,r)\mapsto \E(V_{d-k}(Y_{E,r}+\Pi_{E^\perp}L))
  \end{equation}
  is measurable.

[Definition 33 of arXiv:2606.14564, 'Upper tails for irregular graphs \\ beyond the mean-field regime'] Suppose that $J_0, J \in \cJ_\emptyset^*$ satisfy $J_0 \subsetneq J$.
  The \emph{span} of a set $E$ of edges of $J$ over $J_0$ is the graph
  \[
    \spn_{J_0}E \coloneqq \bigcap \bigl\{J' \in \cJ^* : J_0 \cup E \subseteq J'\bigr\}.
  \]
  The \emph{dimension} of $J$ over $J_0$ is
  \[
    \dim_{J_0}J \coloneqq \min\bigl\{|E| : E \subseteq J \wedge \spn_{J_0}E = J\bigr\}.
  \]
  A set $E$ of edges of $H$ is a \emph{basis} of $J$ over $J_0$ if $\spn_{J_0}E = J$ and $|E| = \dim_{J_0}J$.
  Finally, a vertex $v \in V(J_0)$ is a \emph{root} of $J$ over $J_0$ if $\deg_Jv > \deg_{J_0}v$;
  the set of all roots of $J$ over $J_0$ is denoted by $R_{J_0}(J)$.

[Lemma 12 of arXiv:2608.19832, 'Sharp Convex Concentration for Symmetric Random Tensors with Subgaussian Coordinates'] For \(\Phi_d(x)=x^{\otimes d}\), with the second term in
\eqref{eq:differential-exact} omitted when $d=1$,
\begin{align}
 D\Phi_d(x)h
 &=\sum_{j=1}^d
 x^{\otimes(j-1)}\ot h\ot x^{\otimes(d-j)},
 \\
 \norm{D\Phi_d(x)h}^2
 &=d\norm{x}^{2d-2}\norm{h}^2
 +d(d-1)\norm{x}^{2d-4}\ip{x}{h}^2.
 
\end{align}
In particular, if \(h\perp x\), then
\[
 \norm{D\Phi_d(x)h}=\sqrt d\norm{x}^{d-1}\norm h.
\]

body:
[Prop 21 (Domain Markov property) of arXiv:2510.23423, 'One-arm exponents of the high-dimensional Ising model'] Let $d\geq 2$ and $\beta\geq 0$. Let $G=(V,E),H=(V',E')$ be subgraphs of $\mathbb Z^d$ with $G\subset H$. Let $\xi\in \{0,1\}^{E'\setminus E}$. Then, for every event $\mathcal A\subset \{0,1\}^E$, one has
 \begin{equation}
 	\phi_{H,\beta}^0[\mathcal A \: |\: \omega_{|E'\setminus E}=\xi]=\phi_{G,\beta}^\xi[\mathcal A].
 \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Domain Markov property

body:
[Lemma MC of arXiv:2411.05204, '\Large\bf Sample Path Properties of the Fractional Wiener--Weierstrass Bridge'] Let $ Y $ be the Wiener--Weierstrass  process with $H<K$, then there exists $L>0$ such that
for all $s, t\in[0,1]\text{ satisfying }|s-t|\leq b^{-L}$,
\[ \frac{1}{L}|t-s|^{2H}\leq {\mathbb E}[|Y(t)-Y(s)|^2]\leq L|t-s|^{2H}.
\]In particular, $ Y $ is a quasi-helix in the sense of [Kahane1981,kahane1993some].
title: Lemma MC of arXiv:2411.05204

body: Lemma (campaign status: audited-pass): In the greedy weighted batching: |Us| ≥ as + 1 for every batch, the sets Us are pairwise disjoint, and an earlier witness support is disjoint from every later Ut. The batching is weighted: a witness meeting many disjoint matching pairs is charged by its full Littlewood-Offord atom loss rather than by a single 3/4 factor multiplied by its support size. This is the step that improves the old common-core size O((1+ell)*4^ell) to O(4^ell). Notes: Extraction 'O((1 + ℓ)4ℓ)' and 'O(4ℓ)' reconstructed as O((1+ell)*4^ell) and O(4^ell) (superscripts flattened).

body:
[Theorem T:half-space-full-tails of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] For $n, m\in \mathbb{N}$ and any $\alpha>0$, let
$$
\Delta_\alpha(n) = \mu_\alpha(n) - \mu(n)
$$
be the gap in the limit shape on the diagonal, and
$$
\nu_\alpha(n, m) = \mu(n, m) +  \Delta_\alpha(m).
$$
Fix $\alpha_0>0$, and take any $\alpha \ge \alpha_0$.
Then there exists a constant $c> 0$ depending only on $\alpha_0$, such that for all $v + (1, 1), v + (n, m) \in \mathbb{Z}^2_\ge$ with $n/m \in [\alpha_0, \alpha_0^{-1}]$ and all $\epsilon \in (0, m^{-1/3}]$ we have
\begin{align}

	\mathbb{P}\Big(X_\alpha(v + (1, 1); v + (n, m)) \ge \nu_\alpha(n, m) + \epsilon n\Big) &\le 2\exp\left(-c \epsilon^{3/2}n \left(1 \wedge \frac{\epsilon^{1/2}}{(1/2 - \alpha)\vee 0}\right) \right).
    \end{align}
Moreover, for all $v + (1, 1), v + (n, m) \in \mathbb{Z}^2_\ge$ with $n/m \in [\alpha_0, \alpha_0^{-1}]$ and all $\epsilon \in (0, 1)$ we have
    \begin{align}
	
	\mathbb{P}\Big(X_\alpha(v + (1, 1); v + (n, m)) \le \mu(n, m) - \epsilon n\Big) &\le 2 \exp\left( - c\epsilon^3 n^2 \right).
\end{align}
title: Theorem T:half-space-full-tails of arXiv:2604.10020

body:
Let H be a Hilbert space, X a Banach space, and T : H → X a bounded linear operator. Let T* : X* → H be its adjoint with respect to the pairing of X with X* (identifying H* with H by the Riesz map). Then ‖T‖_{H→X}² = ‖T*‖_{X*→H}² = ‖T T*‖_{X*→X}. In particular, T is bounded with norm A if and only if T T* is bounded with norm A². In practice one verifies the hypotheses on a dense subspace (e.g. Schwartz functions) and extends by density; this is the standard route from a dispersive kernel bound on TT* to a space-time estimate for T.
H Hilbert, X Banach
T : H → X bounded linear (or densely defined with an a priori bound on a dense subspace)

[Lemma 31 of arXiv:2604.22159, 'Adapted optimal transport between filtered Gaussian processes'] Let $\mu = \cN_{Nd}(a, A)$ and $L = \cC_{\min}(A)$. Then
\begin{equation} 
\mu_{t}(\dd x_{t} \mid x_{1:(t-1)}) = \cN_{d}\left( m_{t}, \Sigma_{t+1}    \right),
\end{equation}
where
\[
m_{t+1} = a_{t+1} + L_{t+1, 1:t} (L^{\ominus})_{1:t,1:t} (x_{1:t} - a_{1:t}) 
\]
and
\[
\Sigma_{t+1} = L_{t+1,t+1} L_{t+1,t+1}^{\intercal}.
\]

[Dfn 77 of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] The \textbf{zeroth-order almost periodic} (`\textbf{AP}') \textbf{entropy of $\phi$ along $\bspi$} is
\[\rmh^0_{\bspi}(\phi) := \inf_O \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{d_n}\log \bbP(\X(\pi_n,O) \ne \emptyset),\]
where the infimum runs over all neighbourhoods of $\phi$.  Similarly, the \textbf{lower zeroth-order AP entropy of $\phi$ along $\bspi$} is
\[\ul{\rmh}^0_{\bspi}(\phi) := \inf_O \liminf_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{d_n}\log \bbP(\X(\pi_n,O) \ne \emptyset),\]
where the infimum runs over all neighbourhoods of $\phi$.
title: Definition 77 of arXiv:2507.08909

body: [Lem connected of arXiv:2606.01627, 'The geometry of the giant component of random geometric graphs'] Let $M$ be a connected compact $d$-dimensional Riemannian manifold of volume $1$ and fix $\beta \in (0,1/d)$. There are constants $n_0 = n_0(M,\beta)$ and $c = c(M,\beta)$ so that for all $n \geq n_0$ and $r \geq n^{-\beta}$ $$\mathbb{P}(G_M^n(r) \text{ is connected}) \geq 1 - \exp(- c n^{1 - d\beta})\,.$$
title: Lem connected of arXiv:2606.01627

[Dfn 3. dfn: topological subfunctor of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{Topological subfunctor}] 
  Let $\tilde{\tau}$ and $\tau$ be functors.
  We say that $\tau$ is a \textit{topological subfunctor} of $\tilde{\tau}$ 
  if and only if the following conditions are satisfied.
  \begin{enumerate} [label = (T\arabic*)]
    \item 
      For every $(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S}) \in \mathfrak{M}$,
      there exists a topological embedding of $\tau(S)$ into $\tilde{\tau}(S)$,
      that is,
      there exists a homeomorphism from $\tau(S)$ to a subset of $\tilde{\tau}(S)$.
      Using this map, we always regard $\tau(S)$ as a subspace of $\tilde{\tau}(S)$.
    \item  
      For every $(S_{i}, d^{S_{i}}, \rho_{S_{i}}),\, i=1,2$ 
      and root-and-distance-preserving map $f: S_{1} \to S_{2}$, 
      it holds that $\tau_{f} = \tilde{\tau}_{f}|_{\tau(S_{1})}$.
  \end{enumerate}
title: Dfn 3. dfn: topological subfunctor of arXiv:2412.08236

[Defn d.moment of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] \ 
The real-valued marks of \\
$(\tilde\mathcal{P}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}=\bigl(\{(x_i,\xi_{i,n})\}_{x_i \in \mathcal{P}_n}\bigr)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$,
namely $\xi_{i,n}\in\mathbb{R}$, satisfy a $p$-moment condition, $p \in [1, \infty)$, if there are constants $M_p^{\xi} < \infty$
 such that 
 
\begin{equation}

\sup_{1 \leq n< \infty} \sup_{1 \leq q \leq p} \sup_{x_1,\ldots,
  x_{q} \in W_n} \mathbb {E} _{\bk x1{q}}[ \max(1,|\xi_{1,n}|^p)]
\leq M_p^{\xi} < \infty,
\end{equation}
where $\xi_{1,n}$ is the score  of $x_1$ under the Palm distribution of  $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n$ given the ground points $x_1,\ldots,x_q$. Here and elsewhere, we adopt the convention that the sup with respect to $\bk x1p$ is to be understood as $\text{ess}\sup$ with respect to the factorial moment  measures $\rho^{(p)}(\bk x1p) \mathrm{d} \bk x1p$ of the common ground process~$\mathcal{P}$, where  $\rho^{(p)}$ is tacitly assumed to be uniformly bounded by $\kappa_p$. Without loss of generality we assume that $M_p^{\xi}$
  is increasing in $p$ whenever (equation e:xinpmom of the paper) holds.
title: Moment conditions of scores

[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2607.22470, 'A Logarithmic Fluctuation Hierarchy for Sequential Interacting Diffusions'] Fix \(n\ge0\) and let \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\R^d)\). Then, as
\(N\to\infty\),
\begin{equation}
\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}
\left|
\int_0^t I_{s,0}^{N,n}(\varphi)\,\dd s
-
\int_0^t
\langle Y_s^{N,n+1},\Gamma_s^\varphi\rangle\,\dd s
\right|
\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
Consequently, along any subsequence for which
\(Y^{N,n+1}\LawConv Y^{n+1}\) in \(E\),
\[
  \left(
  Y^{N,n+1},
  \left(\int_0^t I_{s,0}^{N,n}(\varphi)\,\dd s\right)_{t\in[0,T]}
  \right)
  \LawConv
  \left(
  Y^{n+1},
  \left(\int_0^t
  \langle Y_s^{n+1},\Gamma_s^\varphi\rangle\,\dd s
  \right)_{t\in[0,T]}
  \right)
\]
weakly in \(E\times C([0,T];\R)\).  The second coordinate of the limit is
equivalently
\[
\left(\int_0^t
\left\langle
\bar\rho_s,(K*Y_s^{n+1})\cdot\nabla\varphi
\right\rangle\,\dd s\right)_{t\in[0,T]}.
\]

body:
[Corollary 20 (Gaussian functional inequalities after centering) of arXiv:2607.10769, '\fontsize{14}{17}\selectfont\bfseries Sharp Poincar\'e interpolation along Wasserstein geo'] Let $\mu$ be $1$-strongly log-concave, let $m=\int x\,\d\mu$, and denote
\[
 \mathcal D=\Ent_\gamma(\mu)-\frac12|m|^2,
 \quad
 \mathcal I=\FI_\gamma(\mu)-|m|^2,
 \quad
 \mathcal W^2=W_2^2(\mu,\gamma)-|m|^2.
\]
Then $\mathcal D\geq0$, $\mathcal I\geq0$, and
$0\leq\mathcal W^2\leq n$.  Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 e^{\mathcal D/n}
 \leq
 \cos\!\left(\sqrt{\frac2n}\,\mathcal W\right)
 +\frac{\sin\!\left(\sqrt{2/n}\,\mathcal W\right)}{\sqrt{2n}}
  \sqrt{\mathcal I},
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
 4\mathcal D
 \leq2n\left(e^{2\mathcal D/n}-1\right)
 \leq\mathcal I,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal W^2
 \leq-n\log\cos\!\left(\sqrt{\frac2n}\,\mathcal W\right)
 \leq\mathcal D.
\end{equation}
Moreover, for every $s\geq0$,
\begin{equation}
 \Ent_\gamma(P_s^*\mu)
 \leq e^{-4s}\left(\Ent_\gamma(\mu)-\frac12|m|^2\right)
      +\frac12e^{-2s}|m|^2.
\end{equation}

[Definition 150 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Let $\boldsymbol{\chi}_{\N}^{(1)}$ and $\boldsymbol{\chi}_{\N}^{(2)}$ be two families (indexed by a large parameter $\N$) of discrete random $d$-dimensional real vectors. We say that the distribution of $\boldsymbol{\chi}_{\N}^{(1)}$ is asymptotically equal to the distribution of $\boldsymbol{\chi}_{\N}^{(2)}$ if
\begin{equation}

 \lim_{\N\rightarrow\infty} \sup_{f \in \textnormal{Lip}_1} \big|\E\big[f(\boldsymbol{\chi}_{\N}^{(1)})\big]-\E\big[f(\boldsymbol{\chi}_{\N}^{(2)})\big]\big| =0,
\end{equation}
where $\textnormal{Lip}_1$ is the set of $1$-bounded $1$-Lipschitz functions
\[
 \textnormal{Lip}_1=\big\{f:\amsmathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \amsmathbb{R} \quad \big|\quad \forall \boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y} \in \amsmathbb{R}^d \quad |f(\x)-f(\y)| \leq |\!|\x-\y|\!|_{\infty}\,\,\textnormal{ and }\, |f(\x)|\leq 1\big\}.
\]
If \eqref{eq_asymptotic_equivalence} holds, we write $\chi_{\N}^{(1)} \stackrel{\textnormal{d}}{\sim} \chi_{\N}^{(2)}$.

[Lemma spectral_radius of arXiv:2606.16609, 'On stability of outliers from the circular law'] Let $\{ \lambda_k^{(N)} \}_{1 \leq k \leq N}$ be an array of random complex numbers such that for every $N$, $\{ \lambda_1^{(N)}, \dots, \lambda_N^{(N)} \}$ is distributed like the spectrum of a complex Ginibre matrix conditioned on $\{ \lambda_1 = z \}$ with fixed $z \in \mathbb{C}$; then almost surely, for any fixed $\epsilon > 1$ there exists an integer $N_0 >0$ such that
$$
\forall N \geq N_0, \  \forall k \in [\![ 2,N ]\!] \ |\lambda_k| < 1+\epsilon.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Thm tailsmat of arXiv:2605.31054, 'On the empirical spectral distribution of matrix perpetuities'] Assume that $N\geq 2$ and
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] ${\mathbf A},{\mathbf B}\in\mathrm{Sym}_{\geq0}(N)$ a.s.,
        \item[(ii)] $({\mathbf u}{\mathbf A} {\mathbf u}^\top, {\mathbf u} {\mathbf B} {\mathbf u}^\top)\stackrel{d}{=}({\mathbf A},{\mathbf B})$ for any orthogonal matrix ${\mathbf u}$,
        \item[(iii)] there exists $\eta>0$ such that 
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item ${\mathbb E}[{\mathbf A}_{11}^\eta]=1$,
             \item ${\mathbb E}[{\mathbf A}_{11}^\eta \log^+({\mathbf A}_{11})]<\infty$,
             \item ${\mathbb E}[{\mathbf B}_{11}^\eta]<\infty$,
             \item ${\mathbb E}[ \det( {\mathbf A}^{[2]})^{\eta/2}]<1$,
        \end{enumerate}
        \item[(iv)] the conditional law of $\log {\mathbf A}_{11}$ given $\{{\mathbf A}_{11}\neq 0\}$ is non-arithmetic,
        \item[(v)] ${\mathbb P}({\mathbf A}_{11}x+{\mathbf B}_{11}=x)<1$ for $x\in{\mathbb R}$.
    \end{enumerate}
   Then, there exists a unique solution ${\mathbf X}$ to
\begin{align}
{\mathbf X}\stackrel{d}{=}{\mathbf A}^{1/2} {\mathbf X} {\mathbf A}^{1/2} +{\mathbf B},\qquad ({\mathbf A},{\mathbf B})\mbox{ and }{\mathbf X}\mbox{ are independent},
\end{align} 
which satisfies 
\[
\mu_{\mathbf X}\big( (t,\infty)\big) \sim \frac{1}{N}{\mathbb P}(\lambda_{\max}({\mathbf X}) > t) \sim \frac1N \frac{\sqrt{\pi}\, \Gamma\left(\eta+\dfrac{N}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\left(\dfrac{N}{2}\right)\, \Gamma\left(\eta+\tfrac12\right)} {\mathbb P}({\mathbf X}_{11}>t)
\]
and
    \begin{align}
\lim_{t\to+\infty} t^\eta\, {\mathbb P}({\mathbf X}_{11}>t) = \frac{ {\mathbb E}\left[ ({\mathbf A}_{11}{\mathbf X}_{11}+{\mathbf B}_{11})^\eta - ({\mathbf A}_{11}{\mathbf X}_{11})^\eta \right]}{\eta \,{\mathbb E}[{\mathbf A}_{11}^\eta \log{\mathbf A}_{11} ]}\in(0,+\infty).
    \end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm tailsmat of arXiv:2605.31054

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Source-specific calculation, conditional implication or exact obstruction Result: Finite-volume derivatives of log Z are energy cumulants: the second is a variance and the kth derivative is the kth centered cumulant up to sign. Analyticity in a beta neighborhood requires control at all orders, typically |cumulant_k|/volume bounded by C^k*k!, not merely a two-point decay estimate. Even real-analytic finite-volume functions can converge to a nonanalytic limit: f_n(beta)=sqrt((beta-beta0)^2+1/n) tends to |beta-beta0| for any fixed positive beta0. Check: Each f_n has a positive radicand on the real axis and is real analytic there, while the limit has different one-sided derivatives at beta0. Its complex singularities approach beta0 at distance1/sqrt(n), showing the missing uniform analytic radius. Obstruction: Uniform higher-order cumulant estimates or a convergent expansion are needed throughout the desired temperature range. The existing two-point control does not by itself provide them. No full analyticity theorem is established here.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0324-analyticity-of-the-one-dimensional-riesz-free-energy
No independent review

body:
A scaling limit for critical length-weighted honeycomb self-avoiding paths between prescribed domain boundary points does not by itself establish a scaling limit for uniformly sampled n-step honeycomb self-avoiding walks from the origin. The former randomizes length and fixes both endpoints; the latter fixes length and leaves the endpoint random. An application to the fixed-length question needs an additional theorem controlling the length disintegration, endpoint law, spatial rescaling, and curve topology. No such theorem is supplied by the cited conjectures or this draft.
the two sampling rules are as stated in the cited primary questions

[Corollary cor:gradient of arXiv:2510.22778, 'Free denoising diffusion models'] The velocity field of the reversed marginal family is
$-V_{T-s}=\tfrac{\beta}{2}\nabla_{\!W_{2}}\mathcal{F}[\mu_{T-s}]$, so the reverse process
ascends the free energy: generation is the time reversal of a $W_{2}$-gradient descent
toward the semicircular equilibrium. Moreover the deterministic \emph{probability-flow}
equation
$\dot y=-V_{T-s}(y)=\tfrac{\beta}{2}\big(y-\xi_{\mu_{T-s}}(y)\big)$
transports $\gamma$ to $\mu_{0}$ with the same marginals as (equation eq:reversesde of the paper).

[Theorem 22 of arXiv:2609.02444, 'The Hasse norm principle for $A_4$-quartic extensions of global function fields'] Let \(n_1 > 0\) and \(n_{2} \geq 0\) be integers and \(p \geq 5\) a prime.
  Let \(q\) be a power of \(p\) such that all geometric components of \(\widetilde H^{\rm fail}(n_1,n_2) \otimes \FF_p\) are defined over \(\FF_q\).
  Let \(\phi \colon  H^{\rm fail}(n_1,n_2) \to H(n_{1},n_2)\) be the natural forgetful map. 
Let \(H \subset H(n_1,n_2) \otimes \FF_q\) be a (geometric) component and let \(H^{\rm fail}\) be the pre-image of \(H\) in \(H^{\rm fail}(n_1,n_2) \otimes \FF_q\).
  Then,
   \[ \lim_{m \to \infty} \frac{|\phi(H^{\rm fail}(\FF_{q^m}))|}{|H(\FF_{q^m})|} = rb_{n_2},\]
  where $r\leq 2$ is the number of geometric components of \(\widetilde H^{\rm fail}(n_1,n_2) \otimes \FF_q\) lying above $H$. Consequently,
   \[ \lim_{m \to \infty} \frac{|\phi(H^{\rm fail}(n_1,n_2)(\FF_{q^m}))|}{|H(n_1,n_2)(\FF_{q^m})|} \leq 2 b_{n_2}.\]

body:
[Theorem thm:berkowitz-devlin-one-step-clt of arXiv:2608.06159, 'Majority Dynamics on Resampled Sparse Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi Graphs:\\[0.5ex] Gaussian Winner '] Let \(\gR_0,\gB_0\) be a deterministic partition of \([N]\). Independently
sample \(\gG\sim\mathbb{G}(N,p)\) and perform one synchronous majority update with
ties retaining their current colors. Define
\[
\sigma_N\coloneqq\sqrt{Np(1-p)}.
\]
For independent random variables
\[
W_R\sim\Bin(|\gR_0|,p),
\qquad
W_B\sim\Bin(|\gB_0|,p),
\]
set
\[
\chi_N
\coloneqq
\P(W_R\ge W_B)\P(W_R\le W_B).
\]
Then the following conclusions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item For arbitrary parameter choices,
\begin{align}
\Var(|\gR_1|)
=
N\chi_N
+O\left(
|\Delta_0|+\frac{N}{\sigma_N}
\right).

\end{align}
\item Suppose that
\[
\sigma_N\longrightarrow\infty,
\qquad
\log(1/\chi_N)=o(\log\sigma_N).
\]
Then
\[
\Var(|\gR_1|)\sim N\chi_N,
\]
and, for every fixed \(a<c\),
\begin{align}
\P\left(
a\le
\frac{|\gR_1|-\E|\gR_1|}{\sqrt{N\chi_N}}
\le c
\right)
\longrightarrow
\Phi(c)-\Phi(a).

\end{align}
\end{enumerate}
In particular, the assumptions and conclusions in \textup{(ii)} hold if
\(\sigma_N\to\infty\) and
\[
|\Delta_0|p=O(\sigma_N).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 30 of arXiv:2506.10494, 'Geometric Jensen-Shannon Divergence Between Gaussian Measures On Hilbert Space'] Let $\mu = \Ncal(m,C) \in \Gauss(\Hcal)$, $C \in \Sym^{++}(\Hcal) \cap \Tr(\Hcal)$.
	Assume that $A \in \SymTr(\Hcal)_{< I}$, $b \in \Hcal$. Consider
	the orthogonal projection $P_N = \sum_{k=1}^N e_k \otimes e_k$, $N \in \Nbb$, where $\{e_k\}_{k \in \Nbb}$
	are the orthonormal eigenvectors of $C$.
	Define
	\begin{align}
	&\la C^{-1/2}(x-m), AC^{-1/2}(x-m)\ra + \la C^{-1/2}(x-m),b\ra 
	
	\\
	&\doteq \lim_{N \approach \infty}\la C^{-1/2}P_N(x-m), AC^{-1/2}P_N(x-m)\ra + \la C^{-1/2}P_N(x-m),b\ra,
	\nonumber
	\end{align}
	where the limit is in the $\Lcal^2(\Hcal,\mu)$ sense.
	Then
	\begin{align}
		&\int_{\Hcal}\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\la C^{-1/2}(x-m), AC^{-1/2}(x-m)\ra + \la C^{-1/2}(x-m),b\ra\right)\Ncal(m,C)(dx)
		\nonumber
		\\
		& = [\det(I- A)]^{-1/2}\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}||(I-A)^{-1/2}b||^2\right).	
	\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:free-small-loss of arXiv:2607.05693, 'Free multiplicative convolution and Erlang moments in monitored quantum transport'] Fix $\tau>0$. For $n>\tau$, let $c_n=\tau/n$. Then
\[
  \nu_{c_n}^{\boxtimes n}
  \xrightarrow{w}
  \mu_\tau,
\]
where $\mu_\tau$ is the compactly supported probability measure on $[0,1]$
characterized by
\[
  S_{\mu_\tau}(z)
  =
  \exp\left(\frac{\tau}{1+z}\right).
\]
Equivalently, $(\mu_\tau)_{\tau\ge 0}$ is a free multiplicative convolution
semigroup:
\[
  \mu_{\tau_1}\boxtimes\mu_{\tau_2}=\mu_{\tau_1+\tau_2},
  \qquad
  \mu_0=\delta_1.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Their actual LSI constants lie between D^100/96 and O(D^206(log D)^2); norm-one selector observations with noise Theta((log D)^-2) put their ratios between Omega(D^100(log D)^4) and O(D^206(log D)^6). {"artifact_digest":"sha256:8bfe2dd3dee1928439f3e1a6945b93ee70e30494cdc63885a90691768a186c40","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/8b/8bfe2dd3dee1928439f3e1a6945b93ee70e30494cdc63885a90691768a186c40.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:dd45cc5a37eb2bdf6ee694037d47cb625d9da2c201909daabff05ac8adbb64c5","bundle_entry_key":"draft-posterior-hardness-polynomial-lsi-regularization","bundle_id":"population.w740-t411-polynomial-lsi-hardness-v1","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"posterior sampling and functional inequalities","draft":"w740/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.sampling:draft-posterior-hardness-polynomial-lsi-regularization","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Posterior-sampling hardness with polynomial log-Sobolev priors

Status: proof (unaudited). Source/interface inspection and 31 exact supporting checks recorded; independent review remains required. This is a proposed proof of T411 Target 2. It makes no novelty claim. Target 1 remains open.

## Computational scope and statement

Use the computational model of Gupta, Jalal, Parulekar, Price and Xun, arXiv:2402.12727v2: a diffusion prior is supplied through polynomial-size, polynomially bounded, effectively constructible approximate forward-score networks. Gaussian sampling primitives and polynomial-precision computations are understood as in that source. This is not a lower bound against a unit-cost oracle for exact prior scores.

Assume one-way functions exist. For all sufficiently large ambient dimensions D in the source's hard family, there are positive smooth priors M_D, coordinate-selector matrices A_D of norm one, and Gaussian observation standard deviations sigma_D=Theta((log D)^(-2)), with the following properties.

* The priors have explicit polynomial-time generative descriptions, bounded covariance operator, and polynomially accurate forward scores witnessed by polynomial-size ReLU networks (specifically 8-well-modeled in Definition 1.1).
* Their actual optimal LSI constants satisfy

  D^100/96 <= C_LS(M_D) <= C D^206 (log D)^2.

* Therefore their actual observation ratios satisfy

  c D^100 (log D)^4 <= ||A_D||^2 C_LS(M_D)/sigma_D^2
       <= C' D^206 (log D)^6.

* There is no polynomial-time sampler which, with probability at least 1-10^(-6) over observations, outputs a law within TV 10^(-6) of the posterior, using the stated computable score interface and the generative description. Such a sampler would invert a one-way function.

Constants may depend on the fixed source construction, not on D. The polynomial exponents are chosen to keep the approximation budget explicit; no optimal exponent or matching boundary is asserted.

The LSI convention is Ent(f^2)<=2 C_LS E||grad f||^2. The final priors contain nondegenerate Gaussian noise: the finite-coin approximation below is of the center sampler, not a claim that a discrete finite-grid output approximates a continuous law in TV.

## 1. Primary-source input

Take the hard family P_D from Theorem 1.8 / Lemma 3.5 of Gupta et al. The construction is Definition 3.2, scaled in Definition 3.3; its well-modeled score networks are Corollary 3.6, with their construction completed in Appendix C.8. It has these properties:

1. A_D selects the encoded last coordinates, so A_D A_D^T=I and ||A_D||=1. Observation noise is beta_D=Theta((log D)^(-2)). A (1/10,1/10) posterior sampler, in Definitions 1.2 and 1.5, would contradict one-way-function hardness. The success probability is over the observation.
2. P_D is 10-well-modeled: at every D^(-10)<=v<=D^10 its smoothed score has squared L2 approximation error less than D^(-10)/v^2, by a polynomial-size network with polynomially bounded weights. These are the source's effective constructions from the forward one-way-function circuit; no preimage is supplied.
3. Each seed is uniform fair bits. Given the seed, the first coordinates are independent N(seed_i,1/R_D^2). Each remaining coordinate is an independent phase-0 or phase-half discretized centered Gaussian, divided by R_D, where R_D=Theta(log D), and its phase is specified by the forward function of the seed. The unscaled grid spacing and its reciprocal are polynomially bounded.

Uniformity of the score construction is used, rather than inferred from mere network existence. Lemma C.15 (PDF p.32) writes the small-scale network explicitly as a vertex-decoding network followed by evaluation of the forward circuit, one-dimensional score networks and ReLU switches. Lemmas C.19/C.20 (PDF p.38) use a product-mixture score at large scales. The scalar functions here are Gaussian densities or smoothed phase-lattice Gaussian sums. On the polynomial truncation windows used for these networks, their values and derivatives are computable to polynomially many bits by truncated Gaussian sums and elementary series: the reciprocal smoothing scale and lattice spacing are polynomial, so a polynomial summation window suffices, with Gaussian tails bounded by exp(-poly(D)). Denominators on a polynomial window can be exponentially small in a polynomial, requiring polynomially many bits, rather than exponentially many. Thus the one-dimensional piecewise-linear tables can be generated to the source error tolerance with polynomial work; their finitely many coefficients can be rounded with a further polynomial precision budget. Circuit composition and switches are explicit. No conditional seed probability or circuit inverse is computed. This is the finite-precision Gaussian-primitive model of the source, not an exact-real oracle assertion.

Both phase lattices are symmetric about zero. Therefore E P_D=0; its raw second-moment operator is bounded by an absolute constant, also stated in the well-modeled condition. The first coordinate is exactly

(1/2)N(1,1/R_D^2)+(1/2)N(-1,1/R_D^2).

The conditional lattice Gaussian has uniform Gaussian-type tails for the source spacings <=1: its normalizer is bounded below by c/epsilon, and its tail sums are bounded above by C exp(-T^2/4)/epsilon. These bounds follow by counting grid points in [-1,1] and comparing the tails with the Gaussian integral. In particular all coordinate fourth moments are uniformly bounded and E||X||^4=O(D^2). No independence between the different encoded phase choices is needed for this fourth-moment conclusion.

## 2. A finite-coin center sampler

There is a polynomial-coin deterministic map S_D:{-1,1}^k->R^D, k=O(D log D), such that

W2(P_D,Law(S_D)) <= D^(-130),
||S_D(b)|| <= B_D:=4D^2 for all b,
E[S_D S_D^T] <= K I

for an absolute K and all sufficiently large D. Here is a finite algorithmic construction, not an enumeration of the exponentially many seeds.

Sample the seed with its exact fair bits and evaluate its forward circuit. For each scalar Gaussian or phase-lattice Gaussian primitive, truncate the unscaled variable at absolute value D. The tail second-moment contribution is exponentially small in D^2, uniformly in the two lattice phases; this uses the preceding elementary tail-sum comparison. For a continuous Gaussian, quantize its truncated value to mesh D^(-300). For a lattice primitive retain the actual grid points in [-D,D]. There are polynomially many points because the grid reciprocal is polynomially bounded.

For each of the Gaussian and two lattice-phase tables, approximate its finite probabilities by nonnegative dyadic probabilities, of common denominator 2^b, with total mass one and total variation error at most D^(-1000). One can round all but one weight down and assign the remaining mass to the last cell; use b large enough that the number of cells times 2^(-b) is below the requested error, and compute each weight to a further fixed number of guard bits. Thus b=O(log D), with a sufficiently large fixed constant. The Gaussian bin probabilities and lattice weights are computable to this precision in polynomial time, for example by Taylor approximation and integration on the bounded interval; their arguments have polynomial size. Standard elementary series likewise approximate R_D and the grid spacing to the finer mesh precision. No inversion of the forward circuit occurs.

Use b fresh fair bits and the dyadic CDF to choose a cell exactly, independently for each primitive. Couple this with the ideal primitive by a common-part coupling on the finite cells. On a table mismatch the squared unscaled error is at most O(D^2); the total mismatch probability over O(D) coordinates is O(D^(-999)). On a match, continuous quantization contributes at most D^(-300) per coordinate, and parameter rounding can be made smaller. Gaussian and lattice tail second moments contribute exp(-cD^2) times a polynomial. Summing the squared errors proves the stated global W2 bound for sufficiently large D. All values after division by R_D>=1 have absolute value at most 3D, so the norm bound 4D^2 is valid. The tables and the circuit have polynomial descriptions and are built in polynomial time. The number of random bits is O(D log D), even if a deliberately inefficient polynomial-size table is used.

Finally, for each unit vector v, this coupling gives

E(v.S_D)^2 <=2E(v.X)^2+2E||S_D-X||^2 <=K.

Thus bounded covariance is preserved without multiplying a tiny TV error by the square of an unnecessarily enormous output cutoff.

## 3. Regularize to polynomial LSI

Put r=D^(-20), a=D^(-100), h=a/k. Apply C006 to S_D, using fresh standard Gaussians Z in R^k and W in R^D:

c(z)=min(1,min_i |z_i|/h),
F(z)=c(z)S_D(sign z),
M_D=Law(F(Z)+rW).

It has a positive smooth density, bounded covariance operator, and

C_LS(M_D)<=B_D^2 k^2/a^2+r^2
 <=16 k^2 D^204+r^2 <=C D^206(log D)^2.

It is explicitly samplable using the given forward circuit and Gaussian randomness.

Let P_r=P_D*N(0,r^2 I). Gaussian translation gives

TV(Law(S_D+rW),P_r) <=W2(P_D,Law(S_D))/r <=D^(-110).

For clarity, the translation estimate follows by integrating the absolute directional derivative of the Gaussian density: TV(N(x,r^2I),N(x',r^2I))<=||x-x'||/r. Integrate this over the displayed coupling and use Cauchy--Schwarz. No density of the unsmoothed P_D is required.

C006 and the triangle inequality therefore give TV(M_D,P_r)<=a+D^(-110)<=2a.

The prior score is also globally Lipschitz with a polynomial bound: if V=F(Z), then ||V||<=B_D, and Gaussian convolution gives Hess log p(x)=-I/r^2+Cov(V|V+rW=x)/r^4. Its operator norm is at most r^(-2)+B_D^2 r^(-4)=poly(D). This is a regularity statement, not a polynomial exact-score evaluation algorithm.

## 4. Preserve effective forward-score networks

For D^(-8)<=u<=D^8 put v=sqrt(u^2+r^2). For large D, D^(-10)<=v<=D^10. The u-smoothed score of P_r equals the v-smoothed score of P_D. Use its source network and clip each output to [-D/u,D/u]. The clipping is an explicit ReLU operation with coefficients polynomially bounded on the scale interval.

Apply C005 with P=P_r, Q=M_D, L=D and TV distance at most 2a. The squared score error under (M_D)_u is at most

[2D^(-10)+12D exp(-D^2/2)+16aD(D^2+1)]/u^2 <=D^(-8)/u^2

for all sufficiently large D. This estimate is uniform over the full scale interval. For an explicit eventual bound, the degree-nine Taylor term gives exp(D^2/2)>12D^11 once D>=32; the remaining polynomial terms are smaller than D^(-10) for sufficiently large D. Hence the numerator is at most 4D^(-10), below D^(-8).

Together with bounded covariance, these clipped networks witness 8-well-modeledness. Their descriptions are computed by taking the source network at v and adding the clipping layer. The construction uses only the forward circuit and polynomial-precision scalar parameters. It does not approximate exact prior scores to arbitrarily requested accuracy and does not furnish unit-cost exact-score access.

## 5. The actual optimal LSI lies in a polynomial regime

The first marginal of P_r is the symmetric mixture of N(+1,t^2) and N(-1,t^2), where t^2=R_D^(-2)+r^2. Its probability in [-1/4,1/4] is at most 2 exp(-9/(32t^2)). Since R_D=Theta(log D) and r=D^(-20), this is at most a=D^(-100) for sufficiently large D. The symmetry makes each outside plateau have mass at least (1-a)/2.

The TV bound to M_D gives belt mass at most 3a and each outside plateau mass at least (1-5a)/2>=2/5. Let f be zero for x_1<=-1/4, one for x_1>=1/4, and linear between. Its squared gradient is 4 in the belt and zero outside, so its energy is at most 12a. Two independent copies show Var(f)>=4/25>1/8. Therefore

C_P(M_D)>=1/(96a)=D^100/96,
C_LS(M_D)>=C_P(M_D).

This is a lower bound on the actual optimal LSI constant. No irrelevant dummy coordinate or inflated LSI certificate is used to obtain a large observation ratio.

## 6. Transfer a posterior sampler back to the hard source

Write beta=beta_D, A=A_D, and choose sigma=sqrt(beta^2-r^2)>0. Positivity and sigma=Theta(beta) hold for sufficiently large D. Under the common coupling

X~P_D,  X_r=X+rW,  Y=A X_r+sigma E,

the joint law of (X,Y) is exactly the source model with noise beta: A A^T=I, so rAW+sigma E is N(0,beta^2 I), independent of X. The marginal law of (X_r,Y) is the P_r prior with independent observation noise sigma. This equality is before conditioning; W need not be independent of Y afterward.

For tau=1/100 let e_y be the conditional probability that ||X_r-X||>tau in this coupling. Since E||rW||^2=D^(-39),

E_Y e_y <=10^4 D^(-39).

Markov's inequality implies e_y<=1/100 outside an observation set of probability at most 10^6 D^(-39).

Suppose a polynomial-time M_D posterior sampler has TV error <=epsilon_0=10^(-6) with probability at least 1-epsilon_0 over its observations. Denote its output law at y by Q_y and let q(y)=TV(Q_y,M_D(.|y)). Since TV is at most one, E_{(M_D)_Y}q<=2epsilon_0. Observation marginalization contracts TV, so changing the Y law to that of P_r costs at most 2a. The conditional-TV averaging inequality proved in C002 gives

E_{(P_r)_Y} TV(M_D(.|Y),P_r(.|Y)) <=2TV(M_D,P_r)<=4a.

Consequently

E_{(P_r)_Y} TV(Q_Y,P_r(.|Y)) <=2epsilon_0+6a.

Markov at 1/100 makes the bad-observation probability at most 200epsilon_0+600a=0.0002+600a. On the remaining observations, couple Q_y to P_r(.|y) with failure at most 1/100, and then use the conditional coupling of X_r to X, with norm error at most 1/100 except on probability 1/100. The gluing lemma for couplings and a union bound give (1/100,2/100)-closeness to P_D(.|y).

The total bad-observation probability is at most

0.0002+600D^(-100)+10^6 D^(-39),

which is below 1/10 for sufficiently large D. This is stronger than the forbidden (1/10,1/10) source posterior guarantee. All wrapper computations, forward-score network calls and generative descriptions are polynomial, so the hypothetical sampler contradicts the source's one-way-function lower bound.

## 7. Observation ratio and conclusion

The same selector A has norm one and sigma^2=Theta((log D)^(-4)). Combining the two-sided prior LSI bounds with this noise scale gives exactly the two-sided polynomial bounds in the statement. Thus the construction lies in the polynomial-LSI class and the polynomial observation-ratio regime of Target 2, in the stated approximate-score interface.

This proof neither resolves Target 1 nor establishes a sharp transition. Its cryptographic assumption and hardness source are Gupta et al.; the proposed extension consists of the explicit polynomial-LSI regularization and preservation of their computable score interface. [Definition 1 of arXiv:2607.20646, 'The Independence-Preserving Property and Planar Web Geometry'] Let $d$ be a positive integer and $\Omega\subset\R^2$ be an open connected set.
    A \emph{nonsingular planar $d$-web} on $\Omega$ is a $d$-tuple $\W=(h_i)_{i=1}^d$ of real-analytic functions such that $\dd h_i\neq 0$ and $\dd h_i\wedge\dd h_j\neq 0$ everywhere on $\Omega$ whenever $i\neq j$.
    \footnote{
    Geometrically, each function \(h_i\) represents the family of its level curves $\mathcal{F}(h_i) = \{\{(x,y)\in\Omega \mid h_i(x,y)=t\} \mid t\in h_i(\Omega) \}$. 
    Since for a one-variable diffeomorphism $\rho_i$ one has $\mathcal{F}(h_i) = \mathcal{F}(\rho_i\circ h_i)$, the web $(\rho_i\circ h_i)_{i=1}^d$ is identified with $(h_i)_{i=1}^d$.
    }

    A \emph{measurable Abelian relation} for $\W$ is a $d$-tuples $(\Phi_i)_{i=1}^d$ of real-valued measurable functions $\Phi_i$ on $h_i(\Omega)$ satisfying
    \begin{align}
        \Phi_1(h_1(x, y)) + \cdots + \Phi_d(h_d(x, y)) = (\text{constant})
    \end{align}
    for every $(x, y)\in\Omega$.
    This equation is called an \emph{Abelian functional equation}.
    For differentiable components, this is equivalent to
    \[
        \Phi_1'(h_1(x, y)) \dd h_1 + \cdots + \Phi_d'(h_d(x, y)) \dd h_d = 0.
    \]
    Continuous and real-analytic Abelian relations are defined analogously.
    Two measurable Abelian relations are identified if their corresponding components differ by additive constants.
    The real vector space of real-analytic Abelian relations modulo this equivalence is denoted by $\A(\W)$, and its dimension is called the rank of $\W$.
title: Definition 1 of arXiv:2607.20646
