# T419-C014 v1: empirical GD boundedness with an initialization-dependent step

Kind: bound. Target: 2. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claimed.
This is an explicit anisotropic version of the published Gram-imbalance/descent method, not a solution of Target 2. It proves a trajectory component without assuming the iterates are bounded. The prior source is Du-Hu-Lee, arXiv:1806.00900, Theorem 2.2 and Appendix B, Claim B.1; its full convergence theorems have different initialization/step hypotheses. C009 already identifies the exact covariance metric and C010 the positive-noise empirical landscape.

## Statement

Let C be any real positive definite p-by-p matrix, D any real m-by-p matrix, and r>=1. Put lambda=lambda_min(C)>0, c=||C||op, ell=||D||op, W=D C^(-1), and

 q(B,A)=(1/2)||(BA-W) C^(1/2)||F^2,

with B m-by-r and A r-by-p. This is the empirical regression objective up to a constant when C=XX^T/n and D=ZX^T/n. Initialize at any finite deterministic factors B0,A0, and define

 q0=q(B0,A0), J=||A0 A0^T-B0^T B0||F+1,
 R=||W||F+sqrt(2q0/lambda),
 K=sqrt(r)(J+2R), L=6Kc+ell.

For any fixed

 0<eta<=min{1/(1+2q0),1/L},

simultaneous ordinary factor GD satisfies, for every integer t>=0,

 q_t<=q0,
 ||B_t||F^2+||A_t||F^2<=K,
 ||(A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t)-(A0 A0^T-B0^T B0)||F<=2eta q0<1,
 sum_(t>=0) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/eta.

In particular the gradient tends to zero, every accumulation point is critical, and for every integer T>=1,

 min_(0<=t<T) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/(eta T).

All constants are finite and computable from C,D and the initialization. There is no Gaussian assumption and no low-rank assumption on W. No iterate-convergence, saddle-avoidance or statistical-risk assertion is included.

## Exact identities and product/factor bounds

Let G=BA C-D. The two factor gradients are G_B=G A^T and G_A=B^T G. With E_t=A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t the first-order cross terms cancel exactly, giving

 E_(t+1)-E_t=eta^2(G_A G_A^T-G_B^T G_B),
 ||E_(t+1)-E_t||F<=eta^2(||G_A||F^2+||G_B||F^2).

This cancellation only uses dependence on BA and does not require isotropic C. Also

 (||B||F^2+||A||F^2)^2
 <=r [||AA^T-B^TB||F^2+4||BA||F^2].

To verify it, write P=B^TB,Q=AA^T. Scalar trace Cauchy-Schwarz gives (tr(P+Q))^2<=r tr((P+Q)^2), and cyclicity of trace gives tr((P+Q)^2)=||P-Q||F^2+4 tr(PQ), tr(PQ)=||BA||F^2. No commutation is assumed.

When q<=q0, positivity of C gives ||BA-W||F<=sqrt(2q0/lambda), hence ||BA||F<=R. If additionally ||E-E0||F<=1, then ||E||F<=J, so the preceding trace bound implies

 ||B||F^2+||A||F^2<=sqrt(r) sqrt(J^2+4R^2)<=K.

The initialization meets these conditions and therefore has pair norm at most sqrt(K).

## Descent established before closing the boundedness induction

Suppose at the current iterate the pair norm is at most sqrt(K), and preceding steps have valid descent inequalities. Then

 ||grad q||F<=||BA C-D||op sqrt(||B||F^2+||A||F^2)
             <=(Kc/2+ell)sqrt(K).

Because eta<=1/(6Kc+ell), the proposed next point has pair norm at most 2sqrt(K). The connecting segment also lies in that ball. On that ball the Hessian quadratic form in a perturbation (dB,dA) is

 ||(dB A+B dA) C^(1/2)||F^2+2<BA C-D,dB dA>.

Its absolute value is at most

 [c(||A||op^2+||B||op^2)+||BA C-D||op]
 times (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2)
 <=[4Kc+(2Kc+ell)] (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2).

Here the first summand uses Cauchy-Schwarz on dB A+B dA; the cross term uses |<G,dB dA>|<=||G||op||dB||F||dA||F. Thus the Hessian operator norm on the segment is at most L. Taylor's theorem along that segment proves

 q_next<=q-eta||grad q||F^2+(L eta^2/2)||grad q||F^2
        <=q-(eta/2)||grad q||F^2.

In particular q_next<=q0. Telescoping the descent inequalities, including the proposed step, and using q>=0 yields

 sum_(j=0)^t eta^2||grad q_j||F^2<=2eta q0
 <=2q0/(1+2q0)<1.

Summing the imbalance increments now proves ||E_next-E0||F<=2eta q0<1. The product/factor bound therefore puts the endpoint back in the smaller ball of pair radius sqrt(K). This closes the induction without assuming a bound before proving descent on the required larger segment. The q0=0 case is included: both gradients vanish, the sequence is constant, and all inequalities still hold.

## Consequences and exact remaining gap

Telescoping for every finite horizon gives the infinite summability bound. A nonnegative summable sequence tends to zero, so the gradients vanish. Bounded finite-dimensional factor pairs have convergent subsequences; gradient continuity makes every subsequential limit critical. The running-minimum bound follows by averaging the finite sum. These statements do not require that the entire sequence converges to one point.

For B0=0 and a Gaussian A0, this provides an allowed positive step after observing the initialization, conditional on every full-row-rank design. It does not supply a single positive step independent of the unbounded Gaussian initializer. C013 shows that unconditional expected-limit risk with such an initialization-independent fixed step can diverge even at rank one.

Combining this bound with the already verified empirical strict-saddle landscape C010 is insufficient to conclude global optimization. One must additionally show that the specified zero/Gaussian initialization does not approach a nonglobal critical point, with all hypotheses of a saddle-avoidance theorem checked for its lower-dimensional initial support and step rule. Vanishing gradients do not establish that. Even convergence almost surely would not by itself justify passing to expected population risk; a failure-tail/integrability or finite-stopping argument is separately required. The usual full-ambient absolutely-continuous random-initialization theorem cannot simply be cited for the plane B0=0.

Independent reviewer audit and any novelty assessment remain pending. [Theorem \cite{mountford2005motion}, Theorem 1,  \cite{aggarwal2023asep}, Theorem 1.1 of arXiv:2512.19897, 'On the convoy of the ASEP speed process'] Let $Y_0\left(t\right)$ denote the position of the second class particle at time $t$ in the ASEP with step initial condition and a single second-class particle. Then
    \[
    \lim_{t \to \infty}\frac{Y_0\left(t\right)}{\left(1-q\right)t} \overset{\text{a.s.}}{=} U,
    \]
    where $U$ is a uniform random variable on $\left[-1,1\right]$. We define $U$ to be the speed of the second-class particle. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \cite{mountford2005motion}, Theorem 1,  \cite{aggarwal2023asep}, Theorem 1.1

[Lemma Truth lemma of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] Let $L \supseteq \textbf{FIK}$,
  then for any $x = (\Gamma_x, \Delta_x) \in W_L^*$ and any $\varphi \in \mathscr{L}_{\Box\Diamond}$,
  $x \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \varphi$ iff $\varphi \in \Gamma_x$.
  \begin{proof}
    We use an induction on the construction of $\varphi$.
    We shall only consider the cases for $\to$, $\Box$, and $\Diamond$, as the other cases are trivial.

    If $\varphi = \psi \to \chi$, then we shall prove it in both directions.
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[($\Rightarrow$)]
            Suppose $\psi \to \chi \notin \Gamma_x$, then by Proposition (prop:truth-lemma-imp-left of the paper),
            there is $x' = (\Gamma_x', \Delta_x') \in W_L^*$ such that $x \leq^* x'$, $\psi \in \Gamma_x'$, and $\chi \in \Delta_x'$.
            Here, $x' \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \psi$ and $x' \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \chi$ by the induction hypothesis.
            Therefore, $x \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \psi \to \chi$.
      \item[($\Leftarrow$)]
            Suppose $\psi \to \chi \in \Gamma_x$ and take any $x' = (\Gamma_x', \Delta_x') \in W_L^*$ such that $x \leq^* x' \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \psi$,
            then $\psi \in \Gamma_x'$ by the induction hypothesis, and $\psi \to \chi \in \Gamma_x \subseteq \Gamma_x'$ by the definition of $\leq^*$,
            so $\chi \in \Gamma_x'$ by Corollary (cor:saturation of the paper).
            Therefore, $x \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \psi \to \chi$.
    \end{itemize}

    If $\varphi = \Box \psi$, then we shall prove it in both directions.
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[($\Rightarrow$)]
            Suppose $\Box \psi \notin \Gamma_x$, then by Proposition (prop:truth-lemma-box-left of the paper),
            there are $x' = (\Gamma_x', \Delta_x') \in W_L^*$ and $y' = (\Gamma_y', \Delta_y') \in W_L^*$
            such that $x \leq^* x' \sqsubset^* y'$ and $\psi \notin \Gamma_y'$.
            Here, $y' \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \psi$ by the induction hypothesis.
            Therefore, $x \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \Box \psi$.
      \item[($\Leftarrow$)]
            Suppose $\Box \psi \in \Gamma_x$ and take any $x' = (\Gamma_x', \Delta_x'),\ y' = (\Gamma_y', \Delta_y') \in W_L^*$
            such that $x \leq^* x' \sqsubset^* y'$,
            then $\Box \psi \in \Gamma_x \subseteq \Gamma_x'$,
            then $\psi \in \Box^{-1} \Gamma_x' \subseteq \Gamma_y'$,
            so $y' \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \psi$ by the induction hypothesis.
            Therefore, $x \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \Box \psi$.
    \end{itemize}

    If $\varphi = \Diamond \psi$, then we shall prove it in both directions.
        \begin{itemize}
      \item[($\Rightarrow$)]
            Suppose $\Diamond \psi \notin \Gamma_x$, then $\Diamond \psi \in \Delta_x$ by maximality.
            Take any $y = (\Gamma_y, \Delta_y)$ such that $x \sqsubset^* y$,
            then $\psi \in \Diamond^{-1} \Delta_x \subseteq \Delta_y$ by definition,
            then $\psi \notin \Gamma_y$ by maximality,
            then $y \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \psi$ by the induction hypothesis,
            so $x \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \Diamond \psi$.
      \item[($\Leftarrow$)]
            Suppose $\Diamond \psi \in \Gamma_x$.
            Here, $(\Box^{-1} \Gamma_x \cup \set{ \psi }, \Diamond^{-1} \Delta_x)$ is $L$-consistent;
            as otherwise, there are finite $A \subseteq \Box^{-1} \Gamma_x$ and $B \subseteq \Diamond^{-1} \Delta_x$ such that
            $L \vdash \left(\bigwedge A \land \psi\right) \to \bigvee B$, then it contradicts $x$ being $L$-consistent by:
            \begin{center}
              \AxiomC{$L \vdash \left(\bigwedge A \land \psi\right) \to \bigvee B$}
              \UnaryInfC{$L \vdash \psi \to \left(\bigwedge A \to \bigvee B\right)$}
              \RightLabel{\scriptsize{$\textsf{M}_\Diamond$}}

[Proposition 12 of arXiv:2609.03112, '2609.03112'] Let $g$ be irrational and Diophantine of finite type.
For $r=1,2$, the values $\xi_g(z)$ with $z\in\Lambda_r\cap\cC$ have Poissonian
pair correlation of intensity $\pi/(3\sqrt3)$.  For $r=0$, the values with
$z\in\Lambda_0\cap\cC^+$ have Poissonian pair correlation of intensity
$\pi/(6\sqrt3)$.

body:
For complex matrices A (n by n) and B (m by m), S(X) = AX - XB on n by m matrices X, and the Frobenius separation is sep_F(A, B) = min over ||X||_F = 1 of ||AX - XB||_F. The equation AX - XB = C has a unique solution for every C if and only if spec A and spec B are disjoint, equivalently sep_F(A, B) > 0. Then ||X||_F <= ||C||_F / sep_F(A, B), and 1/sep_F(A, B) is exactly the largest ratio ||X||_F / ||C||_F over C != 0.

body:
[Proposition 19 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(n\ge2\).  Every tangent space at \(\xi\) is a metric soliton
flow with a distinguished probability measure.  Its time-\((-1)\) model
has the following properties.
\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Metric-flow conclusions.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(H\arabic*)},leftmargin=3em,
series=limitingpackage]
\item The regular locus \(\mathcal R\) is connected and dense,
\(d|_{\mathcal R}\) is its intrinsic length distance, and \(Z\) is a
complete locally compact length space equal to the metric completion of
\(\mathcal R\).
\item There is a smooth function \(f\) on \(\mathcal R\) for which
\begin{equation}
 \Rc_g+\nabla^2f=\frac12g\qquad\text{on }\mathcal R;
\end{equation}
the distinguished probability measure satisfies
\begin{equation}
 d\mathfrak m=(4\pi)^{-n}e^{-f}\,dV_g\quad\text{on }\mathcal R,
 \qquad \mathfrak m(Z\setminus\mathcal R)=0,
 \qquad \mathfrak m(Z)=1,
\end{equation}
and \(\mathfrak m\) has finite second moment.
\item The tangent space is an exact self-similar metric soliton flow.
On regular convergence charts, in time-compatible gauges, the rescaled
metrics and distinguished densities converge smoothly to \(g\) and the
positive density in \eqref{sp:eq:measure}.
\item For every compact \(K\subset Z\) and every \(p\in(2,4)\), the
zero extension of \(r_{\rm Rm}\) is one-Lipschitz and
\begin{equation}
 \Vol_g\bigl(\{r_{\rm Rm}<\varepsilon\}\cap K\cap\mathcal R\bigr)
 \le C_{K,p}\varepsilon^p,
 \qquad 0<\varepsilon<1;
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{K\"ahler conclusions.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(H\arabic*)},leftmargin=3em,
resume=limitingpackage]
\item The regular soliton \((\mathcal R,g,J)\) is K\"ahler, \(J\) is
parallel and time invariant, and the rescaled complex structures converge
smoothly to \(J\) on regular convergence charts.
\item If \(n=2\), then \(Z\) is a K\"ahler orbifold and
\(\Sing Z\) consists of isolated orbifold points.
\end{enumerate}

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Complex-analytic conclusions.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(H\arabic*)},leftmargin=3em,
resume=limitingpackage]
\item The space \(Z\) is a normal klt complex space.  Its analytic and
metric topologies agree, and its analytic and metric regular loci
coincide.  The regular K\"ahler form extends locally across \(\Sing Z\)
as a positive current with bounded potential.  Every point has a local
closed analytic embedding \(V\hookrightarrow\Omega_V\subset\C^L\) such
that, on \(V\cap\mathcal R\),
\begin{equation}
 \omega_g\ge c_V\omega_{\C^L}|_V.
\end{equation}
\item The function \(f\) extends uniquely to a locally Lipschitz function
on \(Z\).  The flow of \(\nabla f\) is complete, preserves
\(\mathcal R\), and extends to a one-parameter group of biholomorphisms
of \(Z\).
\end{enumerate}

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author_checked_criterion_controlled_against_the_papers_own_deterministic_benchmark] This is the proved range of the campaign answer to the first case (w_1 = |x|^delta) of the open question in Remark 5.3(ii) of arXiv:2607.07410. Let Q denote the law of a two-sided, nontrivial, (r_0,alpha)-semi-selfsimilar Levy process V with cadlag paths and V(0)=0, where alpha is in (0,2), Q(V(1)>0)>0 and Q(V(1)<0)>0. Strictly alpha-stable processes are included. Let nu be its Levy measure and suppose nu((-infinity,0)) > 0. Let delta > 1. Put w(x) = |x|^delta + V(x) and mu^w(dx) = exp(-w(x))dx. Let L^w be the self-adjoint operator associated with the closure on L^2(R,mu^w) of E^w(f,f) = (1/2) integral_R |f'(x)|^2 exp(-w(x))dx, f in C_c^infinity(R). For any fixed x_0 > 0 define B_l(x) = (integral_{x_0}^x exp(w(y))dy)(integral_x^infinity exp(-w(y))dy). Then, Q-almost surely: limsup_{x->infinity} B_l(x) = infinity, and this holds with x_0 replaced by any R; the bottom lambda_ess of the essential spectrum of -L^w is 0; and the semigroup exp(tL^w) is noncompact. For 0 < delta <= 1/alpha the same conclusion is the paper's Proposition 5.2. The record's claim for alpha in (1,2) and 1/alpha < delta <= 1 is not covered by the written proof. This is an unrefereed campaign result.

[Lemma of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The localization ${\mathpalette\ulhelper{{\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{lvl}\to{\mathpalette\ulhelper{\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\textup{gl}$ has a fully faithful right adjoint.
    \begin{proof}
        If $G$ is any compact Lie group, then Proposition~(prop:L-gl-Bousfield of the paper) shows that the localization functor ${\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\text{$G$-lvl}={\mathpalette\ulhelper{{\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{lvl}(\mathbb B{G})\to{\mathpalette\ulhelper{\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\textup{gl}(\mathbb B{G})={\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\text{$G$-gl}$ admits a right adjoint, which is fully faithful with essential image given by the $G$-global $\Omega$-spectra. It therefore only remains to verify the Beck--Chevalley condition. By full faithfulness of the right adjoints, this reduces to proving that the restriction functors preserve the essential images, which is clear from the definition of $G$-global $\Omega$-spectra. 
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 39 (Composition and interpolation) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] Schatten-stable maps are closed under composition, and
\begin{equation}

 \kappa_r(\Psi\circ\Phi)
 \le\kappa_r(\Psi)\kappa_r(\Phi).
\end{equation}
More generally, let
\[
 1\le r_0<r<r_1\le\infty,
 \qquad
 \frac1r=\frac{1-\theta}{r_0}+\frac\theta{r_1},
 \qquad 0<\theta<1.
\]
If $\kappa_{r_0}(\Phi)$ and $\kappa_{r_1}(\Phi)$ are finite, then
\begin{equation}

 \kappa_r(\Phi)
 \le \kappa_{r_0}(\Phi)^{1-\theta}
      \kappa_{r_1}(\Phi)^\theta.
\end{equation}
In particular, interpolation applies on both sides of the Hilbert endpoint;
for $2<r<\infty$ it gives
$\kappa_r(\Phi)\le
\kappa_2(\Phi)^{2/r}\kappa_\infty(\Phi)^{1-2/r}$.

Bradley, Basic properties of strong mixing conditions: a survey and some open questions (arXiv:math/0511078), Question 7 (Section 4.2, p. 19) asks: given an arbitrary nonincreasing sequence (b_1, b_2, ...) in [0,1], is there a strictly stationary sequence X with phi(n) = b_n for all n >= 1? Our result (id D0035, 2026-09-08): NO, refuted in one line from a result Bradley himself quotes - if phi(n) < 1/2 for some n >= 1 then X is phi-mixing, i.e. phi(n) tends to 0. The constant sequence b_n = 1/4 is nonincreasing and lies in [0,1] and gives phi(1) = 1/4 < 1/2, which forces phi(n) to tend to 0 and contradicts phi(n) = 1/4 for every n; the same argument rules out every sequence that dips below 1/2 without tending to zero. Verification as the source words it: this one came from the intake agent rather than from the author, and was verified by pulling the archived source, reading Question 7 at the stated locator word for word, and locating the quoted dichotomy in the survey. Honest scope, in the memo's own words: the literal general form is refuted from the survey's own material, not that a question its author believed open has been settled.
X strictly stationary
phi the uniform mixing coefficient as defined in the survey

[Definition def:extended.filtered.gaussian of arXiv:2604.22453, 'Adapted Wasserstein Barycenters of Gaussian Processes'] Let
\[
\mathscr L_K(T,d):=\{\mathbf L = (\mathbf{L}_{t,s})_{s,t = 1}^T \in (\mathbb{R}^{d\times Kd})^{T \times T}: \mathbf L_{t,s}=0\textup{ whenever }s>t\},
\]
where each $\mathbf{L}_{t,s}$ has $K$ column blocks $\mathbf{L}_{t,s}^{k} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$. For $a \in \mathbb{R}^{Td}$ and $\mathbf{L} \in \mathscr{L}_K(T, d)$, define the filtered process
\[
\mathbb{G}_K^{a,\mathbf L}:=\left(\mathbb{R}^{TKd},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{TKd}),\mathcal{N}_{TKd}(0,I),\mathbb{F}^{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}},X=a+\mathbf {L}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right),
\]
where $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}=(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t)_{t=1}^T$, $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t=(\epsilon_t^1,\ldots,\epsilon_t^K)$, is the canonical process and $\mathbb{F}^{\boldsymbol\epsilon}$ is the filtration generated by $\boldsymbol\epsilon$. Explicitly, for each $t$ we have
\begin{equation} 
X_t = a_t + \sum_{s = 1}^t \mathbf{L}_{t,s} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_s = a_t + \sum_{s = 1}^t \sum_{k = 1}^K \mathbf{L}_{t,s}^{k} \epsilon_s^k. 
\end{equation}
We call $\mathbb{G}_K^{a,\mathbf L}$ an ensemble filtered Gaussian process and denote the corresponding space by $\mathcal{FG}_K(T,d)$, and its $\mathcal{AW}_2$-completion by $\mathrm{FG}_K(T,d)$. Letting $K=1$ recovers the standard filtered Gaussian process.
title: Ensemble filtered Gaussian process

[Lemma l:markfnspin of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Consider the marked point  process  $\tilde{\mathcal{P}} = \sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}\delta_{(x,U(x))}$
where $U(x)$ are i.i.d. uniform random variables on $[0,1]$. Consider the  spin-marking function $\xi$ given in~(equation e.spin-marking of the paper), related to the Gibbs specification~(equation eqn:gibbs of the paper) via~(equation e.Gibbs-partition of the paper).
For any bounded Borel set $B\subset\mathbb{R}^d$, jointly the values of this function 
$\{\xi(\tilde{x}, \tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n \cap B)\}_{x \in \mathcal{P}\cap B}$, 
given a realization of $\mathcal{P}\cap B$,  are distributed as the spin configuration 
$\{V_x(\Psi(\mathcal{P} \cap B))\}_{x \in \mathcal{P}\cap B}$ under this Gibbs model. Further, if $B_1 \cap B_2 = \emptyset$ then the two collections of marks $\{\xi(x,\mathcal{P} \cap B_1)\}_{x \in \mathcal{P}\cap B_1}$ and $\{\xi(x,\mathcal{P} \cap B_2)\}_{x \in \mathcal{P}\cap B_2}$ are conditionally independent given $\mathcal{P}$. 
Moreover, if the mapping $\mu \mapsto \Psi(\mu)$ is translation invariant, 
then the marking function can also be constructed to be translation invariant.
title: Marking function for spin systems
Continuity for truncations

[Lemma 33 (Finite quotients of a circle collapse) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(\Gamma\) be a finite group acting on a compact space \(\widehat X\),
and let \(\widehat d_t\), \(t\geq T\), be a family of
\(\Gamma\)-invariant length metrics that is continuous in the uniform norm on
\(\widehat X\times\widehat X\).  Put
\(X_t=(\widehat X,\widehat d_t)/\Gamma\).  Suppose that
\[
        (\widehat X,\widehat d_t)\longrightarrow C_L
\]
in the Gromov--Hausdorff sense, where \(C_L\) is a metric circle of length
\(L>0\).  Then \(X_t\) has a full Gromov--Hausdorff limit.  The limit is
either a metric circle of length \(L/m\) or a closed interval of length
\(L/(2m)\), for some positive integer \(m\) dividing \(|\Gamma|\).  If every
limiting action of \(\Gamma\) on \(C_L\) is orientation preserving, then the
limit is a circle.

THE NOVELTY CLAIM IS DOWNGRADED to NEW IN THIS SPECIFIC FORM, NOT NEW IN KIND, on a literature pass run as a declared debt: (i) Chatterjee, 'The universal relation between scaling exponents in first-passage percolation', Annals of Math 177 (2013), arXiv 1105.4566, proves chi = 2 xi - 1 and states it is universal, independent of dimension AND of the law of the weights under moment assumptions - so distribution-independence of FPP exponents is an established theme; (ii) Damron-Hanson-Sosoe, arXiv 1306.1197 (PTRF), prove sublinear variance for GENERAL distributions directly (absolutely continuous, discrete, singular continuous, mixtures) under only 2 + log moments via a geometric average replacing BKS's randomised starting point - so the field gets distributional generality with NO transfer argument, under a moment condition strictly WEAKER than the bounded support the continuity lemma needs. The transfer principle is therefore narrower than the state of the art on the axis it trades in. It is not vacuous - the target transferred is the POLYNOMIAL n^{1-eps} that nobody has for any single law - but it must never be presented as a new idea about universality. chi = 1/3 UNMOVED.

[Lemma 20 (Pointwise fixed-fiber improvement) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Fix \(\delta_0>0\), \(0<\lambda_{\mathrm{p}}<\delta_0/10\), and
\(\theta_{\max}>0\).  There are constants
\[
        0<\theta<\theta_{\max},\qquad
        \beta_{\mathrm{fib}}>0,\qquad
        \eps_{\mathrm{fib}}>0,
\]
with the following property.

Let \(q\) be a metric on a closed three-manifold \(M\) such that
\begin{equation}
        \diam(M,q)\geq\delta_0.
\end{equation}
Let \(\pi:M\to S^1\) be a torus fibration, and let \(r\) be an invariant metric for \(\pi\).  Suppose that
\begin{equation}
        \|q-r\|_{C^1(M,r)}<\beta_{\mathrm{fib}},
        \qquad
        d_{\TT^2}(r)\leq\theta.
\end{equation}
Suppose also that \(M\) has a second torus fibration
\(\pi_B:M\to S_B^1\) and an invariant metric \(h_B\)
for \(\pi_B\) such that
\begin{equation}
        \|h_B-q\|_{C^1(M,q)}<\eps_{\mathrm{fib}},
        \qquad
        \diam_q(F_B)\leq\eps_{\mathrm{fib}},
\end{equation}
for every \(\pi_B\)-fiber \(F_B\).  Then \(\pi_B\) is fiber-equivalent to \(\pi\), and
\begin{equation}
        d_{\TT^2}(r)<\frac{\theta}{2},
        \qquad
        L(S^1,r_{S^1})\geq\lambda_{\mathrm{p}}.
\end{equation}
title: Pointwise fixed-fiber improvement

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:90ca2cb818dbaf98d544c187986a9a2cd71ebbb38231c3dc56dc8c54b98b0454","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/90/90ca2cb818dbaf98d544c187986a9a2cd71ebbb38231c3dc56dc8c54b98b0454.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:6cc85f6627aee7f83c3d1d43848b94925a2ddc088a5d0c34737969270e49bb92","bundle_entry_key":"i0005-c19","bundle_id":"population.i0005-correlation-energy-and-active-moments-006","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"parking and comparison fields","draft":"w661/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.particle-hole:particle-hole-signed-susceptibility-conservation-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# I0005-C19 v1: conserved signed susceptibility forces correlation mass

Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty: KNOWN stationary divergence/conservation
method; UNCHECKED this exact parking formulation and density-normalized
consequence. This concerns the actual source process, not a Gaussian proxy.

For the sparse critical synchronous particle-hole law on Z^d, d>=1,
P(eta=1)=P(eta=-1)=p, P(eta=0)=1-2p, 0<p<1/2, define
S_t(x)=A_t(x)-H_t(x), h_t=E A_t(0)=E H_t(0), r=p/(1-2p).
At each finite time t,

    sum_z Cov(S_t(0),S_t(z))=Var eta(0)=2p.

The sum is finite by finite propagation. Using C18's active-count bound,

    Var S_t(0)<= (2+r)h_t,
    sum_z |Cov(S_t(0),S_t(z))| / Var S_t(0)
                         >=2p/[(2+r)h_t].

The denominator is positive: otherwise stationarity would make all
covariances zero, contradicting the conserved sum. In particular as the
source's h_t tends to zero, normalized signed correlation mass diverges.
This does not imply that the hole-only Palm count in C9 diverges: mixed
and active-active correlations also enter this sum rule.

## 1. Pathwise current divergence

Let J_i(x) be net particle transport through time t across the edge
x to x+e_i: departures in that direction minus departures across the
same edge in reverse. Settlement removes one active particle and one
hole at the same site, leaving their signed difference unchanged. Thus
the exact pathwise charge identity is

    S_t(x)=eta(x)+D_t(x),
    D_t(x)=sum_i[J_i(x-e_i)-J_i(x)].

At fixed finite t the source's finite propagation makes S_t and each
current a function of finitely many independent initial site/noise
variables in a bounded neighborhood. The bounded sparse initial values
also give bounded local particle counts and currents at this horizon.
Consequently they have finite second moments, and any covariance sums
below have finite support. No limiting interchange or summability
assumption at infinite time is used.

Mean stationarity makes E D_t(x)=0, and E eta(x)=0, so E S_t(x)=0.

## 2. Telescoping the covariance sum

For any of these local stationary fields X, summing a covariance with a
divergence in its second entry gives

    sum_z Cov(X(0),D_t(z))
      =sum_i sum_z [Cov(X(0),J_i(z-e_i))-Cov(X(0),J_i(z))]=0.

The cancellation is a finite-support reindexing. Similarly stationarity
gives

    sum_z Cov(D_t(0),eta(z))
      =sum_i sum_z [Cov(J_i(-e_i),eta(z))-Cov(J_i(0),eta(z))]
      =sum_i sum_z [Cov(J_i(0),eta(z+e_i))-Cov(J_i(0),eta(z))]=0.

Apply these identities to S_t=eta+D_t:

    sum_z Cov(S_t(0),S_t(z))
      =sum_z Cov(eta(0),eta(z))
       +sum_z Cov(D_t(0),eta(z))
       +sum_z Cov(S_t(0),D_t(z))
      =Var eta(0)=2p,

because the initial excesses are independent across sites.

## 3. One-point variance and normalized mass

A_t H_t=0 at each site and H_t^2=H_t. Therefore

    Var S_t(0)=E S_t(0)^2=E A_t(0)^2+h_t
                                      <=(2+r)h_t

by C18. The absolute covariance sum is at least the absolute value of
the signed sum, which is 2p. Divide by the positive variance and use its
upper bound to obtain the assertion.

## What this excludes

For fixed p at sufficiently late times, the full signed field cannot
have independent site values: that would make the covariance sum equal
to its vanishing one-point variance. The argument does not exclude
approximately Poisson local hole geometry, or independence after a
specified scaling with correlations retained at other scales. It does
not supply a closer-hole probability estimate or decide I0005.

Sources: Bou-Rabee--Panagiotis arXiv:2609.02820v1, conservation (19),
critical mean identity (47), source finite propagation; I0005-C18 v1
for the active-label factorial bound. Current reindexings are proved

PROOF (UNAUDITED), w741-T422-C06 v1. Not independently checked.
# T422 Target 2: a finite-sample-span upper confidence bound

Status: proof (unaudited), C06 v1. The constants below are explicit but the
bound is not asserted to have the sharp epsilon exponent of a typical noise
scale. The fixed-time theorem does not depend on C02 or C03; its final optional
optimal-step corollary inherits their unaudited status.

## Statement

Use the fresh Gaussian online least-squares model: H=diag(h_j),
h_j=j^(-alpha), alpha>1, deterministic initial errors satisfying
h_j e_0,j^2=j^(-gamma), gamma>1. Gaussian L2 predictions are used if the
coefficient vector is not in ordinary l2, as explained in model_conventions.md.
Labels have independent centered noise of finite variance sigma2>=0.
Each of t>=1 deterministic steps uses B>=1 independent fresh samples,
B an integer. A fixed positive step suffices. More generally, the proof
only requires that every update be a finite linear combination of that
step's input vectors, that the Bt inputs remain mutually independent with
law N(0,H), and that expected risk at t is finite.

For ell=1,2 define

    V(e)=sum_j h_j e_j^2,
    W_(ell+1)(e)=sum_j h_j^(ell+1)e_j^2,
    v_t=E V(e_t), Z_r=zeta(r),
    R_ell(e)=1+Z_(ell alpha)(V(e)+sigma2)/W_(ell+1)(e).

These are the single-example instantaneous noise scales: ell=1 is unweighted,
ell=2 is Hessian-weighted. Fix confidence parameter theta in (0,1), and put

    K=Bt, d=K+1,
    A_d=sum_(j=1)^d e_0,j^2/h_j=sum_(j=1)^d j^(2alpha-gamma)>0,
    L_den=h_d^(ell+2) A_d theta^2/(16d)>0.

Then

    P(W_(ell+1)(e_t)>=L_den)>=1-theta/2.                  (S1)

Consequently, with probability at least 1-theta, e_t!=0 and

    1+Z_(ell alpha) <= R_ell(e_t)
      <=1+[16d Z_(ell alpha)/(h_d^(ell+2)A_d theta^2)]

The probability of e_t=0 is zero. If t is a finite first EXPECTED-risk

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:530b3407cc440bb66ad26e9fbdb5a3d335df5cfbc4caa8bd6dc24ed288f59636","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/53/530b3407cc440bb66ad26e9fbdb5a3d335df5cfbc4caa8bd6dc24ed288f59636.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:2bd8b9e6abc4f8fa035f6be7c61fd833cd181cd8922fe129b0678ea163cee574","bundle_entry_key":"t422-random-span-upper-confidence","bundle_id":"population.t422-random-span-upper-confidence-004","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"stochastic optimization","draft":"w741/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.stochastic:gaussian-sgd-sample-span-instantaneous-noise-upper-confidence-bound","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T422 Target 2: a finite-sample-span upper confidence bound

Status: proof (unaudited), C06 v1. The constants below are explicit but the
bound is not asserted to have the sharp epsilon exponent of a typical noise
scale. The fixed-time theorem does not depend on C02 or C03; its final optional
optimal-step corollary inherits their unaudited status.

## Statement

Use the fresh Gaussian online least-squares model: H=diag(h_j),
h_j=j^(-alpha), alpha>1, deterministic initial errors satisfying
h_j e_0,j^2=j^(-gamma), gamma>1. Gaussian L2 predictions are used if the
coefficient vector is not in ordinary l2, as explained in model_conventions.md.
Labels have independent centered noise of finite variance sigma2>=0.
Each of t>=1 deterministic steps uses B>=1 independent fresh samples,
B an integer. A fixed positive step suffices. More generally, the proof
only requires that every update be a finite linear combination of that
step's input vectors, that the Bt inputs remain mutually independent with
law N(0,H), and that expected risk at t is finite.

For ell=1,2 define

    V(e)=sum_j h_j e_j^2,
    W_(ell+1)(e)=sum_j h_j^(ell+1)e_j^2,
    v_t=E V(e_t), Z_r=zeta(r),
    R_ell(e)=1+Z_(ell alpha)(V(e)+sigma2)/W_(ell+1)(e).

These are the single-example instantaneous noise scales: ell=1 is unweighted,
ell=2 is Hessian-weighted. Fix confidence parameter theta in (0,1), and put

    K=Bt, d=K+1,
    A_d=sum_(j=1)^d e_0,j^2/h_j=sum_(j=1)^d j^(2alpha-gamma)>0,
    L_den=h_d^(ell+2) A_d theta^2/(16d)>0.

Then

    P(W_(ell+1)(e_t)>=L_den)>=1-theta/2.                  (S1)

Consequently, with probability at least 1-theta, e_t!=0 and

    1+Z_(ell alpha) <= R_ell(e_t)
      <=1+[16d Z_(ell alpha)/(h_d^(ell+2)A_d theta^2)]
                   [2v_t/theta+sigma2].                  (S2)

The probability of e_t=0 is zero. If t is a finite first EXPECTED-risk
hit v_t<=epsilon Z_gamma, substitute that upper bound for v_t in (S2).
The hitting index is deterministic here; a realized-risk stopping time
requires an additional argument.

## Finite-coordinate sample-span separation

List the K input vectors used up to time t as x_1,...,x_K. Whatever the
update coefficients, coordinatewise the error has the form

    e_t=e_0+sum_(i=1)^K b_i x_i,                           (S3)

where the random coefficients can depend on all observed data. No independence
of the b_i from the inputs is asserted or needed.

On the first d coordinates set

    a_j=e_0,j/sqrt(h_j),
    Z_(j,i)=x_i,j/sqrt(h_j),
    D=diag(h_j^((ell+2)/2)).

All dK entries of Z are independent standard real Gaussians. The vector of
weighted error coordinates is exactly

    (h_j^((ell+1)/2)e_t,j)_(j<=d)=D(a+Zb).

The smallest singular value of D is h_d^((ell+2)/2). Since a+Zb differs
from a by an element of col(Z), pointwise

    W_(ell+1)(e_t)
      >= ||D(a+Zb)||^2
      >= h_d^(ell+2) dist(a,col(Z))^2.                    (S4)

This uses neither a conditional product bound nor an assumed distribution
for the data-dependent coefficients.

## A uniform random line and its explicit small-ball bound

The d by d-1 standard Gaussian matrix has full column rank almost surely.
For example, its first d-1 rows have a determinant which is a nonzero
polynomial; the zero set has Lebesgue measure zero, by induction on the
number of variables and Fubini. Their joint density is absolutely continuous.

Its orthogonal complement is consequently a random line. Orthogonal
invariance of the matrix law makes this line uniformly distributed: the
unique orthogonally invariant line distribution is the image of uniform
spherical measure under the map taking a unit vector to its line. A randomly
chosen sign therefore lifts it to a uniform spherical vector U. Equivalently,
U has the law g/||g|| for d independent standard Gaussians. Orthogonal
invariance and a rotation of the fixed nonzero a give

    dist(a,col(Z))^2 has law ||a||^2 U_1^2=A_d U_1^2.     (S5)

For completeness the needed spherical small-ball constant can be bounded
without gamma-function asymptotics. Let S=sum_(j=2)^d g_j^2, independent of
g_1. For 0<q<=1/2,

    {|U_1|<=q} = {|g_1|<=q sqrt(S)/sqrt(1-q^2)}.

The one-dimensional Gaussian density is at most 1/sqrt(2pi), so
P(|g_1|<=z)<=sqrt(2/pi)z<=z for z>=0. Conditioning on S, then applying
Cauchy--Schwarz and 1/sqrt(1-q^2)<=2, yields

    P(|U_1|<=q)<=2q E sqrt(S)<=2q sqrt(d-1)<=2q sqrt(d).  (S6)

Choose q=theta/(4sqrt(d))<1/2. The right side of (S6) is theta/2.
Combining (S4)--(S5) proves (S1). In particular, for every theta>0 the
probability of W_(ell+1)(e_t)=0 is at most theta/2, hence is zero.

## Numerator and confidence bound

Markov's inequality gives V(e_t)<=2v_t/theta with probability at least
1-theta/2 when v_t>0. If v_t=0, nonnegativity gives V(e_t)=0 almost surely;
in fact (S1) excludes this case under the stated nonzero initialization and
finite-sample assumptions. No use of independence is made when intersecting
the numerator and denominator events: a union bound gives probability at
least 1-theta.

On that intersection the denominator is at least L_den, giving the upper
bound in (S2). For every nonzero error, W_(ell+1)(e)<=V(e) because 0<h_j<=1.
Thus the displayed expression for R_ell also gives its lower bound in (S2).
The conditional Gaussian covariance identity remains valid for the finite-risk
Gaussian-series model; conditioning fixes a finite-H-norm error, and its
prediction is an L2 Gaussian scalar. This is the same model convention as C02.

## Explicit operational-knee corollary, conditional on C02 and C03

At an exactly optimal constant step, set t=S*(B,epsilon), and use C02's
explicit t<=c_plus Phi(B,epsilon). Define the integer

    D_max=B ceil(c_plus Phi(B,epsilon))+1 >=d.

Since A_d>=1 and h_d=d^(-alpha), (S2) implies with probability >=1-theta

    R_ell(e_t)
      <=1+16 Z_(ell alpha) D_max^(1+alpha(ell+2)) theta^(-2)
                   [2epsilon Z_gamma/theta+sigma2].       (S7)

Using C03's L_J J_epsilon<=Bcrit_op<=U_J J_epsilon then gives

    (1+Z_(ell alpha))/(U_J J_epsilon)
      <=R_ell(e_t)/Bcrit_op
      <=[the right side of (S7)]/(L_J J_epsilon).         (S8)

All constants and cutoffs are explicit functions of alpha,gamma,B,epsilon,
sigma2,theta and C02's displayed constants. The power-law exponent gamma maps
to the two beta conventions as specified in C02. Equations (S7)--(S8) are
conditional on the unaudited C02/C03 results, not independent validations of them.

## Scope, checks, and the unpaid step

The numerator Markov step costs theta^(-1) and the random-line denominator
costs theta^(-2). More seriously, retaining only Bt+1 coordinates introduces
a large factor D_max^(1+alpha(ell+2)). This bound provides an explicit
high-probability comparison for the full finite-risk exponent range, not
a matching exponent-level calibration or a sharp upper tail. The next unpaid
step is to exploit the actual SGD coefficients or effective dimension to
remove this raw sample-count loss.

The span identity applies to data-dependent update coefficients; independence
is needed only for the fresh Gaussian input matrix. Nonzero deterministic
initialization, d>K, positive selected h_j, deterministic t and finite
v_t are all used. If d<=K, the random span fills the selected coordinates
almost surely and this particular lower-bound route collapses. If the inputs
are selected adversarially to span a, the distance in (S4) is zero.

Finite exact rational checks and a scalar confidence-union calculation are
recorded separately; they do not certify the random-line distribution or the
infinite-dimensional theorem. No independent PASS or whole-theorem Lean
certificate is asserted.

Provenance: the conditional covariance conventions are from the settled
T422 diagnostics and McCandlish et al., arXiv:1812.06162, equations (2.8)--(2.9).
The elementary Gaussian projection and small-ball facts are derived above;
they are not claimed as new standalone probability theorems.

[Prop choquet inegral properties of arXiv:2411.00663, 'Ergodicity and Mixing of invariant capacities and applications'] Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mu)$ be a capacity space, $f$ and $g$ be two $\mathcal{F}$-measurable functions. Then
	\begin{longlist}
		\item (Positive homogeneity): $\int_\Omega\alpha fd\mu=\alpha \int_\Omega fd\mu$ for each $\alpha \geq 0$.
		\item (Translation invariance): $\int_\Omega (f+\alpha 1_{\Omega})d\mu=\int_\Omega fd\mu+\alpha$ for each $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$.
		\item (Monotonicity): $\int_\Omega fd\mu \geq \int_\Omega gd\mu$ if $f \geq g$.
	\end{longlist} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop choquet inegral properties of arXiv:2411.00663

[Proposition 29 of arXiv:2506.10494, 'Geometric Jensen-Shannon Divergence Between Gaussian Measures On Hilbert Space'] [\cite{Minh2024:FisherRaoGaussian}, Proposition 8]
	
	Let $\mu_0 = \Ncal(m_0, C_0)$ be fixed, with the associated white noise mapping $W:\Hcal \mapto \Lcal^2(\Hcal,\mu_0)$.
	Assume that $T \in \Sym(\Hcal) \cap \Tr(\Hcal)$, with eigenvalues $\{\alpha_k\}_{k \in \Nbb}$ and
	corresponding orthonormal eigenvectors $\{\phi_k\}_{k \in \Nbb}$. 	Let $P_N = \sum_{j=1}^Ne_j \otimes e_j$, with $\{e_j\}_{j\in \Nbb}$ being the orthonormal eigenvectors of $C_0$. Then in the $\Lcal^2(\Hcal,\mu_0)$ sense,
	
	
	

	
	\begin{align}
		&\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}{\alpha_k}W^2_{\phi_k}(x)
		=\lim_{N \approach \infty}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}{\alpha_k}W^2_{P_N\phi_k}
		\\
		
		
		
		& = \lim_{N \approach \infty}\la C_0^{-1/2}P_N(x-m_0), TC_0^{-1/2}P_N(x-m_0)\ra
		\\
		&\doteq\la C_0^{-1/2}(x-m_0), TC_0^{-1/2}(x-m_0)\ra.
	\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 29 of arXiv:2506.10494

body:
[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2506.10522, 'On the Law of the Iterated Logarithm for $m$-dependent stationary random variables under s'] Suppose that  $\{X_1,\ldots, X_n\}$ is a sequence  of independent random variables
on $\sles$. Set
$A_n(p,y)=\sum_{i=1}^n\mbE[(X_i^+\wedge y )^p]$ and
$ \breve{B}_{n,y}=\sum_{i=1}^n \mbE[(X_i\wedge y)^2]$.   Then  for all $p\ge 2$, $x,y>0$, $0<\delta\le 1$,
\begin{align}
    & \hV\Big( \max_{k\le n}  \sum_{i=1}^k(X_i-\bE[X_i])\ge x\Big)
    \le    \hV\big(\max_{k\le n} X_k> y \big)
    +\exp\left\{-\frac{x^2}{2(xy+\breve{B}_{n,y})   }\right\}.
    
\end{align}
and
\begin{align}
& \hV\Big( \max_{k\le n}  \sum_{i=1}^k(X_i-\bE[X_i])\ge x\Big) \nonumber\\
\le &  \hV\big(\max_{k\le n} X_k> y \big)
  +2\exp\{p^p\}\Big\{\frac{A_n(p,y)}{y^p} \Big\}^{\frac{\delta x}{10y}}
+\exp\left\{-\frac{x^2}{2\breve{B}_{n,y}(1+\delta)   }\right\}.
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 10 of arXiv:2506.10522

[Cor Cor_x4 of arXiv:2606.22183, 'Expected loss of quasi-arithmetic means of exchangeable random variables'] Let $I\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be a nonempty open interval, $f:I\to\mathbb{R}$ be a continuous and strictly increasing function, and let $(\xi_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables with values in $I$
 such that $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}((f(\xi_1))^4)<\infty$.
Further, let $L:I\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function such that the function $L\circ f^{-1}: f(I)\to\mathbb{R}$ is strongly $\alpha$-convex,
where $\alpha:(f(I)-f(I))\to\mathbb{R}_+$, $\alpha(x):=x^4$, $x\in (f(I)-f(I))$, and $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}(\vert L(\xi_1)\vert)<\infty$.
Then
 \begin{itemize}
  \item[(i)] $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\big(L\big( \mathscr{A}_n^{f}(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n) \big)\big)\in[-\infty,\infty)$, $n\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}$,
  \item[(ii)] for each $n\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}$,
          \begin{align*}
               &\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\big(L\big( \mathscr{A}_n^{f}(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n) \big)\big)\\
               &\qquad \leqslant \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\big(L\big( \mathscr{A}_{n-1}^{f}(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{n-1}) \big)\big) 
                 - \frac{1}{(n-1)^3n^3} \Big( (n^2-3n+3) M_4 + 3(2n-3) M_2^2 \Big),
           \end{align*}
           where $M_k := \operatorname{\mathbb{E}} ( ( f(\xi_1) - \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}(f(\xi_1)) )^k )$, $k\in\{2,4\}$.
 \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Cor Cor_x4 of arXiv:2606.22183

body:
[Lemma 26 of arXiv:2604.07207, 'Mixing times of step-reinforced random walks'] Let $\tilde{S}$ be the lazy simple random walk on $G=(\ZZ_2^d,+)$ with step distribution $\mu$ given in Theorem \ref{slowhycu} starting from $\tilde{S}_0=e_G$, and let $S$ be its step-reinforced version with reinforcement parameter $\alpha \in (0,1)$, in particular, the step distribution of $S$ is also $\mu$. Then for any $y\geq 0$ and $n \geq 1$ and $\delta \in (0,1)$, one has 
    $$
\PP(W(S_n) \geq y) \leq \PP(W(\tilde{S}_{n_{\alpha,\delta}}) \geq y) + C_0 e^{-C n},
    $$
    for some $C_0= C_0(\alpha,\delta)$ and $C=C(\alpha,\delta)$.
title: Lemma 26 of arXiv:2604.07207

[Lemma 16 (Base length and fiber diameter control diameter) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(h\) be an invariant metric for a torus
fibration \(\pi:M\to S^1\), with quotient metric \(h_{S^1}\).  Let \(g\) be
another metric satisfying \(g\leq B h\); no invariance is assumed for \(g\).  If every \(\pi\)-fiber has
\(g\)-diameter at most \(d_f\), then
\[
        \diam(M,g)\leq B^{1/2}L(S^1,h_{S^1})/2+d_f.
\]
In particular, if \(d_{\TT^2}(h)\leq d\), then
\[
        \diam(M,g)\leq B^{1/2}\bigl(L(S^1,h_{S^1})/2+d\bigr).
\]

[Propn PR4 of arXiv:2509.20657, 'Scaling limit for Brownian motions \\ on the $l$-level Sierpinski gaskets: \\ The fractal '] If $f_l$ is in $L^2(\mathrm{SG}(l), \mu^l)$, then $P^{l}_{\tau^l t}f_l$ is almost-surely equal to a function that is H\"older continuous. Specifically, for this version of $P^{l}_{\tau^l t}f_l$, it holds that
\[\left|P^{l}_{\tau^l t}f_l (x)-P^{l}_{\tau^l t}f_l (y)\right|\leq Ct^{-(1+d/2)}\left(|x-y|\vee l^{-1}\right)^{\gamma} \|f_l\|_2,\qquad\forall x,y\in\mathrm{SG}(l),\:t\in[2l^{-2},1],\]
where $\gamma$ is the constant of Proposition (PR3 of the paper) and $C$ is a constant independent of all the other variables.

\begin{equation*}
 p\geq c_4,

 0<\sigma\leq\min\left\{\frac12,c_5p^{-1/2}\right\},

 \int_{M_t}f_+^p\,d\mu
 \leq\int_{M_0}f_+^p\,d\mu
 +C(n,\alpha,\eta,\sigma,p)|M_0|t.
\end{equation}
The constant is independent of $\kappa$ and $T$.

[Lem 6 of arXiv:2606.03661, '2606.03661'] Let $\sideset{_1^{}}{_1^{}}{\operatorname{\mathfrak{F}}}(a;b;z)$ be the
$G$-hypergeometric function of type $(1,1)$, 
\begin{equation}

 \sideset{_1^{}}{_1^{}}{\operatorname{\mathfrak{F}}}(a;b;z) = 
\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{\Lbrack a \Rbrack_n}{\Lbrack b \Rbrack_n} \frac{z^n}{n!} .

[Lemma lem:bernoulli-smoothing of arXiv:2512.04371, 'Constructive Approximation under Carleman's Condition, \\ with Applications to Smoothed An'] For any fixed sequence $\{a_l\}_{l=0}^k \subset \RR$, there exists a polynomial $p_k:\RR\to \RR$ of degree $k+1$ such that $p_k^{(l)}(1) - p_k^{(l)}(0) = a_l$ for all $0\le l\le k$.

[Defin def:spect of arXiv:2605.31054, 'On the empirical spectral distribution of matrix perpetuities'] \ 
    For any $N\times N$ real  random matrix ${\mathbf Y}$ with eigenvalues $(\lambda_k({\mathbf Y}))_{k=1}^N$, we define the empirical spectral distribution and the expected empirical spectral distribution by $\hat{\mu}_{{\mathbf Y}}$ and $ \mu_{{\mathbf Y}}$ respectively, by 
    \[
    \hat{\mu}_{\mathbf Y} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^N \delta_{\lambda_k({\mathbf Y})},\qquad \mu_{{\mathbf Y}}={\mathbb E}[\hat{\mu}_{\mathbf Y}], 
    \]
    where $\lambda_k({\mathbf Y})$ for $k=1,\ldots,N$ are the eigenvalues of ${\mathbf Y}$ listed with multiplicities.

[Defn 4 of arXiv:2609.00723, 'An integral Hyodo--Kato isomorphism'] An $F$-pre-log algebra over $\sR$ is a pair $(\sA,F_A)$ consisting of a pre-log algebra 
$\sA=(A,\alpha\colon L \to A)$ over $\sR$ and a $F_R$-homomorphism $F_A\colon A\to A$ such that $F_A(a)\equiv a^p\mod pA$ (so, $F_A$ is a   lift of the absolute Frobenius of $A/p$).

 An $F$-pre-log algebra $(\sA,F_A)$ over $\sR$ is called \emph{special} if there is a decomposition $L=L^o\oplus N$ as monoids such that the structure map $N\to L$ is the inclusion into the second factor and that 
\eq{eq;def;Flogalgebra}{F_A(\alpha(l))=\alpha(l)^p\qfor l\in L^o.}
 A map $(\sA,F_A) \to (\sB,F_B)$ of $F$-pre-log algebras is a map $\sA\to \sB$ of pre-log rings which is compatible with $F_A$ and $F_B$.
title: Definition 4 of arXiv:2609.00723

[Corollary 18 of arXiv:2511.13559, 'Asymptotic analysis of rare events in high dimensions'] Suppose $|g(x)|\leq 1$ for all $x\in D$, and Assumption~\ref{assume1} holds. Let $N\geq1,M\geq1$, and
\be
R \geq  4\left(1+\frac{\log d}{d}+(M+1/2)\frac{\log\la}{d}\right).\ee 
Suppose $R\e \leq\rho_0\wedge1$, $R\e\delta_2(R\e/2)\leq 4$,  $\pa_tz(u)\geq1/2$ for all $u\in D_1\cup D_2=\Theta(\us(R\e)\times[0,R\e])$, and $z(u)-z(0_{d+1})\geq \e\|u\|_{H,1}$ for all $u\in D_3=D\setminus \U(R\e/2)$. Then

\bs
\frac{1}{\mathcal Z}\int_{D} g(u)e^{-\la z(u)}\dd u &=\frac{1}{\la}\left(\sum_{m=1}^{N}c_m\la^{-(m-1)} +\Rem_{N}\right),\\
 c_m &= \sum_{k=1}^m\nu_{m-k}(\g_k),\quad m=1,\dots,L-1.
\es The remainder $\Rem_N$ is bounded as follows, with $\|f\|_\infty=\sup_{x\in \us(R\e),y\in[0 ,(R\e)^2]}|f(x,y)|$:
\bs
|\Rem_{N}| \les\; &\sum_{k=1}^{N}|\Rem_{N+1-k}^\Lap(\g_k)|\la^{-(k-1)} + \mu\|D_{\z}^N\g\|_\infty\la^{-N}\\
&+(1\vee\mu)\big(1+\max_{1\leq k\leq N}\|D_{\z}^{k-1}\g\|_\infty\la^{-(k-1/2)}\big)\la^{-M}.
\es Here, $\Rem_{N+1-k}^\Lap(\g_k)$ is as in~\eqref{lap-gz-L}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Thm Kuratowski--Ryll-Nardzewski measurable selection theorem of arXiv:2605.31054, 'On the empirical spectral distribution of matrix perpetuities'] Let $X$ be a standard Borel space, let $Y$ be a Polish space, and let
\[
\Psi\colon X\to 2^Y
\]
be a set-valued map with nonempty closed values. If $\Psi$ is weakly measurable, then there exists a Borel measurable map
\[
f\colon X\to Y
\]
such that
\[
f(x)\in \Psi(x)\qquad\text{for all }x\in X.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Kuratowski--Ryll-Nardzewski measurable selection theorem
Application to heavy tails -- random thresholds

body:
[Theorem 2 (Boundary) of arXiv:2606.07290, 'Boundary behaviour of the Volterra square-root process'] Suppose that $K \in C^1(\R_+)$, and let 
    \[
        \gamma_-(t) = \frac{2(x_0 L_0(t) + b)}{\sigma^2 K(0)} \ \text{ and } \ \gamma_+(t) = \frac{2\Lambda(t)}{\sigma^2 K(0)},
    \]
    with $\Lambda$ given by
    \[
        \Lambda(t) = x_0 L_0(0)\mathrm{e}^{\beta^+ K(0) t} + b \begin{cases} 1 + L_0(0) \frac{\mathrm{e}^{\beta K(0)t} - 1}{\beta},&  \beta \geq L_0(t)
        \\  \frac{L_0(0) - \beta}{L_0(t) - \beta},& \beta < L_0(t). \end{cases}
    \]
    Then $\P[X_t = 0] = 0$ for all $t > 0$. Moreover, let $p > 0$ and $t > 0$ satisfy $\gamma_-(t) > p$. If $x_0 = 0$, then 
   \[
     \frac{1}{\theta(t)^{p}} \frac{\Gamma(\gamma_{+}(t) - p)}{\Gamma(\gamma_{+}(t))} \leq \E[X_t^{-p}] \leq \frac{\Gamma(\gamma_{-}(t) - p)}{\Gamma(\gamma_{-}(t))} \frac{1}{\theta(t)^{p}},
    \]
    and if $x_0 > 0$, then 
    \[
        \frac{1}{\theta(t)^{p}} \mathrm{e}^{-C(t)} \frac{\Gamma(\gamma_+(t)-p)}{\Gamma(\gamma_+(t))} \leq \E[X_t^{-p}] \leq \frac{1}{\theta(t)^{p}} \left[ \left( \frac{C(t)}{2} \right)^{-p} + \mathrm{e}^{-C(t)/2} \frac{\Gamma(\gamma_-(t) - p)}{\Gamma(\gamma_-(t))} \right].
    \]
    If $p \geq \gamma_+(t)$, then $\E[X_t^{-p}] = \infty$ for any $x_0 \geq 0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let $A>0$ and let $F$ be an entire function on $\mathbb C$. The following are equivalent: (i) $F$ is of exponential type at most $A$ (there is $C$ with $|F(z)|\le Ce^{A|z|}$ for all $z\in\mathbb C$) and $\int_{\mathbb R}|F(x)|^2dx<\infty$; (ii) there is $\varphi\in L^2(-A,A)$ with $F(z)=\int_{-A}^{A}\varphi(t)e^{itz}\,dt$ for all $z\in\mathbb C$. Under these conditions one automatically has the sharper bound $|F(x+iy)|\le\|\varphi\|_{L^1(-A,A)}e^{A|y|}$. Equivalently, in the convention $\hat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\xi}dx$: a function $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ has $\hat f=0$ a.e. outside $[-W,W]$ if and only if $f$ agrees a.e. with the restriction to $\mathbb R$ of an entire function of exponential type at most $2\pi W$ that is square integrable on $\mathbb R$. Both the growth bound in every complex direction and the integrability on the real line are needed.
F entire on C
exponential type bound |F(z)| <= C e^{A|z|} holding in ALL complex directions, not only on the real axis
F square integrable on the real line
A > 0 fixed; in the e^{-2 pi i x xi} convention the type is 2 pi W for band [-W,W]

body: [Theorem 9 of arXiv:2504.16254, 'New bounds on the modularity of $G(n,p)$'] Let n ∈N, d ≥1, p = p(n) = d/n, and G(n, p) be a binomial random graph. Then with high probability, for large d mod(G(n, p)) ≥P∗+ od(1) √ d , where P∗= 0.76321 ± 0.00003 and od(·) relates to d →∞. For completeness let us also comment on the value of mod(G(n, p)) when d ≤ 1 + o(1). Then, if only dn →∞, the modularity score of the partition dictated by connected components with high probability tends to 1.
title: Theorem 9 of arXiv:2504.16254: New bounds on the modularity of $G(n,p)$

[Defn def.A2 of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] \begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),labelindent=0pt]\ 
\item  The marked point process  $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$, is  said to have {\em summable exponential $\mathbb{B} $-mixing correlations}  if it  has fast $\mathbb{B} $-mixing  correlations 
 as in Definition (B-omega-mixing of the paper)(Bmixing-fast of the paper) with functions
 $\omega_k(s) = C_k \phi(s)$, $k\in\mathbb{N}$,  
such that the $C_k$ are non-decreasing 
and where the $\omega_k(s)$ satisfy the twin growth conditions
\begin{equation} 
\sup_{k\in\mathbb{N}} \frac{C_k}{k^{ak}}  < \infty
\end{equation}
for some constant $a\in[0,1)$ and  
\begin{equation} 
\limsup_{r \to \infty} \frac{\log \phi(r)}{r^b } \in [-\infty,  0),
\end{equation}
for some constant $b \in (0, \infty)$. 

\item  Similarly, the 
 family  
 $(\tilde\mathcal{P}_l = \{(x,U_l(x))\}_{x \in \mathcal{P}})_{l \in \mathbb{N}}$
 of marked point processes has 
{\em summable exponential $\mathbb{B} $-mixing correlations} 
if~(equation e.Bmppmixing of the paper) holds
for functions
 $\omega_k(s) = C_k \phi(s)$, $k\in\mathbb{N}$, with non-decreasing constants $C_k$,  satisfying~(equation eqn:sum of the paper) and~(equation phibd of the paper)
that is to say 
for all $l, p,q \in \mathbb{N}$, and all $f \in \mathbb{B} (\mathbb{K}^p), g \in \mathbb{B} (\mathbb{K}^q)$, we have
 \begin{align} \nonumber
& \left|\mathbb {E} _{\bk x1{p+q}}[f(\bk {U_l}1{p})g(\bk {U_l}{p+1}{p+q})]\rho^{(p+q)}(\bk x1{p+q}) - \mathbb {E} _{\bk x1p}[f(\bk {U_l}1p)] \rho^{(p)}(\bk x1{p})\mathbb {E} _{\bk x{p+1}{p+q}}[g(\bk {U_l}{p+1}{p+q})]\rho^{(q)}(\bk
x{p+1}{p+q})\right|\\
 &\hspace{0.1\linewidth}\le C_{p + q} \phi(s),  \qquad x_1,\ldots,x_{p+q} \in \mathbb{R}^d.
\end{align}

\item  The  point process $\mathcal{P}$ has
{\em summable exponential mixing correlations}
 if it has mixing correlations as in Definition (d.omegamixing of the paper)(i.mixing-ground of the paper) with 
$\omega_k(s) = C_k \phi(s)$, $k\in\mathbb{N}$, and where $\phi$ and $(C_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ satisfy the above conditions. 

\end{enumerate}

[Theorem 1 (Finite-horizon directional response) of arXiv:2608.19762, '2608.19762'] Consider the scaled perturbation
\[
    g_t^{\mathrm s}(\alpha)
    =
    g_t^{\mathrm c}+\alpha\xi_t.
\]
Suppose that the control trajectory lies in the interior of the smooth regions
used to define $\widetilde f_s$, that the corresponding AdamW transitions are
differentiable along the trajectory, and that $F_s$ is differentiable at the
relevant control states. In particular, the second-moment coordinates involved
in the derivatives satisfy $\widehat v_{s,i}^{\mathrm c}>0$.
Let $\delta x_{t+h}(\alpha)$ and $\delta F_{t+h}(\alpha)$ denote the resulting
paired state and probe-loss responses. Then, for every fixed $h\geq1$,
\begin{align*}
    \left.
    \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\alpha}
    \delta x_{t+h}(\alpha)
    \right|_{\alpha=0}
    &=
    \Phi_{t+h,t+1}B_t\xi_t,\\
    \left.
    \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\alpha}
    \delta F_{t+h}(\alpha)
    \right|_{\alpha=0}
    &=
    c_{t+h}^{\top}
    \Phi_{t+h,t+1}
    B_t\xi_t.
\end{align*}
Define the horizon-$h$ input--output operator
\[
    \mathcal G_{t,h}
    :=
    c_{t+h}^{\top}
    \Phi_{t+h,t+1}
    B_t.
\]
Then
\[
    \delta F_{t+h}(\alpha)
    =
    \alpha\mathcal G_{t,h}\xi_t
    +
    o(\alpha),
    ~~
    \alpha\rightarrow0.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Finite-horizon directional response

    \begin{itemize}
        \item In dimension $d = 2$, there exists an inverse temperature $\beta_{\mathrm{KT}}^{\mathrm{Ann-Vil}}(\kappa) < \infty$, such that, for any $\beta \geq \beta_{\mathrm{KT}}^{\mathrm{Ann-Vil}}(\kappa)$, the function $x \mapsto  \left\langle \cos  ( \theta_0 - \theta_x ) \right\rangle^{\mathrm{Ann-Vil}}_{\kappa , \beta}$ decays polynomially fast in $|x|$.
        \item In dimension $d \geq  3$, there exists an inverse temperature $\beta_{c}^{\mathrm{Ann-Vil}}(d, \kappa) < \infty$, such that, for any $\beta \geq \beta_{c}^{\mathrm{Vil}}(d, \kappa)$, the function $x \mapsto  \left\langle \cos  ( \theta_0 - \theta_x ) \right\rangle^{\mathrm{Ann-Vil}}_{\kappa , \beta}$ is bounded away from $0$.
    \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Proposition 9 of arXiv:2603.28226, '2603.28226'] Let $\Omega=E\sqcup E^c$ with $\mathbb P(E)=p\in(0,\tfrac12]$, and define
\[
 \mathcal F_1=\{\varnothing,\Omega\},
 \qquad
 \mathcal F_n=\mathcal F_\infty=\{\varnothing,E,E^c,\Omega\},\qquad n\ge2.
\]
Fix $\lambda>0$ and let
\[
 f:=\frac{\lambda}{p}\mathbf1_E,
 \qquad
 \|f\|_1=\lambda.
\]
Assume that
\[
 f=g+h+k
\]
with $g,h,k\in L^1(\mathcal F_\infty)$ and
\[
 0\le k\le \beta\lambda\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]
for some $\beta\in[0,p^{-1}]$. Then one of the following alternatives holds:

\smallskip
\noindent\textup{(i)}
\[
 \mathbb P\Bigl(\sup_{n\ge1}|\mathbb E_n[g]|>0\Bigr)=1;
\]

\noindent\textup{(ii)} $g=0$ almost surely and
\begin{equation}

 \Bigl\|\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|\mathbb E_n[h]-\mathbb E_{n-1}[h]|\Bigr\|_1
 \ge
 \begin{cases}
 (3-\beta-2p)\lambda, & 0\le \beta\le1,\\[4pt]
 2(1-p\beta)\lambda, & 1\le \beta\le p^{-1}.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Both lower bounds are sharp.

body:
[Definition def:supernode of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] After a weak chronological order has been fixed, a \emph{supernode} is
one equality block: all occurrences assigned to one physical time after
the complete same-time rule has been applied.  It is \emph{hard} if the
equality block contains at least two occurrences, or if its fused tensor
contains a nonsingleton packet, the time-indexed $-2N^{-1}W_i$ Jacobi
child, or a special root.  In particular, every surviving same-time
nonsingleton is hard, whether or not its occurrences are
column-connected.  Otherwise the block consists of exactly one occurrence
and is a passive singleton supernode carrying one of the four star
statuses defined after (eq:3.2.10n of the paper).  Ordered supernodes are always
ordered by their actual physical times; no fragment of one equality block
is counted as a second node.
title: Fused chronological supernode

[Thm solution space to null and ward of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] The following four types of Coulomb gas integrals (see definitions in Section~(Classification of screening solutions of the paper)) solve the null vector equation (equation null vector equation angular coordinate constant h of the paper) and the rotation equation (equation rotation_invariance of the paper):
\begin{itemize} 
    \item[(1)] For any link pattern \( \alpha \in LP(n,m) \), with \( m,n \in \mathbb{Z} \) and \( 1 \leq m \leq \frac{n}{2} \), the Coulomb gas integral \( \mathcal{J}_{\alpha}^{n,m}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \) defined in ((radial ground solution of the paper)) solves the null vector equation (equation null vector equation angular coordinate constant h of the paper) with 
    \[
    h = \frac{1 - (n - 2m)^2}{2\kappa},
    \]
    and the rotation equation (equation rotation_invariance of the paper) with \( \omega = 0 \).
    
    \item[(2)] For any link pattern \( \alpha \in LP(n,m) \), with \( m,n \in \mathbb{Z} \), \( 1 \leq m \leq \frac{n}{2} \), and \( n \) even, the corresponding Coulomb gas integrals $\mathcal{K}^{(m,n)}_{\alpha}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ defined in ((radial excited soultion of the paper)) solve the null vector equation (equation null vector equation angular coordinate constant h of the paper) with 
    \[
    h = \frac{1 - \left(n - 2m + \frac{\kappa}{2} \right)^2}{2\kappa},
    \]
    and the rotation equation (equation rotation_invariance of the paper) with \( \omega = 0 \).

    \item[(3)] For any link pattern \( \alpha \in LP(n,m) \), with \( m,n \in \mathbb{Z} \) and \( 1 \leq m \leq \frac{n}{2} \), the Coulomb gas integral \( \mathcal{J}^{n,m}_{\alpha}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \eta) \) solves the null vector equation (equation null vector equation angular coordinate constant h of the paper) with 
    \[
    h = -\frac{(n - 2m)^2}{2\kappa} + \frac{1 + \eta^2}{2\kappa},
    \]
    and the rotation equation (equation rotation_invariance of the paper) with 
    \[
    \omega = \frac{\eta(n - 2m)}{\kappa}.
    \]

    \item[(4)] For any link pattern \( \alpha \in LP(n,\frac{n}{2}) \), with \( n \) even, the Coulomb gas integral \( \mathcal{L}_{\alpha}^{n}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \) defined in ((Chordal Coulomb gas Solution of the paper)) solves the null vector equation (equation null vector equation angular coordinate constant h of the paper) with 
    \[
    h = \frac{(6 - \kappa)(\kappa - 2)}{8\kappa},
    \]
    and the rotation equation (equation rotation_invariance of the paper) with \( \omega = 0 \).
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let $X = Z\Sigma^{1/2}$ be $n \times p$ with $Z$ having i.i.d. entries of mean $0$ and variance $1$, $\Sigma$ positive semidefinite, and let $S = \frac{1}{n}X^T X$. Assume $p/n \to c \in (0, \infty)$ and that the empirical spectral distribution of $\Sigma$ converges weakly to a probability measure $H$ on $[0, \infty)$. Then almost surely the empirical spectral distribution of $S$ converges weakly to a nonrandom probability measure $F = F^{c, H}$, characterised as follows: with $\underline F = (1 - c)\delta_0 + cF$ (the limiting spectral distribution of the $n \times n$ companion $\frac{1}{n}XX^T$) and $\underline m(z) = \int \frac{d\underline F(t)}{t - z} = -\frac{1 - c}{z} + c\,m_F(z)$, for every $z \in \mathbb{C}^+$ the value $\underline m(z)$ is the unique solution in $\mathbb{C}^+$ of $$z = -\frac{1}{\underline m} + c\int \frac{\tau\, dH(\tau)}{1 + \tau\,\underline m}.$$ Equivalently, $m_F$ solves $m_F(z) = \int \frac{dH(\tau)}{\tau\,(1 - c - c z\, m_F(z)) - z}$. For $H = \delta_1$ (identity population covariance) the equation reduces to the quadratic $z\,\underline m^2 + (z + 1 - c)\,\underline m + 1 = 0$ for the companion transform (equivalently $c z\, m_F^2 + (z - 1 + c)\, m_F + 1 = 0$ for $m_F$ itself), whose solution is the Stieltjes transform of the Marchenko-Pastur law with ratio $c$; the support of $F$ and its density are read off by Stieltjes inversion, and the density is analytic inside the support and behaves like a square root at its edges.
entries of Z i.i.d., mean zero, variance one (finite second moment suffices for the almost-sure convergence in the Bai-Silverstein form)
the spectral distribution of Sigma converges weakly to H; p/n -> c in (0, infinity)

body:
[Proposition prop:construction-until-explosion of arXiv:2608.05105, 'Cluster-Cluster model in $\mathbb{Z}^d$'] Let \(\alpha<0\), and write \(\beta=-\alpha>0\). The Cluster-Cluster dynamics
admits a maximal local construction as follows. For every finite
\(\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb Z^d\) there is a stopping time
\(\tau^\Lambda\in[0,\infty]\) such that the restriction of the process to
\(\Lambda\) is well defined on \([0,\tau^\Lambda)\), has càdlàg paths there,
and has only finitely many jumps on every compact subinterval of
\([0,\tau^\Lambda)\). If \((\Lambda_j)_{j\ge1}\) is an increasing exhaustion of
\(\mathbb Z^d\) by finite boxes, the maximal lifetime is
\[
    \tau_{\rm exp}:=\inf_{j\ge1}\tau^{\Lambda_j}.
\]
For every \(T<\tau_{\rm exp}\), the process is defined on every finite set up to
time \(T\). If \(\tau_{\rm exp}<\infty\), then local stabilization of the cutoff
processes fails at \(\tau_{\rm exp}\); equivalently, arbitrarily large cutoff
levels influence the evolution in finite boxes arbitrarily close to
\(\tau_{\rm exp}\).

[Lem boundsrho of arXiv:2605.06488, 'Continuous-state branching processes with L\'evy-Khintchine drift-interaction: Laplace dua'] Assume $\mathrm{a}=0$ and $\neg \hatHone$. 

	\begin{enumerate}
		\item Let $\eta$ be the L\'evy measure associated to $\Sigma$. Then, $$\overline{\varrho}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle\Sigma,\hat\Phi}=\underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\limsup}\,x\int_0^{\infty}\bar{\eta}(u)\Big(\frac{1}{\hat\Phi(x)}-\frac{1}{\hat{\Phi}(x+u)}\Big)\mathrm{d} u,$$
        and similarly for $\underline{\varrho}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle\Sigma,\hat\Phi}$ with $\liminf$.
        \item
		If $\Sigma\sim \Sigma_1$ at $\infty$, then $$\overline{\varrho}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle\Sigma, \hat{\Phi}}=\overline{\varrho}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle \Sigma_1,\hat\Phi}\text{ and } \underline{\varrho}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle \Sigma, \hat{\Phi}}=\underline{\varrho}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle\Sigma_1, \hat{\Phi}}.$$ 
		
		\item  There is no loss of generality in assuming that the measure $\hat{U}$ admits a density $\hat u$, moreover
\[\underline{\varrho}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle\Sigma,\hat\Phi}=\underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\liminf}\,\mathbb{E}[B(\mathbbm{e}_x)], \quad \overline{\varrho}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle\Sigma,\hat\Phi}=\underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\limsup}\,\mathbb{E}[B(\mathbbm{e}_x)],\]
where 
\begin{center}
$B:(0,\infty)\ni z \mapsto \frac{\Sigma(z)\hat{u}(z)}{z}$ and $\mathbbm{e}_x$ is an exponential r.v. with parameter $x$.\end{center}
One has also the bounds
		\[\liminf_{z\rightarrow \infty}\frac{\Sigma(z)\hat{u}(z)}{z}\leq \underline{\varrho}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle\Phi, \hat{\Sigma}}\leq \overline{\varrho}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle\Phi, \hat{\Sigma}}\leq \underset{z\rightarrow \infty}\limsup\frac{\Sigma(z)\hat{u}(z)}{z}.\]    
		In particular, if $\varrho:=\underset{x\rightarrow \infty}{\lim}\frac{\Sigma(z)\hat{u}(z)}{z}\text{ exists in } [0,\infty]$, then $\underline{\varrho}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle\Sigma, \hat{\Phi}}=\overline{\varrho}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle \Sigma, \hat{\Phi}}=\varrho.$

body: In information theory, the noisy-channel coding theorem, establishes that for any given degree of noise contamination of a communication channel, it is possible to communicate discrete data nearly error-free up to a computable maximum rate through the channel. This result was presented by Claude Shannon in 1948 and was based in part on earlier work and ideas of Harry Nyquist and Ralph Hartley.
title: Noisy-channel coding theorem

body: In mathematics, the Mordell–Weil theorem states that for an abelian variety over a number field , the group of K-rational points of is a finitely-generated abelian group, called the Mordell–Weil group. The case with an elliptic curve and the field of rational numbers is Mordell's theorem, answering a question apparently posed by Henri Poincaré around 1901; it was proven by Louis Mordell in 1922. It is a foundational theorem of Diophantine geometry and the arithmetic of abelian varieties.
title: Mordell–Weil theorem

body:
[Prop evanescent of arXiv:2507.09421, 'Stability of randomly switching stochastic reaction networks with asymptotically linear tr'] Let $X$ be a CTMC on $\mathbb S\subseteq \mathbb Z^d$, and let $x\in\mathbb S$. Then $x$ is evanescent for $X$ iff when started from state $x$ with positive probability the process never enters a recurrent state.
\begin{proof}[Proof Sketch]
    First, assume that $\lim\limits_{t\to\infty}\@ifstar{\oldnorm}{\oldnorm*}{X(t)}_{\ell^1}\to\infty$ occurs with positive probability. Given this event, the process almost surely does not enter a recurrent state because if a recurrent state is visited once then it is a.s.~visited infinitely many times [Norris_1997].
    
    For the reverse implication, suppose that $\liminf\limits_{t\to\infty}\@ifstar{\oldnorm}{\oldnorm*}{X(t)}_{\ell^1}$ is finite with probability one. Note that for all $R\in\mathbb R$, the event that the process ever enters a recurrent state contains, up to a set of measure zero, the event that $\liminf\limits_{t\to\infty}\@ifstar{\oldnorm}{\oldnorm*}{X(t)}_{\ell^1}\le R$. Indeed, otherwise we could use the fact that $\{y\in\mathbb Z^d:\@ifstar{\oldnorm}{\oldnorm*} y_{\ell^1}\le R\}$ is finite to conclude that there existed a specific transient state $y$ which was visited infinitely often with positive probability, contradicting transience of $y$. Sending $R\to\infty$, the result follows from continuity of probability. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop evanescent of arXiv:2507.09421

[Theorem 17 (Bernstein inequalities, Lemma 2.1, \cite{MR2768550}) of arXiv:2609.02197, '2609.02197'] Let $\left(n,\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\gamma_3\right) \in \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{R}_+^*\times\mathbb{R}_+^*\times\mathbb{R}_+^*$ such that $\gamma_2<\gamma_3.$
\begin{enumerate}
\item There exists $\mu \in \mathbb{R}_+^*$ such that for any $\left(r,\beta\right) \in \left[1,+\infty\right[^2$ and all $\varphi \in \mathscr{S},$ if \\ $\left\{x \in \mathbb{Z}^d,\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\varphi\left(y\right)\mathrm{e}^{-2\pi \mathrm{i}\left\langle x,y\right\rangle}\,\mathrm{d}y\neq 0\right\}\subset \left\{x \in \mathbb{R}^d,\left|x\right|\leq \beta\gamma_1\right\},$ then $$\max_{\substack{q\in\mathbb{N}^d \\ \left|q\right|=n}}\left\Vert \partial^q \varphi\right\Vert_{L^\infty\left(\mathbb{T}^d\right)}\leq \mu\beta^{n+\frac{d}{r}}\left\Vert \varphi\right\Vert_{L^r\left(\mathbb{T}^d\right)}.$$
\item There exists $\left(\mu_1,\mu_2\right) \in \left(\mathbb{R}_+^*\right)^2$ such that for any $\beta \in \left[1,+\infty\right[$ and all $\varphi \in \mathscr{S},$ if \\ $\left\{x \in \mathbb{Z}^d,\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\varphi\left(y\right)\mathrm{e}^{-2\pi \mathrm{i}\left\langle x,y\right\rangle}\,\mathrm{d}y\neq 0\right\}\subset\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}^d,\beta\gamma_2\leq \left|x\right|\leq\beta\gamma_3\right\},$ then $$\mu_1\beta^{n}\left\Vert \varphi\right\Vert_{L^\infty\left(\mathbb{T}^d\right)}\leq \max_{\substack{q\in\mathbb{N}^d\\\left|q\right|=n}}\left\Vert \partial^{q}\varphi\right\Vert_{L^\infty\left(\mathbb{T}^d\right)}\leq \mu_2\beta^{n}\left\Vert \varphi\right\Vert_{L^{\infty}\left(\mathbb{T}^d\right)}.$$
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have independent coordinates with finite ranges, f a real function of X, and f = sum over S of f_S its Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition over subsets S of {1, ..., n}: f_S depends only on X_S, f_empty = E f, and E[f_S | X_T] = 0 unless S is inside T. Put w_S = E[f_S^2] and W_k = sum over |S| = k of w_S, the variance at interaction order k. Let A_q be a random set, independent of X, containing each coordinate independently with probability q in [0, 1], and M(q) = E over A_q of E Var(f | X_{A_q^c}). Then M(q) = sum over nonempty S of [1 - (1 - q)^|S|] w_S = Var(f) - J(1 - q), with J the Bernoulli reveal profile, and M(q) = (1/2) E[(f(X) - f(X^(A_q)))^2], where X^(A) redraws X_A independently from its own law. For every r >= 1, (-1)^(r+1) M^(r)(q) = sum_{k=r}^n (k)_r (1 - q)^(k - r) W_k >= 0 with (k)_r = k(k - 1)...(k - r + 1); so M is increasing and concave, M'(0) = sum_k k W_k = sum_i E Var(f | X_{-i}), and the derivatives at any q determine the spectrum. For a pure order-d function, J(p) = p^d Var(f) and M(q) = [1 - (1 - q)^d] Var(f).

body:
[Lem pcp-cumulant-functional of arXiv:2605.13004, 'Orientation in Poisson Cluster Processes via Imaginary Bispectra'] Let
\[
N=\sum_j\vartheta_{U_j}C_j
\]
be a stationary Poisson cluster process with immigrant rate $\nu$, where the $C_j$ are i.i.d. copies of a finite simple cluster $C$ and $\mathbb{E} C(\mathbb{R})<\infty$; if multiplicities are allowed, products and sums below are over atoms counted with multiplicity. Whenever the following logarithms are finite, for instance for bounded compactly supported $q$ with $-1<q\le0$ and bounded compactly supported $f\le0$ under the preceding finite-mean assumption, the Poisson product formula gives
\[
K_{\mathrm{fac}}^N(q)
=
\nu\int_\mathbb{R}
\left\{
\mathbb{E}\prod_{y\in C}(1+q(u+y))-1
\right\}\,du
\]
and
\[
K_{\mathrm{comp}}^N(f)
=
\nu\int_\mathbb{R}
\left\{
\mathbb{E}\exp\big(C(f(u+\cdot))\big)-1
\right\}\,du .
\]
The derivative identities used below require only finite moments: for every $n\ge1$ with $\mathbb{E}[C(\mathbb{R})^n]<\infty$ and bounded compactly supported $f_0,\ldots,f_{n-1}$,
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1} f_j(t_j)\,
\kappa_n(dt_0,\ldots,dt_{n-1})
=
\nu\int_\mathbb{R}
\mathbb{E}\sum_{x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}\in C}^{\neq}
\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}f_j(u+x_j)\,du,
\]
whereas
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1} f_j(t_j)\,
\gamma_n(dt_0,\ldots,dt_{n-1})
=
\nu\int_\mathbb{R}
\mathbb{E}\sum_{x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}\in C}
\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}f_j(u+x_j)\,du.
\]
Equivalently, for $n\ge2$,
\[
\kappa_n^{\mathrm{red}}(d\tau_1,\ldots,d\tau_{n-1})
=
\nu\,\mathbb{E}\sum_{x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}\in C}^{\neq}
\prod_{r=1}^{n-1}\delta_{x_r-x_0}(d\tau_r),
\]
and
\[
\gamma_n^{\mathrm{red}}(d\tau_1,\ldots,d\tau_{n-1})
=
\nu\,\mathbb{E}\sum_{x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}\in C}
\prod_{r=1}^{n-1}\delta_{x_r-x_0}(d\tau_r).
\]
In particular, if $\mathbb{E}[C(\mathbb{R})^3]<\infty$ and
\[
W(\omega):=\widehat C(\omega)=\sum_{x\in C}e^{-\mathrm{i}\omega x},
\]
then
\[
\widehat{\gamma_3^{\mathrm{red}}}(\omega_1,\omega_2)
=
\nu\,\mathbb{E}\{W(\omega_1)W(\omega_2)W(-\omega_1-\omega_2)\}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Cumulant functionals for Poisson cluster processes

body: [Thm main-random-walk of arXiv:2604.14122, 'The scaling limit of random walk and\\ the intrinsic metric on planar critical percolation'] There exists a sequence $(b_n)_{n\in\mathbf N}$ such that the following is true. Let $m \in \mathbf N$ and sample $\rho_n \in \mathcal{X}^{(m)}_n$ and $\rho \in \mathcal{X}^{(m)}$ such that $(\mathcal{X}^{(m)}_n,d^{{\mathrm {path}}}_n,\pi_n,\rho_n) \to (\mathcal{X}^{(m)},d^{{\mathrm {path}}},\pi,\rho)$ in law in the rooted GHf topology. Then there exists a coupling such that the following holds almost surely. Let $X^{(n)}$ be the continuous-time simple random walk on $\mathcal{X}^{(m)}_n$ that jumps to each open neighboring site at rate $b_n$, started from $\rho_n$. Then there exists a diffusion process $X$ on $\mathcal{X}^{(m)}$ with $X_0=\rho$ such that $\pi_n(X^{(n)})$ converges in law to $\pi(X)$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ in the space of c\`adl\`ag processes on $[0,1]^2$ equipped with the topology of uniform convergence on compact sets. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Own-work proof draft (unaudited); no novelty priority claimed. Fix one oracle O. Assume that for every NP^O predicate and every strict uniform polynomial-time O-samplable ensemble there is one deterministic O-relative heuristic scheme, polynomial in input length and inverse error, whose error is bounded by the requested tolerance at every length. Then every uniform nonnegative rational efficient-weight law with polynomial numerator/denominator bit bounds and positive normalizer has uniform strict polynomial-time approximate samplers at every inverse-polynomial TV accuracy. Every uniform polynomial-time O-map also has all-length distributional inverters at every inverse-polynomial joint-TV accuracy. A conditional-set affine-hashing sampler proves both: random bucket counting, unique-witness extraction, and an explicit virtual-row union bound avoid assuming a sampler or CDF for the target weighted law. Under the existing C003 AR conversion this gives nonuniform polynomial-size forward-KL approximations in the SAME oracle. The 1995 Impagliazzo survey defines DistNP using samplable ensembles and reports an IR2 heuristic oracle with NP circuit hardness, but its unpublished construction and full O-relative sampler coverage have not been verified here. This card proves the bridge under the precise hypothesis; it does not claim an independently established Target 2 oracle.
One fixed final oracle O; full O-relative NP and strict uniform polynomial-time samplable ensembles
For every such distributional NP problem, one fixed deterministic scheme with runtime polynomial in input length and inverse error and error <=eta for every length and every eta in (0,1)
For A: uniform nonnegative rational weight evaluator with polynomial numerator/denominator bounds and positive normalizer; for B: a uniform polynomial-time map on fixed polynomial-length uniform seeds
