body: The phrase 'general position' carries two conventions in the theory of hyperplane arrangements, and they are incompatible. For a CENTRAL arrangement, where every hyperplane contains the origin, the useful condition is on the NORMAL vectors: every $d$ or fewer of them are linearly independent. This is the condition under which the central orthant count is exact. For an AFFINE arrangement, a widespread convention instead requires that any $p$ of the hyperplanes with $p$ greater than the ambient dimension have empty intersection. No central arrangement can ever satisfy the affine condition, because all of its hyperplanes share the origin. A central arrangement is therefore never in 'general position' in the affine sense, however generic its normals. Sources using the affine convention will appear to exclude exactly the case a central count is about, and citing one for the other is a live error.
title: General Position: Two Incompatible Conventions

body:
[Definition Lipschitz maps and Lipschitz model classes of arXiv:2609.03129, 'A Closed-Form Formula for Consistent Lipschitz Regression on Metric Spaces with Sparse Neu'] Let $(X,\rho_X)$ and $(Y,\rho_Y)$ be metric spaces, and let $L\ge0$.  A map
$f:X\to Y$ is called $L$-Lipschitz if
\[
    \rho_Y(f(x),f(y))
    \le
    L\,\rho_X(x,y)
\]
for every $x,y\in X$.  Its Lipschitz constant is
$
    \operatorname{Lip}(f)
\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \sup_{x\neq y}
    \,
        \tfrac{\rho_Y(f(x),f(y))}{\rho_X(x,y)}
$.
When $h:X\to\mathbb R$ is real-valued, we also write $
    |\nabla h|(x)
    \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \limsup_{y\to x}
        \tfrac{|h(x)-h(y)|}{\rho(x,y)}
$ for its pointwise upper slope, with the convention that the value is $+\infty$ if the corresponding $\operatorname{limsup}$ is infinite.
\hfill\\
\noindent
For a metric space $(X,\rho)$, we define the unit Lipschitz model class
\[
    \mathcal F_1
    \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \operatorname{Lip}((X,\rho),[-1,1];1)
    =
    \left\{
        f:X\to[-1,1]
        :
        |f(x)-f(y)|
        \le
        \rho(x,y)
        \text{ for all }x,y\in X
    \right\}.
\]
If $(X,\rho)$ has doubling dimension $0<d<\infty$, we abbreviate
$
    \mathcal F_{1:d}
\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \operatorname{Lip}((X,\rho),[-1,1];1)
$.
All such classes are equipped with the uniform norm
$
    \|f\|_\infty
\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \sup_{x\in X}|f(x)|
$.
title: Lipschitz maps and Lipschitz model classes

[Lemma 37 of arXiv:2609.02808, 'Minimizers of Laplace eigenvalues under a lower curvature bound'] Let $X=([0,D],|\cdot|,c\,\varphi\,ds)$, where $c>0$ and $\varphi$ satisfies
\eqref{eq:concavity} and \eqref{eq:normalization}, and let
\[
0=\lambda_0(X)\le\lambda_1(X)\le\cdots
\]
be the eigenvalues of its Neumann Laplacian. Then the Cheeger energy of $X$
is the quadratic form
\[
\mathcal E_X(u)=c\int_0^D |u'|^2\varphi\,ds,
\]
and
\[
\lambda_j(X)\ge\mu_j(\varphi)
\qquad\text{for every }j\ge0.
\]

Order the positive integers by the Sharkovskii ordering: 3 lhd 5 lhd 7 lhd 9 lhd ... (odd numbers greater than 1, increasing) lhd 2*3 lhd 2*5 lhd 2*7 lhd ... lhd 4*3 lhd 4*5 lhd ... lhd 8*3 lhd ... (2^k times each odd number greater than 1, for successively larger k) ... lhd ... 16 lhd 8 lhd 4 lhd 2 lhd 1 (ending with the powers of two, in decreasing order). Let f: I -> I be continuous on an interval I subset R. If f has a periodic point of minimal period m, and m lhd n in the Sharkovskii ordering, then f also has a periodic point of (minimal) period n. In particular, since 3 is first in the ordering, a period-3 point forces periodic points of every period.

f: I -> I is continuous

body: A small-world network is a graph characterized by a high clustering coefficient and low distances. In an example of a social network, high clustering implies the high probability that two friends of one person are friends themselves. The low distances, on the other hand, mean that there is a short chain of social connections between any two people (this effect is known as six degrees of separation). Specifically, a small-world network is defined to be a network where the typical distance L between two randomly chosen nodes (the number of steps required) grows proportionally to the logarithm of the number of nodes N in the network, that is: $$L\propto \log N$$

body:
[Lemma 112 of arXiv:2605.03236, 'Stochastic It\^o Equations and Parabolic Second-Order Equations with singular Drift'] Let $\rho\in(0,\infty)$, $C\in\bC_{\rho}$. Let $(\sfd_{0},q,p)$ be properly tight, $f,f^{n(k)}\in L_{(q,p)}(C)$, $f^{n(k)}\to f$ in $L_{(q,p)}(C)$.
Then for any $(t,x)\in\bR^{d+1}$
\begin{equation}
                  
E_{t,x}\int_{0}^{\tau_{C}} f(\sft_{s},x_{s})\,ds
=\lim_{n\to \infty}
E^{ n(k)}_{t,x}\int_{0}^{\tau_{C}} f^{n(k)}(\sft_{s},x_{s})\,ds,
\end{equation}
where $\tau_{C}$ is the first exit time
of $(\sft_{s},x_{s})$ from $C$.
In particular, for any $\rho>0$,
$C\in\bC_{\rho}$, and $(t,x)\in\bR^{d+1}$
$$
E_{t,x}\int_{0}^{\tau_{C}}|b(\sft_{s},x_{s})|\,ds
=\lim_{n\to \infty}
E^{ n(k)}_{t,x}\int_{0}^{\tau_{C}}|b^{ n(k)}(\sft_{s},x_{s})|\,ds
\leq \sfb_{0} \rho.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 112 of arXiv:2605.03236

body:
[Theorem thm:lutz-lutz-point-to-set of arXiv:2608.29561, 'Ball codes: A coding characterization of Hausdorff and packing dimensions'] For every nonempty set \(E\subseteq\mathbb R^n\),
\[
\dim_H(E)
=
\min_{A\subseteq\omega}
\sup_{x\in E}
\liminf_{r\to\infty}\frac{K^A_r(x)}{r},
\qquad
\dim_P(E)
=
\min_{A\subseteq\omega}
\sup_{x\in E}
\limsup_{r\to\infty}\frac{K^A_r(x)}{r},
\]
where \(K^A_r\) denotes the relativization
of~(equation eq:euclidean-point-complexity of the paper) to the oracle \(A\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Point-to-set principle of Lutz and Lutz~\cite{LutzLutz2018}

\begin{align*}
 [ f(\omega), \omega]_{\pi}(t):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{m(n)-1} \left( f(\omega(t^n_{k+1}\wedge t)) - f(\omega(t^n_k\wedge t))\right)\cdot
  \left(\omega(t^n_{k+1}\wedge t)  - \omega(t^n_k\wedge t)\right)
\end{align*}
exists, and is equal to the Riemann–Stieltjes integral
\[
\int_0^t \langle \nabla f(\omega(u)),\, d[\omega]_{\pi}(u)\rangle.
\]

[Corollary 28 (Empirical Fourier sums) of arXiv:2608.22342, 'Completely Positive Entropy and Fourier Central Limit Theorems for Stationary Random Measu'] Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:ball-fourier-clt}, suppose that
$\eta$ is a point process with $\rho_\eta>0$. Then, for every
$\xi\in E_\eta$,
\begin{equation}

    \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathbb S\ind_{B_R}}}
      \sum_{x\in\omega\cap B_R}\chi_\xi(x)
    \dto \mathcal{CN}\bigl(0,S_\eta(\xi)\bigr).
\end{equation}
The left-hand side is defined to be $0$ on
$\{\mathbb S\ind_{B_R}=0\}$. If $(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_q)\in E_\eta^{(q)}$,
the corresponding Fourier sums
converge jointly, and their Gaussian limits are independent.
title: Empirical Fourier sums

[Lemma lem:deformation-discrete of arXiv:2509.08928, 'The near critical random bond Ising model via embedding deformation'] Let $\mathcal{S}$ be an $s$-embedding of $(S,(x_e)_{e\in E})$ associated to the propagator $\mathcal{Y}$. Consider the Ising model on $(S,(\hat{x}_e)_{e\in E})$, where the set of coupling constant only differ at an edge $e_0$. Using the parametrisation (equation eq:x=tan-theta of the paper), define the abstract angles $x_{e_0}=\tan \frac{\theta_0}{2} $ and $\hat{x}_{e_0}=\tan \frac{\hat{\theta}_0}{2}$. Following the identification of double covers made in Section (sub:2-point-fermion of the paper) , fix a 'south-eastern' corner $a_0^+ \in \Upsilon^\times $ such that the branching structures of the double-covers $\Upsilon^\times_{(a_0)}$ and $\Upsilon
	^{\times} $ don't coincide on $z_0$. Similarly, fix a 'north-western' corner $c_0^+ \in \Upsilon^\times $ such that the branching structures of the double-covers $\Upsilon^\times_{(c_0)}$ and $\Upsilon

body:
[Corollary 5 (High-noise reverse-path proximity) of arXiv:2608.21709, 'Posterior Information Dynamics of Diffusion Models for Linear Inverse Problems'] Under Corollary~\ref{cor:reverse-path-kl}, assume
$\Tr\Cov(X_0)<\infty$, and set
\[
\gamma_t=\frac{a_t^2}{\Delta_t},
\qquad
Y_{\gamma_t}=\frac{X_t}{\sqrt{\Delta_t}}.
\]
Then, for every $T>t>0$,
\begin{equation}

\begin{aligned}
\E_R\KL\!\left(
\mathbb Q^{R,\mathrm{rev}}_{[t,T]}
\middle\|
\mathbb P^{\mathrm{rev}}_{[t,T]}
\right)
&=\MI(R;X_t)=\MI(R;Y_{\gamma_t})\\
&\le \MI(X_0;Y_{\gamma_t})\\
&\le \frac12\log\det\!\left(\Id_d+\gamma_t\Cov(X_0)\right)\\
&\le \frac{\gamma_t}{2}\Tr\Cov(X_0).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Consequently, if $d^{-1}\Tr\Cov(X_0)\le C_0$ and
$\Delta_t\ge\Delta_0>0$, the average reverse-path KL per coordinate is at
most $C_0a_t^2/(2\Delta_0)$.  Pinsker's inequality and Jensen's inequality also
give
\begin{equation}

\E_R\left\|
\mathbb Q^{R,\mathrm{rev}}_{[t,T]}
-
\mathbb P^{\mathrm{rev}}_{[t,T]}
\right\|_{\rm TV}
\le
\sqrt{\frac{\gamma_t}{4}\Tr\Cov(X_0)}.
\end{equation}
Here
\(\|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}:=\sup_B|\mu(B)-\nu(B)|
=\tfrac12\int|\dd\mu-\dd\nu|\).
The KL bound is naturally normalized by dimension.  The total-variation bound
vanishes in fixed dimension as \(a_t\to0\), and along dimension sequences for
which \(d a_t^2\to0\) on the high-noise window. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: High-noise reverse-path proximity

[Theorem 50 (Poisson-regime \texorpdfstring{$L^\infty(U)$}{Linfty(U)} profile) of arXiv:2604.09933, 'Explicit cutoff profiles for colored top-\texorpdfstring{$m$}{m}-to-random shuffles'] Assume \eqref{eq:mu-Poisson-assump}, and define

\[
H_{\infty,p}(c):=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \frac{e^{-\lambda}}{1-r}-1, & r<1 \ \ (\text{equivalently }c>\log p),\\[10pt]
+\infty, & r\ge1 \ \ (\text{equivalently }c\le \log p).
\end{cases}
\]
Assume further, in the case \(r<1\), that there exists a summable \((b_u)_{u\ge0}\) such that, for all sufficiently large \(n\) and all \(u\ge0\),
\[
0\le \mu_n(n-u)\,u!\,p^u\le b_u.
\]
Then, with convergence in the extended interval \([0,\infty]\),
\[
\left\|\frac{M_n(\cdot)}{U(\cdot)}-1\right\|_{L^\infty(U)}
\longrightarrow
H_{\infty,p}(c).
\]

[Dfn of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{Electrical networks}]
  Let $(V, E)$ be a connected, simple, undirected graph with finite or countably many vertices,
  where $V$ denotes the vertex set and $E$ denotes the edge set.
  (NB.\ A graph being simple means that it has no loops and no multiple edges.)
  For $x, y \in V$,
  we write $x \sim y$ if and only if $\{ x, y \} \in E$.
  Let $\{\mu(x, y)\}_{x, y \in V}$ be a family of non-negative real numbers such that 
  $\mu(x,y) = \mu(y, x)$ for all $x, y \in V$,
  $\mu(x, y) > 0$ if and only if $x \sim y$,
  and
  \begin{equation}
    \mu(x) 
    \coloneqq 
    \sum_{y \in V} \mu(x, y) < \infty,
    \quad 
    \forall x \in V.
  \end{equation}
  We call $\mu(x,y)$ the \textit{conductance} on the edge $\{x,y\}$
  and $(V, E, \mu)$ an \textit{electrical network}.
  Note that the edge set $E$ is uniquely determined by conductances.
  We equip $V$ with the discrete topology 
  and define a Radon measure $\mu^{\#}$ as the \textit{counting measure} on $V$, 
  which is a Radon measure on $V$ given by 
  \begin{equation}
    \mu^{\#}(A) 
    \coloneqq 
    \# A
    = 
    \sum_{x \in V} \delta_{x}(A)
    \quad 
    A \subseteq V,
  \end{equation}
  where $\delta_{x}$ is the Dirac measure putting mass $1$ at $x$.
  Given an electrical network $G$,
  we write $V_{G}$, $E_{G}$, $\{\mu_{G}(x,y)\}_{x, y \in V_{G}}$, and $\mu^{\#}_{G}$
  for the vertex set, the edge set, the conductances, and the counting measure, respectively.
  When we say that $G$ is a \textit{rooted electrical network},
  there exists a distinguished vertex,
  which we denote by $\rho_{G} \in V_{G}$.

[Definition 5 of arXiv:2606.17452, 'Optional Stopping for Superhedging Supermartingales'] Consider a sequence $\{f_n\}= \{f_n\}_{0 \leq n < T+1}$ of non-anticipative functions $f_n:\mathcal{S} \rightarrow [- \infty, \infty]$, $n\ge0$.

\vspace{.1in}\noindent $\{f_n\}$ is a \emph{supermartingale} sequence if
\begin{equation}  \nonumber 
\overline{\sigma}_j f_{j+1} \leq f_j~~a.e.\;\; 0 \leq j < T,
\end{equation}
$\{f_n\}$ is a \emph{submartingale} if
\begin{equation} \nonumber 
f_j \leq \underline{\sigma}_j f_{j+1}~~a.e.\;\;0 \leq j < T,
\end{equation}
$\{f_n\}$ is a \emph{martingale} if
\begin{equation}\nonumber 
\underline{\sigma}_j f_{j+1}= \overline{\sigma}_j f_{j+1}= f_j~~a.e.\;\; 0 \leq j < T.
\end{equation}
title: Definition 5 of arXiv:2606.17452

[Lemma 19 (Projection Lemma) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] For every $\pi\in\Delta^\circ_{m-1}$ there is, among the points of
the open separatrix $\Sigma^\circ$ --- where the
Fisher--Rao metric is defined --- a unique nearest point to $\pi$,
given in closed form by
\[
p(\pi)=\frac{\bigl(P_L\sqrt\pi\bigr)^2}{\bigl|P_L\sqrt\pi\bigr|^2}
\qquad(\text{componentwise square}),
\]
that is, $\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Sigma^\circ}
d_{\mathrm{FR}}(\pi,q)=p(\pi)$, with
\[
d_{\mathrm{FR}}\bigl(\pi,\Sigma^\circ\bigr)
=2\arccos\bigl|P_L\sqrt\pi\bigr|
=2\arcsin\bigl|P_{L^\perp}\sqrt\pi\bigr|\;<\;\pi.
\]
Since the unique ambient spherical foot already lies in
$\Phi(\Sigma^\circ)$, the same value is obtained if the infimum is
taken over the closure $\bar\Phi(\Sigma)$, whenever the latter is
read as the closure of the Riemannian domain.

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is the remaining-problem reduction in the partial answer to Problem 3.11 of Takahiro Hasebe and Yuki Ueda's Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions, ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374, DOI:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15 (arXiv:1710.08240). A probability measure is unimodal if, for some mode m, it is an atom at m plus an absolutely continuous measure whose density is nondecreasing to the left of m and nonincreasing to the right. Write boxplus for additive free convolution. A law lambda is freely strongly unimodal if lambda boxplus nu is unimodal for every unimodal nu. The source's Theorem 1.4 shows that no nondelta law of finite variance (equivalently, in the free domain of attraction of the semicircle) is freely strongly unimodal. The record's proved Cauchy obstruction excludes every nondelta lambda in the free domain of attraction of a Cauchy law. The same closure argument shows, more generally, that a nondelta lambda is not freely strongly unimodal whenever it lies in the free domain of attraction of a free stable law that is itself not freely strongly unimodal. Problem 3.11 therefore reduces to two questions. (1) Is some free stable law of index alpha in (0,2), alpha != 1, freely strongly unimodal? (The index-1 case is settled by the Cauchy identity, and index 2 by the source's Lemma 3.1.) (2) Is some measure lying in no free domain of attraction freely strongly unimodal? Numerically, for the free stable laws lambda_alpha with K(w)=1/w - i(iw)^{alpha-1}, the unimodal witness nu = (1/10)U[0,0.05] + (9/10)U[0,16] gives lambda_alpha boxplus nu two interior maxima at alpha = 1.95, 1.8, 1.6, 1.4, 1.2, 1.0, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7. This was computed by Belinschi-Bercovici subordination and calibrated against the exact Cauchy case at alpha=1. So those laws, and the laws attracted to them, are excluded numerically; only alpha=1 is a theorem. For alpha = 0.6 down to 0.3 the same nu, and three other one-sided uniform mixtures tried at alpha=0.5, give a single maximum. This is not evidence that those laws are freely strongly unimodal. The case alpha below about 0.65 remains open. This does not answer the existence question. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
This is a reduction of candidates, not a classification or a numerical proof for every stable index.
title: Hasebe-Ueda 3.11: candidate reduction through attracting laws

body:
Let alpha in (0,1) be irrational with continued fraction alpha = [0; a_1, a_2, ...], all a_i >= 1, and let p_n / q_n be its convergents, defined by p_n = a_n p_{n-1} + p_{n-2}, q_n = a_n q_{n-1} + q_{n-2} with q_{-1} = 0, q_0 = 1, p_{-1} = 1, p_0 = 0. Put eta_n = |q_n alpha - p_n| and note the signs alternate: q_n alpha - p_n = (-1)^n eta_n. For n >= 1 one has eta_n < 1/q_{n+1} <= 1/2, so eta_n = ||q_n alpha||; at n = 0 this can fail (if a_1 = 1, i.e. alpha > 1/2, then eta_0 = alpha > 1/2 while ||alpha|| = 1 - alpha), so ALL statements below are for n >= 1. Write R_alpha(x) = x + alpha on T = R/Z. Then:

(a) BEST APPROXIMATION / CLOSEST RETURNS. For n >= 1 and every integer q with 1 <= q < q_{n+1} and q not equal to q_n one has ||q alpha|| > ||q_n alpha|| = eta_n. Consequently the denominators q_n are exactly the closest-return times of the orbit of 0 under R_alpha: q_{n+1} is the smallest integer q > q_n with ||q alpha|| < ||q_n alpha||, and the sequence of record-setting return times is precisely q_1 < q_2 < ....

(b) RECURSION AND SIZE. eta_{n-1} = a_{n+1} eta_n + eta_{n+1}; the eta_n strictly decrease to 0; 1/(q_{n+1} + q_n) < eta_n < 1/q_{n+1}; and the exact identity q_n eta_{n-1} + q_{n-1} eta_n = 1 holds for every n >= 1 (and also at n = 0 with the convention eta_{-1} = |q_{-1} alpha - p_{-1}| = 1).

(c) RENORMALIZATION INTO TWO ROKHLIN TOWERS. Let J_n be the arc of T whose endpoints are the two points q_{n-1} alpha - p_{n-1} and q_n alpha - p_n (of opposite signs), so J_n contains 0 and has length eta_{n-1} + eta_n; it is split by 0 into a piece of length eta_{n-1} and a piece of length eta_n. Then the first-return map of R_alpha to J_n is the exchange of these two subintervals: the return time is q_n on the piece of length eta_{n-1} and q_{n-1} on the piece of length eta_n. Equivalently the q_{n-1} + q_n sets R_alpha^i(base) -- i < q_n over the long piece and i < q_{n-1} over the short piece -- are pairwise disjoint and tile T, which is exactly the content of the identity q_n eta_{n-1} + q_{n-1} eta_n = 1 in (b). This is the standard renormalization scheme behind Ostrowski expansions and the three-distance theorem.

SHARP EDGES. (a) is a statement about the TWO-SIDED quantity ||q alpha||. The intermediate (mediant) denominators b q_n + q_{n-1} with 1 <= b < a_{n+1} are best ONE-SIDED approximations but in general do not minimize ||q alpha||, so they are NOT closest-return times -- confusing the two is the classic error here. The hypothesis that alpha is irrational is essential: for rational alpha the algorithm terminates, the orbit is finite and periodic, and the tower picture degenerates. Also note eta_n < 1/q_{n+1} is an inequality, not an asymptotic equality: eta_n and 1/q_{n+1} agree only up to a factor between 1/2 and 1, and a proof that needs the exact value must use eta_n = 1/(q_{n+1} + q_n * [0; a_{n+2}, a_{n+3}, ...]).

[Lemma 1 (A sufficient Lyapunov condition for discounted integrability) of arXiv:2606.17517, 'Killed resolvents and measure-valued stopping gains for reflected optimal stopping with ma'] Suppose there exists a function $\Psi\in C^2(\R^2_+)$, $\Psi\ge1$, satisfying
the reflected Neumann condition
\[
   \partial_i\Psi=0
   \quad\text{on }\{x_i=0\},
   \qquad i=1,2,
\]
and constants $K\ge0$, $\lambda<r$, and $C_\Psi>0$ such that
\[
   \mathcal L\Psi(x)\le \lambda\Psi(x)+K,
   \qquad x\in\interior{\R}^2_+,
\]
and
\[
   G(x)^+ + c(x)\le C_\Psi\Psi(x),
   \qquad x\in\R^2_+.
\]
Then
\[
   \mathbb E_x\left[
      \int_0^\infty e^{-rs}c(X_s)\,ds
   \right]<\infty
   \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   \sup_{t\ge0}
   \mathbb E_x\big[e^{-rt}G(X_t)^+\big]<\infty.
\]

[Theorem 10 of arXiv:2605.21424, 'A dice game, a multinomial walk, and the inverted Dirichlet distribution'] Let \(m\ge 2\).  For all \(n_1,\ldots,n_m\in \N_{\ge 1}\) consider
\[
\pi_1(n_1,\ldots,n_m)=\mathbb{P}(A_2\leq n_2-1,\dotsc,A_m\leq n_m-1) 
\]
where $(A_2,\dotsc,A_m)$ has a negative multinomial distribution with parameters $(n_1;p_2,\dotsc,p_m)$, 
where \(p_\ell=\frac{n_\ell}{n_1+\ldots,n_m}\) for \(\ell\in\{2,\ldots,m\}\).

Then we have the following representations:
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
\(\pi_1(n_1,\ldots,n_m)=\mathbb{P}\left(X_2>\frac{n_2}{n_1},\dotsc,X_m>\frac{n_m}{n_1}\right)\)\\
where $(X_2,\dotsc,X_m)\sim \operatorname{ID}(n_2,\dotsc,n_m;n_1)$.
\item \(\pi_1(n_1,\ldots,n_m)=\mathbb{P}\left(\frac{G_2}{n_2} > \frac{G_1}{n_1},\dotsc,\frac{G_m}{n_m} > \frac{G_1}{n_1}\right)\)\\
where \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\) are independent random variables with \(G_j\sim \operatorname{Gamma}(n_j,1)\), \(j=1,\ldots,m\).
\end{enumerate}

body: [Definition def.interval of arXiv:2607.10105, 'The four-dimensional Anderson model: a case study for critical SPDEs'] Let $A$ be a finite index set, with some linear order $<$. We will call it an \emph{interval} (such as $[1,m]=\{1,\cdots,m\}$). A \emph{subinterval} of $A$ is a subset of form $[a,b]=\{x\in A:a\leq x\leq b\}$. Given a partial pairing $\kappa$ (Definition (def.pairing of the paper)), we say a subinterval $B$ is \emph{fully paired} if $\kappa$ induces a full pairing on $B$. Define $\kappa$ to be \emph{primitive} if no \emph{proper} subinterval is fully paired.
title: Definition def.interval of arXiv:2607.10105

[Proposition largeDeviation of arXiv:2608.17031, 'A shape theorem for periodic branching diffusion'] Fix $x\in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $e\in S^{d-1}$. Let $\lambda_e>0$ be the minimizer in (equation eq:prelimCriticalSpeed of the paper), and recall that $\zeta_e = \lambda_e e$. Let $(Y_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be the solution of (equation eq:SDETiling2.0 of the paper) under the measure $\mathbb{P}_x^{\zeta_e}$. Let $\hat{Y}_t:=(1/t)e\cdot(Y_t-Y_0)$. Let $I_e:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow (-\infty,+\infty]$ be the function defined by
    \begin{equation}
        I_e(\lambda)=\sup_{\eta \in \mathbb{R}} \{ \eta \lambda - [\gamma((\lambda_e+\eta)e)-\gamma(\zeta_e)]\}=[\gamma((\lambda_{e}+\cdot)e)-\gamma(\zeta_e)]^{*}(\lambda).
    \end{equation}
    For a set $A\subset \mathbb{R}$, let $I_e(A):=\inf_{\lambda\in A}I_e(\lambda)$. The following holds:
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
        \item For every closed set $\mathcal{C}\subset \mathbb{R}$, $\limsup_{t\rightarrow \infty}\sup_{x\in \mathbb{R}^d}\frac{1}{t}\log \mathbb{P}_x^{\zeta_e}[\hat{Y}_t \in \mathcal{C}]\leq -I_e(\mathcal{C})$.
        \item For every open set $\mathcal{O}\subset \mathbb{R}$, $\liminf_{t\rightarrow \infty}\inf_{x\in \mathbb{R}^d}\frac{1}{t}\log  \mathbb{P}_x^{\zeta_e}[\hat{Y}_t \in \mathcal{O}]\geq -I_e(\mathcal{O})$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition defn:UDS_ of arXiv:2609.02491, 'Generalised Random Parking for Trapeziums on a Strip'] \textbf{Depositing on $\mathcal{P}_x$:} The following scheme defines how we deposit the trapezium $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$ on $\mathcal{P}_x$. Let $x>a$, and let $\tau \sim \mathcal{U}(0,2x-2a).$ 
If $\tau \in (0,x-a)$, we deposit the left-most point of $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$, $\tau$ into the upper baseline of $\mathcal{P}_x$. If $\tau \in [x-a,2x-2a)$, we deposit the left-most point of $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$, $y=\tau+a-x$ into the lower baseline of $\mathcal{P}_x$. (Illustrated in Figure~(fig:trapezium_arriving_possible_strips of the paper)(a) \&~(b).)

\textbf{Depositing on $\mathcal{T}_x$:} The following scheme defines how we deposit the trapezium $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$ on $\mathcal{T}_x$. To do so, we will split into two cases: (i) if $(a+b)/2<
x< (3a-b)/2$, and (ii) $x \ge (3a-b)/2$. 
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=3em]
    \item[{\textbf{(i)}}] Assume that $(a+b)/2
< x< (3a-b)/2$, in which case we can only deposit on the lower baseline of $\mathcal{T}_x$. Hence, let $\tau \sim \mathcal{U}(0,x-(a+b)/2)$, and deposit $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$, $\tau$ into the lower baseline of $\mathcal{T}_x$. (Illustrated in Figure~(fig:trapezium_arriving_possible_strips of the paper)(e).)
\item[{\textbf{(ii)}}] Let $x\ge (3a-b)/2$, and $\tau \sim \mathcal{U}(0,2x-2a)$. If $\tau \in (0,x-(3a-b)/2)$, we deposit the left-most point of $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$, $\tau$ into the upper baseline of $\mathcal{T}_x$. If $\tau \in [x-(3a-b)/2,2x-2a)$, we deposit the left-most point of $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$, $y=\tau-(x-(3a-b)/2)$ into the lower baseline of $\mathcal{T}_x$. (Illustrated in Figure~(fig:trapezium_arriving_possible_strips of the paper)(c) \&~(d).)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Algorithm:} When a trapezium $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$ has been deposited on either $\mathcal{P}_x$ or $\mathcal{T}_x$, there will be two leftover strips. Conditional on the first deposition, the parking procedures on these two strips are defined to be independent copies of the $\mathcal{UDA}$, with the corresponding strip types and sizes. 
This procedure is continued recursively until there are no strips remaining which can fit $\mathcal{T}_{(a+b)/2}$.
title: Definition of $\mathcal{UDA}$

body:
For case weights $s_1, \dots, s_n \ge 0$ not all zero, the effective sample size is $n_{\mathrm{eff}} = (\sum_i s_i)^2 / \sum_i s_i^2$. It satisfies $1 \le n_{\mathrm{eff}} \le n$, with $n_{\mathrm{eff}} = n$ if and only if all nonzero weights are equal and $n_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1$ if and only if a single weight is nonzero. Its meaning: if $X_1, \dots, X_n$ are i.i.d. with variance $\sigma^2$, the weighted mean $\bar X_s = \sum_i s_i X_i / \sum_i s_i$ has variance $\sigma^2 / n_{\mathrm{eff}}$ - the weighted mean is as noisy as an unweighted mean of $n_{\mathrm{eff}}$ observations. The same factor governs every entry of a weighted sample covariance $\sum_i s_i (x_i - \bar x_s)(x_i - \bar x_s)^T / \sum_i s_i$ to leading order, so entrywise concentration bounds for the sample covariance transfer to the weighted one with $n$ replaced by $n_{\mathrm{eff}}$. For the per-sample relative metric of ensemble stacking, $s_i = 1/\|y_i\|^2$, a few small-norm cases can make $n_{\mathrm{eff}}$ far smaller than $n$ (measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT pool: 150 of 932 rows on one component, 8.7 of 60 in the $n = 60$ arm). (Why: $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_s) = \sum_i s_i^2 \sigma^2 / (\sum_i s_i)^2 = \sigma^2 / n_{\mathrm{eff}}$ by independence. The bounds: Cauchy-Schwarz gives $(\sum_i s_i)^2 \le n \sum_i s_i^2$ with equality iff the nonzero weights are equal (restricting to the nonzero ones), and $(\sum_i s_i)^2 \ge \sum_i s_i^2$ since the cross terms are nonnegative, with equality iff at most one weight is nonzero. For the covariance, each entry is a weighted mean of the products $(x_{ik} - \bar x_{s,k})(x_{il} - \bar x_{s,l})$ with the same weights, and the centring changes the variance only at second order in $1/n_{\mathrm{eff}}$.)

[Proposition prop:carpet-clock of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] The amplitude flow $s \mapsto u_{s}$ has period $1$, so the flow of
		laws is periodic in $\tau$ with period $4/\pi$. The density flow
		$s \mapsto w_{s}$ has minimal period $\tfrac18$: for every law and
		every $\tau$,
		\begin{equation}
			f_{\tau + \frac{1}{2\pi}} = f_{\tau},
			\qquad
			u_{s+1/8} = e^{-i\pi/4}\,u_{s}.
			
		\end{equation}
		Within one period the density flow is a palindrome,
		$w_{1/8 - s} = w_{s}$, and at every time the kernel is symmetric
		about the median rank, $w_{s}(1-z) = w_{s}(z)$.
title: The observable clock

[Prop Aut-h-Vect of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The only automorphism of $\ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus$ in $\CMon(\textup{Ho}(\Spc_\textup{Glo}))$ is the identity.
    \begin{proof}
        If $f$ is any such automorphism, then $f({\mathbb{R}})\cong{\mathbb{R}}$ since this is the only object of $\ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus(1)$ generating it under the symmetric monoidal product. As $f$ is symmetric monoidal up to incoherent equivalence, we conclude that $f({\mathbb{R}}^n)\cong{\mathbb{R}}^n$, and hence $\dim f(V)= \dim V$ for any representation $V$ by naturality. Thus, $f$ preserves the decomposition $\ul\textup{Rep}\simeq\coprod_{n\ge0}\BGcat{{\textup{O}}(n)}$, and we can therefore identify it with a family of conjugacy classes of isomorphisms $f_n\colon{\textup{O}}(n)\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}{\textup{O}}(n)$ such that the diagram
        \[
            \begin{tikzcd}
                {\textup{O}}(m)\times{\textup{O}}(n)\arrow[r,"f_m\times f_n"]\arrow[d,hook] &[1em] {\textup{O}}(m)\times{\textup{O}}(n)\arrow[d,hook]\\
                {\textup{O}}(m+n)\arrow[r,"f_{m+n}"'] & {\textup{O}}(m+n)
            \end{tikzcd}
        \]
        commutes up to conjugation for every $m,n\ge0$. We want to show that all $f_n$ are inner automorphisms, which is trivial for $n=0,1$, while for $n=2$ this is an instance of the previous lemma. For $n\ge3$, we then see by applying the compatibility condition inductively that $f_n$ sends any block matrix of the form $((eq:orth-normal-form of the paper))$ to an element conjugate to itself, so it is an inner automorphism by Corollary~(cor:uniqueness-maps-to-O(n) of the paper).
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop Aut-h-Vect of arXiv:2608.28504

body: Let G be a connected finite simple graph with maximum degree Delta(G). If G is neither a complete graph nor an odd cycle, then the chromatic number satisfies chi(G) <= Delta(G). (If G is a complete graph K_n, chi(G) = n = Delta(G)+1; if G is an odd cycle, Delta(G) = 2 and chi(G) = 3 = Delta(G)+1.) [Brooks (1941); see Diestel, Graph Theory]
title: Brooks' Theorem (Vertex-Chromatic Number Bound)

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, The stationary law of the leftmost particles in Aldous's drift-jump process (2026). In Aldous's drift-jump process, k particles 0 < X_1 < ... < X_k move right with velocity equal to their position, and at the events of a rate-one space-time Poisson process the nearest particle to the right of the event jumps to it; Aldous (open problem, February 2018) asked for a fairly explicit description of the stationary distribution. The paper proves that the stationary distribution is unique and the law at time t converges to it in total variation from every start, and that in stationarity X_i = Gamma_{tau_i}, where Gamma_1 < Gamma_2 < ... is a rate-one Poisson process and, independently, tau_i is the first n at which the longest increasing subsequence of n independent uniforms reaches length i (a form of representation (42) in the 1993 notes of Aldous and Diaconis). Every joint survival probability P(X_{k_1} > s_1, ..., X_{k_r} > s_r) equals e^{-s_r} times a finite determinant with modified-Bessel-function entries, of size at most k(k-1) for the first k particles; for one particle it is Gessel's Toeplitz determinant. E(X_i - X_{i-1}) is the constant c(i) of Aldous and Diaconis (1999) for the i-th pile in patience sorting. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/drift-jump-leftmost-particles (commit c315f47b0278). Not refereed.
title: The stationary law of the leftmost particles in Aldous's drift-jump process: a Poisson-process and longest-increasing-subsequence representation with Bessel determinants (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/drift-jump-leftmost-particles)

For a square-integrable function f of finitely many independent coordinates, let f_S be its orthogonal coordinate-average product projections. Refresh each coordinate independently at rate one, and set C_f(t)=Cov(f(W),f(W^t)), E_f(t)=-C_f'(t), and H_f(t)=exp(t)E_f(t). Then L=sum_{|S|=1}||f_S||_2^2 is the limit of H_f(t), R_f(t)=H_f(t)-L=sum_{|S|>=2}|S|exp(-(|S|-1)t)||f_S||_2^2 is nonnegative, and Var(f)=L+integral_0^infinity exp(-t)R_f(t)dt. If L>0, no bound H_f(t)<=A F(Bt) for all t>=0 can hold with finite positive A,B and a nonnegative integrable F. The weighted energy E_f itself tends to zero; the floor concerns the unweighted convention only.

[Proposition 3 (Correctness of \EVIBQ) of arXiv:2608.22227, '\fontsize{18pt}{20pt}\selectfont \bf Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning with Smoothed Q'] Fix an episode \(t\), a target quantile level \(\tau\in(0,1)\), and a buffer
\(\beta_t\in(0,\tau]\). Suppose that \(\mathcal C_\delta^t\) is nonempty and
that the maximizers in Algorithm~\ref{alg:EVI-BQ} exist. Then the returned pair
\((P^t,\pi^t)\) satisfies $P^t\in\mathcal C_\delta^t$ and $V_{\tau,0}^{\pi^t,P^t,\beta_t}(\bar s)
= \max_{P\in\mathcal C_\delta^t}
\max_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{det}}}
V_{\tau,0}^{\pi,P,\beta_t}(\bar s)$. Consequently, Algorithm~\ref{alg:EVI-BQ} exactly implements the optimistic
buffered re-planning step required by Algorithm~\ref{alg:UCB--BQRL}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:cutsets->paths of arXiv:2503.21737, 'High-intensity Voronoi percolation on manifolds'] Assume that $M$ satisfies the conditions of Theorem (thm:main of the paper). 
    Let $\varepsilon>0$ and  $x\in V_\varepsilon$.
    There exists a constant $C_1$ independent of $\varepsilon$ and $x$ as well as constants $C_0=C_0(\varepsilon,x),c_0=c_0(\varepsilon,x)>0$  such that the following holds:
    For every $k\ge 1$ there exists a subset  $V_k^x \subset V_\varepsilon$ such that $|V_k^x|\le C_0e^{C_1\varepsilon k}$ and, for every $n\geq 1$, any
    connected cutset contained in $G_\varepsilon \setminus B_{G_\varepsilon}(x,n)$ separating $B_{G_\varepsilon}(x,n)$ from infinity contains at least one path in
    \[\bigcup_{k\ge c_0\log n-C_0}\bigcup_{v\in V_k^x}\mathcal{P}_{\varepsilon}(v,k).\]

body:
[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2608.12839, 'Spiking Neural Networks with Elephant Reinforcement'] Let
$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_0
=
(\mu_{1,0},\ldots,\mu_{N,0})
\in\mathcal P(E)^N
$
be an arbitrary family of initial probability measures.

Then there exists a unique family of laws
$
\boldsymbol{\mu}(t)
=
(\mu_1(t),\ldots,\mu_N(t))$, 
$t\geq0$,
such that, for every bounded function \(f:E\to\mathbb R\),
\[
\int_E f(x)\,\mu_i(t)(dx)
=
\int_E f(x)\,\mu_{i,0}(dx)
+
\int_0^t
\int_E
\mathcal A_{i,\boldsymbol{\mu}(u)}f(x)
\,\mu_i(u)(dx)\,du.
\]

Equivalently, there exists a unique in law family of nonlinear jump processes
\[
X_i(t)
=
\bigl(V_i(t),S_i(t),K_i(t)\bigr),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,N,
\]
such that
\[
\mathcal L(X_i(t))=\mu_i(t)
\]
and
\[
\beta_i(t)
=
\mathbb E\left[
\mathbf 1_{\{
V_i(t)>\alpha S_i^{+}(t)
\}}
\right].
\]

Moreover, each process is non-explosive.

[Proposition 48 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let \(k\) be a perfect field of characteristic \(p>0\), let \(C\) be a
smooth projective curve over \(k\), and let
\[
\pi\colon Y \to  C
\]
be a smooth projective morphism of relative dimension \(n\).
Assume that
\[
R^{q}\pi_*
\left(
\Omega^b_{Y/C}\otimes\omega_{Y/C}
\right)=0
\]
for every \(0\leq b\leq n\) and every \(q<n\).

body:
[Lemma 3 of arXiv:2609.03669, 'Volterra Integral Reduction \\ for Boundary Diffusion Problems'] For every compact set $K\subset\mathbb R$, we set $K':=\psi(K)$. For $u,v\in K'$, introduce
\begin{equation}

F(t,u,v)
:=
\mathbb E^{t,v}_{0,u}
\left[
\exp\left(
-\int_0^tV(W_s)\,ds
\right)
\right].
\end{equation}
Then, as $t\to0^+$,
\begin{align}
F(t,u,v)
&=
1-t\overline{V}(u,v)
+
O_{K'}(t^2),

\\
\partial_uF(t,u,v)
&=
-t\,\partial_u\overline{V}(u,v)
+
O_{K'}(t^{3/2}),

\end{align}
uniformly for $(u,v)\in K'\times K'$.

$$
\P_{u_0}[X_1=u_1,\dots,X_n=u_n] = \P_{u_0'}[X_1=u'_1,\dots,X_n=u'_n].
$$

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2606.01881, '2606.01881'] For Bernoulli bond percolation with fixed $p\in[0,1]$ on the canonically coupled RRT, define the one-time leadership probabilities and their limiting value by
\[
        q_n(p):=\Pp\bigl(1\in\Pi^{(n),\downarrow}_1\bigr),
        \quad n\ge1,\qquad
        \theta(p):=\lim_{n\to\infty}q_n(p),
\]
whose existence is justified in Remark~\ref{rem:limit-pn}.  Also define
\[
        \rho(p):=\Pp\bigl(1\in\Pi^{(n),\downarrow}_1\text{ for all }n\ge1\bigr).
\]
Then, for every $p\in[0,1]$,
\[
        0<\rho(p)\le \theta(p).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary cor:FP-one-point of arXiv:2608.02772, 'Non-Abelian Hirota-Miwa Equations for the KPZ Universality Class'] For $m = 1$, the Fredholm determinant
$F_{t,x,a} = \det_{L^2(\mathbb{R})}(I - K_{t,x,a})$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
\Bigl[D_{t,a} + \tfrac{1}{4}D_x^2
+ \tfrac{1}{12}D_a^4\Bigr] F \cdot F = 0,
\end{equation}
which is KP-II in Hirota bilinear form.

[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2609.02711, 'Differentiability of the Leading Lyapunov Exponent \\ of a linear differential equation wi'] Assume that Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:un} is satisfied and that for a
  fixed $z\in (a,b)$ we have integral separation for the random
  dynamical system
  \begin{equation}
    \frac{dy}{dt} = A(z,\omega_t) y\,.
  \end{equation}
Assume furthermore that for some $\delta>0$,
$\esp{\Gamma_z^{-(1+\delta)}}< +\infty$. Then for any initial value
$(y_0,0)$ with $y_0\in\rdpp$, the solution $(y(t),\partial_zy(t))$ of the random linear
differential system
\begin{align}
  \frac{dy}{dt} &= A(z,\omega_t) y\\
  \frac{d\partial_z y}{dt} &= A(z,\omega_t) \partial_z y + \partial_z A(z,\omega_t)
  y
\end{align}
satisfies, for any sequence $t_n \ge n^{\unsur{1+\delta}}$,
\begin{equation}
  \lim_{n\to +\infty} \frac{\crochet{\partial_zy(t_n),\vun}}{t_n
    \crochet{y(t_n),\vun}} = \Lambda'(z)\quad a.s.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let rows $w_1,\dots,w_{m-1}$ be i.i.d. isotropic in $\mathbb{R}^m$ ($m=\dim\mathrm{Sym}_d^0$ or $\dim\mathrm{Sym}_d$), let $c$ be the unit null vector of the design they span, and let $A$ be the unit-Frobenius symmetric matrix it encodes. By isotropy $\sqrt d\,A$ converges in moments to the semicircle law, so $d^{k-1}\,\mathbb{E}\,\mathrm{Tr}(A^{2k}) = C_k + b_k/d + O(1/d^2)$ with $C_k$ the Catalan numbers. The correction constant $b_k$ is NOT a function of the row's fourth moment alone. Evidence at $d=14$ over $\sim10^5$ designs per row law: (i) rows with i.i.d. coordinates of kurtosis $\kappa$ give $b_k$ a function of $\kappa$ only, a three-point law and a Gaussian at $\kappa=3$ agreeing to $0.2$--$0.5$ standard errors on $k=2,3,4,5$ while $\kappa\in[1,9]$ moves the excess by a factor $2.3$; (ii) but two constructions with the SAME typical-direction kurtosis and different dependence disagree by an order of magnitude --- a rank-one Veronese row (kurtosis $3+24/d$) and an i.i.d. row matched to that kurtosis give $k=2$ excess $0.462$ versus $0.041$, a factor $11$; (iii) interpolating with $z=(XX^\top-rI)/\sqrt{2r}$, a sum of $r$ independent rank-one forms, the excess falls roughly as $1/r$ ($0.46,0.23,0.13,0.085$ at $r=1,2,4,8$) while the kurtosis $3+12\,\mathrm{Tr}(U^4)/r \to 3$. So within one dependence class the fourth moment tunes $b_k$, but across classes at fixed fourth moment $b_k$ varies by a factor of order ten; a derivation of $b_k$ for the Veronese row ($b_2\approx7.7$, $b_3\approx49$, $b_4\approx248$, $b_5\approx1148$) must use the rank-one dependence of $xx^\top$, not a kurtosis.

[Definition 173 (The fundamental $L^2$-velocity-controlling quantities) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] Let $\blowuprateofwaveWRTnumberofcommutations(N)$ denote the powers of $\weight$ from Def.\,\ref{D:NOTATIONFORPOWERSOFWEIGHT}.  Let $1 \le N \le \Ntop$ be an integer. Then in terms of the null-flux quantities of Def.\,\ref{D:NULLFLUXESFORTHEWAVEANDTRANSPORTVARIABLES} 
	and the differentiated conventions of Def.\,\ref{D:STRINGSOFCOMMUTATIONVECTORFIELDS}, 
	we define the following $L^2$-controlling quantities:
	\begin{subequations}
			\begin{align}  
				\begin{split} 
					\totalfluxcontrolvelocity_N(\ubar,u) 
					& 
					\eqdef 
					\max_{\tander^N \in \mathcal{P}^{(N)}}
					\sup_{\substack{\ubar' \in [\leftubar,\ubar] 
							\\
							u' \in [\moreinterestingu_1,u]}} 					
					\sum_{i=1}^3			
					\left\lbrace 
					 \ingoingfluxwave{\blowuprateofwaveWRTnumberofcommutations(N)}\left[\tander^N v^i\right](\ubar',u') + 
					\outgoingfluxwave{\blowuprateofwaveWRTnumberofcommutations(N)}\left[\tander^N v^i\right](\ubar',u')
					\right\rbrace,  
				\end{split}
				\\
				\strongangularcontrolvelocity_N(\ubar,u) 
				& 
				\eqdef 
					\max_{\tander^N \in \mathcal{P}^{(N)}} \sum_{i=1}^3
						\spacetimecoercive{\blowuprateofwaveWRTnumberofcommutations(N)}\left[\angrmD \tander^N v^i\right] (\ubar,u), 
				  \\			
				\weakspacetimeangularvelocitycontrol_N(\ubar,u) & \eqdef 
					\begin{cases}
						\max_{\tander^N \in \mathcal{P}^{(N)}} \sum_{i=1}^3
						\newspacetimecoercive{\blowuprateofwaveWRTnumberofcommutations(N) - 1}\left[\sqrt{\upmu + 2 \ReciprocaluLunitAppliedtoTimeFunction \upmu} \nullangrmD \tander^N v^i\right] (\ubar,u),  & \blowuprateofwaveWRTnumberofcommutations(N) > 0, \\
						0 & \blowuprateofwaveWRTnumberofcommutations(N) = 0, 
					\end{cases}
					 \\	
				\weakspacetimetransvelocitycontrol_N(\ubar,u) 
				& 
				\eqdef
					\begin{cases}
						\max_{\tander^N \in \mathcal{P}^{(N)}} 
						\sum_{i=1}^3
						\newspacetimecoercive{\blowuprateofwaveWRTnumberofcommutations(N) - 1}\left[ \newuL \tander^N v^i\right] (\ubar,u), & \blowuprateofwaveWRTnumberofcommutations(N) > 0 \\
						0 & \blowuprateofwaveWRTnumberofcommutations(N) = 0,
					\end{cases}   
				\\		
				\totalcontrolwave_N(\ubar,u)
				&				
				\eqdef 
				\totalfluxcontrolvelocity_N(\ubar,u) +
				\strongangularcontrolvelocity_N(\ubar,u) + \weakspacetimetransvelocitycontrol_N(\ubar,u)  + \weakspacetimeangularvelocitycontrol_N(\ubar,u),
				
			\end{align}
		\end{subequations}
title: The fundamental $L^2$-velocity-controlling quantities

[Lemma 14 of arXiv:2608.11031, 'A Bayesian Proof of the Bernoulli Theorem'] Let $\mu\in\cP(T)$, let $X\sim\mu$, and let $k_0<k_1$ be integers
such that
\[
  r_{k_0}\ge2\diam_\infty(T).
\]
Suppose that $U_{k_0},\ldots,U_{k_1}$ are conditionally independent
given $X$ and satisfy $U_k\sim\mu$ for every $k=k_0,\ldots,k_1$.
Assume in addition that $U_{k_0}$ is independent of $X$ and that
$U_{k_1}=X$.  For $k=k_0,\ldots,k_1$, set
\[
  d_k:=\E\varphi_{r_k}(X,U_k),
  \qquad
  q_k:=I(X;U_k).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
  \delta_T(\mu)
  \le
  \frac{17}{2}\sum_{k=k_0+1}^{k_1-1}r_kd_k
  +\frac{9}{2\sqrt2}\sum_{k=k_0}^{k_1}r_k(d_k+q_k).
  
\end{equation}

body:
[Corollary cor:cheeger-uniform of arXiv:2606.27073, 'Retention Profiles and KL Contraction Bounds in Finite Markov Chains'] If $\pi$ is uniform, the Cheeger cut has $|A|\le n/2$, and
$h_P\le 1-|A|/n$, then
\[
  M
  \;\ge\;
  \frac{(1-h_P)\log\frac{n(1-h_P)}{|A|}
  +h_P\log\frac{nh_P}{n-|A|}}{\log n}.
\]
For small $h_P$, $M\gtrsim 1-\log|A|/\log n$.
In particular, if $|A|=O(n^\alpha)$ for $\alpha\in(0,1)$, then
$M\ge 1-\alpha+o(1)$.

[Pre-prop 2.2 of arXiv:2412.00708, 'Stochastic PDE approach to fluctuating interfaces'] Consider the SPDE (equation eq:2.3-1 of the paper) with $n=3$.
Then, $\widetilde{\Psi} = \widetilde{\Psi}^{N,K}$ 
defined by (equation eq:2.stretch of the paper) satisfies the following SPDE in law
\begin{align}  
\partial_t \widetilde{\Psi}(t,z,\underline{x}) = & (- K \mathcal{A}^K_z + \Delta_{\underline{x}})
\widetilde{\Psi}(t,z,\underline{x})  
+ KN^{-d/2} \tfrac12 f''(\bar v^K(z)) \widetilde{\Psi}(t,z,\underline{x})^2  \\
& + KN^{-d}\tfrac16 f'''(\bar v^K(z)) \widetilde{\Psi}(t,z, \underline{x})^3 \notag \\
&+   K^{3/4}\partial_z \big( g_1(\bar v^K(z))\dot{W}^1(t,z,\underline{x})\big) + K^{1/4}
g_1(\bar v^K(z))\nabla_{\underline{x}} \cdot \dot{{\mathbb W}}^2(t,z,\underline{x})  \notag \\
& + K^{3/4} g_2(\bar v^K(z)) \dot{W}(t,z,\underline{x}), 
\notag
\end{align}
for $ (z,\underline{x}) \in \sqrt{K}{\mathbb{T}} \times {\mathbb{T}}^{d-1}$.
Then, $\Psi$ defined by (equation eq:2.2-4 of the paper)  satisfies the SPDE 
\begin{align}  
\partial_t \Psi = & (- K \mathcal{A}_z^K + \Delta_{\underline{x}})\Psi 
+ K^{7/4} N^{-d/2} \tfrac12 f''(\bar v^K(z)) \Psi(t,z,\underline{x})^2 \\
& + K^{5/2}N^{-d}\tfrac16 f'''(\bar v^K(z)) \Psi(t,z, \underline{x})^3  \notag
\\
& +  \partial_z \big( g_1(\bar v^K(z)) \dot{W}^1(t,z,\underline{x})\big) + K^{-1/2}
g_1(\bar v^K(z)) \nabla_{\underline{x}} \cdot \dot{{\mathbb W}}^2(t,z,\underline{x})  \notag  \\
&  + g_2(\bar v^K(z)) \dot{W}(t,z,\underline{x}),  \notag
\end{align}
for $(z,\underline{x})\in \sqrt{K}{\mathbb{T}}\times{\mathbb{T}}^{d-1}$.

[Prop adjshiftproperties of arXiv:2510.23430, 'On the Martin boundary for discrete TASEP'] (1) For any partition $\lambda$ we have $\rho_\gamma^*(g_\lambda^{(\mathfrak a,\mathfrak b)})=g_\lambda^{(\mathfrak a+\gamma,\mathfrak b-\gamma)}$. In particular $\rho^*_\gamma$ defines a map $\Lambda\to\Lambda$.

(2) The action of $\rho_\gamma^*$ on complete symmetric functions is described by
$$
\rho_\gamma^*(H(z))=H\left(\frac{z}{1-\gamma z}\right)=\prod_{i}\frac{1-\gamma z}{1-(x_i+\gamma)z}.
$$
(3) We have $\omega \rho_\gamma^*=\rho_{-\gamma}^*\omega$.

body:
Load-bearing hypothesis: $\hat f\in L^1$. For $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^d)$ the transform $\hat f$ is bounded and continuous but need not be integrable, and then $\int\hat f(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\xi}d\xi$ is not defined as a Lebesgue integral at any $x$. Counterexample: $f=\mathbf 1_{[-1/2,1/2]}$ has $\hat f(\xi)=\sin(\pi\xi)/(\pi\xi)$, which is $O(1/|\xi|)$ and not integrable; only the symmetric improper limit $\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{-R}^R$ exists, and it returns $f(x)$ for $|x|\ne1/2$ but the midpoint value $1/2$ at $x=\pm1/2$. Structural consequence: if $f\in L^1$ and $\hat f\in L^1$ then $f$ equals a continuous function a.e.; so any $f\in L^1$ with an essential jump (an indicator, a sawtooth) automatically has a non-integrable transform - checking $\hat f\in L^1$ is not a formality one may skip. Continuity of $f$ is not sufficient either: the Wiener algebra $A(\mathbb R)=\{\hat g:g\in L^1\}$ is a proper subset of $C_0(\mathbb R)$, and chirps $\varphi(x)e^{i\pi Nx^2}$ with $\varphi$ a fixed bump have bounded sup norm while $\|\widehat{\;\cdot\;}\|_1$ grows like $N^{1/2}$, so no bound $\|\hat f\|_1\le C\|f\|_\infty$ can hold. Safe substitutes when $\hat f\notin L^1$: Gauss-Weierstrass or Abel summation, $\int\hat f(\xi)e^{-\pi\varepsilon^2|\xi|^2}e^{2\pi ix\xi}d\xi\to f(x)$ in $L^1$ and at every Lebesgue point; or work in $\mathcal S'$, where inversion always holds distributionally.

\frac{\mathrm d\bar{\mathbf Z}_t^z}{\mathrm dt}=\bar F_{\mathbf I_t}^1(\bar{\mathbf Z}_t^z),\quad\mathbf Z_0^z=z
\]
with

\end{align*}

body: [Proposition 42 of arXiv:2605.02002, 'Glauber dynamics for random field Ising models on bounded degree graphs and MLSI'] For each $C>0$, suppose that Assumption \ref{thiasssumption} holds for the random field $h$. Then the RFIM $\mu_G$ satisfies $\operatorname{USM}(C)$, and similarly does the RFIM measure $\mu_{\widetilde{G}}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 42 of arXiv:2605.02002

body:
[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] Let $\varphi$ be defined as in Definition \ref{defphi}. Then,
   \[\varphi(i) = {d \choose i}(n-1)^i\]
   \begin{proof}
      Fix $i \in \{0,\dots,d\}$. Now, $\varphi(i)$ counts the number of elements in $\mathbb{Z}_n^d$ with Hamming distance of exactly $i$ from $\hat{1}$. That is, the number of elements with $i$ non-one elements. There are ${d \choose i}$ different choices for which dimensions should be non-one, and $(n-1)$ choices for each of these dimensions. 
   \[\therefore \quad \varphi(i) = {d \choose i}(n-1)^i,\quad \forall i \in \{0,\dots,d\}\]
   \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 6 of arXiv:2604.07478

body:
[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2608.25971, 'Positive \texorpdfstring{$\tau$}{tau}-bi-Ricci curvature and Mean curvature flow with surg'] If the induced metric has nonnegative $\tau$-bi-Ricci curvature, then its
scalar curvature is nonnegative and the norm of its mean-curvature vector is
at least $n\kappa$.  If $\kappa>0$, the mean-curvature vector is nowhere zero.
Thus the normal can be chosen so
that $H\geq n\kappa$.  Under strict positivity, the same conclusion holds for
every $\kappa\geq0$, with $H>n\kappa$.
title: Lemma 4 of arXiv:2608.25971

[Prop sep.comp of arXiv:2412.00822, '\textsc{Ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellations \\ beyond hyperbolic spaces}'] The separation from $z=(z_{1},z_{2}) \in \mathcal{M}$ to $(\theta, \phi, r) \in  \widetilde{\partial \mathcal{M}}$ is given by
\[
\mathbf{d}\bigl(z, (\theta,\phi, r)\bigr)
=
\rcases
{\displaystyle \frac{r}{K(z_{1}, \theta)K(z_{2}, \phi)} &\mbox{in the product of discs model,}\\[10pt]
\displaystyle \frac{r}{\widehat K(z_{1}, \theta)\widehat K(z_{2}, \phi)} &\mbox{in the product of upper half-planes model,}\\
}
\]
where $K(z, \theta)$ and $\widehat K(z, \theta)$ are respectively the hyperbolic Poisson kernel and the modified hyperbolic Poisson kernel defined in~[IPVT23]. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); independent mathematical, priority and target-scope audit pending. # Unsaturated unequal truth unions: exact zero-budget conditional frontier

T379-C017 v3, proof (unaudited), exact reduction and TV-rigidity suites PASS.
Independent mathematical, primary-source priority and target-scope review pending.
Target 1, secondary target 2. The missing general case has saturated
known supports or calibration budget beyond the interval proved below.

## Statement and experiment

Integers d>=1,N>=2d+1,K>=2,1<=r<K. Each of d context pairs has one A
and one S, with VC-d orientation class; N-2d remaining contexts are
known S. S has all K truths; each A has an independent uniform r-subset.
The factual source chooses contexts uniformly, then truths uniformly.
Training consists of actual iid factual context/candidate samples,
without partition tags. An independent verifier may supply ell true
candidates per variable context, uniformly without replacement, also
without orientation labels. Include those identities in the known
truth union C_x. Condition on ANY positive-probability data outcome
with sizes j_x=|C_x|<r in EVERY variable context. Counts and identities
may differ arbitrarily between siblings. Every orientation remains
compatible; compatible A supports contain C_A. The actual posterior
orientation probabilities need not be uniform.

Require exact source Mis_infinity=0 in EVERY compatible world, using
the uniform coarsening within exact g-probability bins. Allow all g.
Set h_i=min(j_left,j_right) for pair i and

 b_h=[1/K+(r-h)/(r(K-h))]/(2N).

The proposed exact CONDITIONAL worst-world false-mass frontier is

 V(0)=sum_{i=1}^d (K-r)*b_{h_i}.                        (1)

An attainer has this risk in every actual compatible world. This is
not an assertion that all other generators have a pointwise lower
bound (C015's varying-count control disproves that). No unconditional
expected minimax value is inferred from (1).

For the same known truths with the partition additionally supplied,
the conditional worst-world oracle value is

 O_worst(0)=sum_i (K-r)*(r-h_i)/(Nr(K-h_i)).              (2)

Thus the exact worst-oracle estimation gap is

 V(0)-O_worst(0)
   =sum_i h_i*(K-r)^2/(2NrK(K-h_i)).                    (3)

The oracle in (2) takes a maximum over supplied orientations; it is
not the average actual-orientation oracle. Formula (3) weights the
conditional 1/N-per-pair classification error of the specified fair
completion of support-consistent ERM. No statistically optimal ERM
rate or general unweighted-error identity is claimed.

## Residual support variability forces one score level

Fix ANY robustly zero-calibrated generator g and its exact score
partition Pi. In every bin B, p_world(B)=g(B) for every compatible
world, hence its source mass is invariant under changing supports or
orientations. For a context x possibly A, let Q_x be its K-j_x
uncertified atoms. Since 1<=r-j_x<K-j_x, any two atoms of Q_x can be
swapped in a compatible A support while all other truth identities
remain fixed. If one were in B and the other outside, this swap would
change p(B) by 1/(Nr), contradicting invariance. Therefore each bin
contains either ALL or NONE of Q_x. Equivalently all Q_x atoms have
one common score; denote their unique bin B_x.

This argument FAILS if j_x=r, since there is then no residual truth
to swap. C016's neutral-bundle counterexample exploits exactly this
boundary, rather than contradicting the present strict hypothesis.

## Classifying each pair's invariant bins

Write s=j_L<=t=j_R<r for one pair; relabel siblings if necessary.
For a bin B let u_x=|B intersect C_x| and epsilon_x=1 if Q_x is in B,
else zero. The difference between its A-context and S-context source
contributions is

 delta_x(B)=(K-r)/(NrK)*(u_x-epsilon_x*j_x).

Independent flipping of this pair's orientation while holding all
other pairs fixed implies delta_L(B)=delta_R(B) for EVERY bin.

If B_L!=B_R, then in B_L the left delta is nonpositive and the right
delta nonnegative. Equality forces u_L=s,u_R=0. Similarly B_R has
u_R=t,u_L=0. Thus each context lies entirely in its own one score bin.

If B_L=B_R=B*, equality gives

 k=s-u_L=t-u_R, 0<=k<=s.

Outside B* every bin contains only known truths from these contexts
and contains the SAME number of known truths from each sibling.
Exactly k known truths from each sibling lie outside B*.

## Reduction to the balanced-count game

For each pair retain the smaller context's complete known set C_L.
In the larger context retain a subset C'_R of size s. If the residual
bins are different, choose any such subset. If they coincide in B*,
retain ALL k larger-context known truths outside B* and choose any
s-k additional known truths inside B*. This is possible since there
are t-k>=s-k such inside truths. The sets may depend on g; this is
a proof comparison, not the algorithm.

Expand the compatible world set by forgetting the t-s surplus truths
in the larger context. In the distinct-bin case both contexts had
one score, so every source bin mass and every false-atom count per
bin are unchanged under this expansion. In the common-bin case all
newly uncertified atoms lie in B*. Every other bin retains the same
known-true counts; in B* the A context always has r-k true atoms and
K-r false atoms, in either orientation and for every expanded support.
Thus again each source bin mass and each actual false-count-per-bin
vector is unchanged.

Do this independently for every pair. For the same fixed g,

* robust zero calibration holds on the EXPANDED balanced-count game;
* the set of possible false masses across its worlds equals the set
  across the original compatible worlds, orientation by orientation.

The expanded game has balanced known counts h_i and arbitrary known
identities. It need not preserve the original sample/verifier labels:
it is an enlarged source-world comparison, not a claimed posterior.
C015's general balanced-count lower bound at c=0 therefore yields
max_original H(g)=max_expanded H(g)>=sum_i(K-r)b_{h_i}.
Dependence of the selected balanced sets on g causes no problem:
the balanced theorem is uniform over all sets of the stated sizes.

## Balanced comparison lower bound, stated here for completeness

For the expanded known sets of balanced sizes h_i, average orientations
fairly and average compatible residual supports uniformly. This is an
artificial lower-bound distribution, not the actual posterior. Its
mean factual law mu gives density a=(1/r+1/K)/(2N) to known truths,
b_h to uncertified atoms in count-h pairs, and 1/(NK) to fixed S.
The false probability of each uncertified atom is tau_h=(K-r)/(2(K-h)).
As h increases b_h decreases and tau_h increases; safe densities are
at least 1/(NK)>=b_h. For E_h the union of uncertified atoms in pairs
with count at least h, every inside density is <=every outside
density. Uniform coarsening in any bin transfers mass INTO E_h, so
mu_Pi(E_h)>=mu(E_h)=T_h with T_h as in (6). Robust feasibility and
TV convexity imply TV(mu_Pi,g)<=c, hence g(E_h)>=(T_h-c)_+.
The artificial average false risk is exactly
tau_0*g(E_0)+sum_{h=1}^{r-1}(tau_h-tau_{h-1})*g(E_h).
It is at least (6), and the maximum original risk equals the maximum
expanded risk and is at least this average. This proves the needed
balanced lower bound directly, for c=0 and throughout (4), without
requiring a prior-card theorem or any actual posterior identity.

## Attainment and oracle comparison

Select h_i known truths from each sibling before constructing g. Put
their two known-true groups at score (1/r+1/K)/(2N); put the remaining
2(K-h_i) pair atoms at b_{h_i}, and fixed S atoms at 1/(NK).
Each pair group has invariant p mass under all original worlds.
Exact-score mergers preserve invariance. This g is robustly calibrated
with zero budget, and each actual world's K-r false atoms per pair
all receive b_{h_i}. This proves the matching upper bound in (1).

If a supplied orientation chooses A at count j, the zero-budget oracle
has risk (K-r)*(r-j)/(Nr(K-j)), by the ordered known-A-group argument
of C009/C015. This quantity decreases with j, so its maximum over
independent orientations picks j=h_i in every pair, proving (2).
Subtracting gives (3) exactly.

This is a whole strict-unsaturation data region for arbitrary d,N,K,r,
not a theorem deduced from nine small finite partition searches. It
uses robust zero calibration critically and does not extend to c>0
by continuity alone. Saturated-context neutral bins are a real excluded
mechanism. Primary source statistic: Kalai--Vempala 2311.14648v3,
Definitions 1--2 pp.8--9. C015 is an own unaudited draft whose balanced
lower-bound proof is required here; its primary-source priority and
all current independent mathematical/target-scope audits are pending.

## A nonzero calibration-budget interval via discrete TV jumps

The reduction extends to EVERY budget

 0<=c<c_star=(K-r)/(2NrK).                               (4)

Let Pi be the exact score partition of any robustly c-feasible g.
For any two compatible worlds w,w', the triangle inequality gives

 TV(p_w,Pi,p_w',Pi)<=2c.                                (5)

If a context's uncertified atoms occupy two different score bins,
swap one true and one false uncertified atom in its A support. This
is possible since j_x<r<K. The coarsened source laws then differ
by exactly 1/(Nr) in TV. But 2c<(K-r)/(NrK)<1/(Nr), contradicting (5).
Thus all uncertified atoms still occupy one score bin, as before.

Consequently coarsened source masses are independent of residual
supports. On flipping a single pair's orientation their bin-mass
changes are integer multiples of

 eta=(K-r)/(NrK),

by the delta formula above. If any bin changes, the changes sum to
zero, so the sum of their positive parts is at least eta. Uniform
coarsening preserves each bin mass, hence the TV of these two
coarsened laws is at least eta. This contradicts 2c<eta. Therefore
ALL coarsened source laws are identical across every compatible world.
In particular the invariant-bin classification and balanced-set
expansion apply without assuming g equals this common coarsened law.
They preserve both calibration distance to g and false mass, bin by
bin, for each orientation. The earlier reduction is valid throughout (4).

Let D_h count pairs with h_i=h,0<=h<=r-1. Put

 tau_h=(K-r)/(2(K-h)), M_h=D_h*(2-h/r-h/K)/N,
 T_h=sum_{t=h}^{r-1}M_t.

C015's balanced-game formula gives the exact all-generator conditional
frontier for the ORIGINAL unequal-count experiment:

 V(c)=tau_0*(T_0-c)_+
      +sum_{h=1}^{r-1}(tau_h-tau_{h-1})*(T_h-c)_+,       (6)

for every c in (4). The matching construction discards surplus truths
and transfers mass from the balanced uncertified groups to fixed S
in decreasing h order. It works even for larger c as an upper bound;
the exact lower bound is asserted only on (4).

For the same-data partition-supplied worst-orientation oracle set

 alpha_h=2tau_h, A_h=D_h*(r-h)/(Nr), Q_h=sum_{t=h}^{r-1}A_t.

Its exact frontier is

 O_worst(c)=alpha_0*(Q_0-c)_+
      +sum_{h=1}^{r-1}(alpha_h-alpha_{h-1})*(Q_h-c)_+.    (7)

For any supplied orientation, ignoring surplus A truths down to h_i
gives a feasible generator attaining the minimum-count oracle bound,
so that orientation's oracle value is at most (7). The orientation
that chooses the smaller-known-count context as A in EVERY pair is
compatible and has exactly that oracle game, proving the reverse
inequality for the worst orientation. Thus (6)-(7) is an exact matching
conditional decomposition; at zero it simplifies to (3).

No endpoint c=c_star is claimed, nor is c_star asserted to be the
largest valid interval. A nonzero TV jump cannot be ruled out by the
triangle argument at the endpoint. No global expected minimax identity
is inferred, and no statement about actual-world-only calibration is
made. The rigidity proof is a deterministic discrete-bin argument;
finite checks validate its steps but do not supply the general proof.

On this interval both formulas simplify: let H=max_i h_i and
tau_H=(K-r)/(2(K-H)). Every nonempty M_h group has mass at least
(K-r)/(NK), whereas c<c_star=(K-r)/(2NrK) is smaller. Every nonempty
A_h group has mass at least 1/(Nr), also greater than c_star.
Therefore no highest-risk group is exhausted and

 V(c)=V(0)-tau_H*c,
 O_worst(c)=O_worst(0)-2*tau_H*c,
 V(c)-O_worst(c)
   =sum_i h_i*(K-r)^2/(2NrK(K-h_i))+tau_H*c.             (8)

This is the exact matching oracle-plus-ambiguity penalty on a nonzero
parameter interval, not merely an upper or lower estimate. The interval
is small and depends on N,K,r; no uniform large-budget assertion follows.

Exact verification: logs/unsaturated_reduction_check.json records
90440 expanded source-bin mass checks, 23634 false-count-vector and
risk-preservation checks, 1401 feasible-partition lower checks, 1396
nonzero-budget generator checks and 200 attainer/world checks. Five
single-pair configurations exhaust all invariant partitions; the
two-pair configuration checks its first 500, explicitly not all.
logs/discrete_tv_rigidity_check.json exhausts all 21147 nine-atom
partitions: 20944 split support groups, 151 violate orientation
invariance, and 52 are invariant. Minimum corresponding nonzero TV
diameters are 1/6 and 1/18. A real generator at radius 1/36 has
non-invariant source bins, so the strict endpoint exclusion is needed
for this rigidity proof. The control does not assert that the exact
frontier formula itself fails there. General proof and finite checks
remain distinct; independent audit is still required.

All variable context known-truth unions arise from actual untagged iid factual data and optional independent uniform partial truth verification
Every known-truth count j_x<r; no supplied orientations; every compatible residual support/orientation considered
Robust exact-level source Mis_infinity<=c for EVERY compatible world, 0<=c<(K-r)/(2NrK); arbitrary generators; conditional worst-world objective

swap one true and one false uncertified atom in its A support. This
is possible since j_x<r<K. The coarsened source laws then differ
by exactly 1/(Nr) in TV. But 2c<(K-r)/(NrK)<1/(Nr), contradicting (5).
Thus all uncertified atoms still occupy one score bin, as before.

Consequently coarsened source masses are independent of residual
supports. On flipping a single pair's orientation their bin-mass
changes are integer multiples of

 eta=(K-r)/(NrK),

by the delta formula above. If any bin changes, the changes sum to
zero, so the sum of their positive parts is at least eta. Uniform
coarsening preserves each bin mass, hence the TV of these two
coarsened laws is at least eta. This contradicts 2c<eta. Therefore
ALL coarsened source laws are identical across every compatible world.
In particular the invariant-bin classification and balanced-set
expansion apply without assuming g equals this common coarsened law.
They preserve both calibration distance to g and false mass, bin by
bin, for each orientation. The earlier reduction is valid throughout (4).

Let D_h count pairs with h_i=h,0<=h<=r-1. Put

 tau_h=(K-r)/(2(K-h)), M_h=D_h*(2-h/r-h/K)/N,
 T_h=sum_{t=h}^{r-1}M_t.

C015's balanced-game formula gives the exact all-generator conditional
frontier for the ORIGINAL unequal-count experiment:

 V(c)=tau_0*(T_0-c)_+
      +sum_{h=1}^{r-1}(tau_h-tau_{h-1})*(T_h-c)_+,       (6)

for every c in (4). The matching construction discards surplus truths
and transfers mass from the balanced uncertified groups to fixed S
in decreasing h order. It works even for larger c as an upper bound;
the exact lower bound is asserted only on (4).

For the same-data partition-supplied worst-orientation oracle set

 alpha_h=2tau_h, A_h=D_h*(r-h)/(Nr), Q_h=sum_{t=h}^{r-1}A_t.

Its exact frontier is

 O_worst(c)=alpha_0*(Q_0-c)_+
      +sum_{h=1}^{r-1}(alpha_h-alpha_{h-1})*(Q_h-c)_+.    (7)

For any supplied orientation, ignoring surplus A truths down to h_i
gives a feasible generator attaining the minimum-count oracle bound,
so that orientation's oracle value is at most (7). The orientation
that chooses the smaller-known-count context as A in EVERY pair is
compatible and has exactly that oracle game, proving the reverse
inequality for the worst orientation. Thus (6)-(7) is an exact matching
conditional decomposition; at zero it simplifies to (3).

No endpoint c=c_star is claimed, nor is c_star asserted to be the
largest valid interval. A nonzero TV jump cannot be ruled out by the
triangle argument at the endpoint. No global expected minimax identity
is inferred, and no statement about actual-world-only calibration is
made. The rigidity proof is a deterministic discrete-bin argument;
finite checks validate its steps but do not supply the general proof.

On this interval both formulas simplify: let H=max_i h_i and
tau_H=(K-r)/(2(K-H)). Every nonempty M_h group has mass at least
(K-r)/(NK), whereas c<c_star=(K-r)/(2NrK) is smaller. Every nonempty
A_h group has mass at least 1/(Nr), also greater than c_star.
Therefore no highest-risk group is exhausted and

 V(c)=V(0)-tau_H*c,
 O_worst(c)=O_worst(0)-2*tau_H*c,
 V(c)-O_worst(c)
   =sum_i h_i*(K-r)^2/(2NrK(K-h_i))+tau_H*c.             (8)

This is the exact matching oracle-plus-ambiguity penalty on a nonzero
parameter interval, not merely an upper or lower estimate. The interval
is small and depends on N,K,r; no uniform large-budget assertion follows.

Exact verification: logs/unsaturated_reduction_check.json records
90440 expanded source-bin mass checks, 23634 false-count-vector and
risk-preservation checks, 1401 feasible-partition lower checks, 1396
nonzero-budget generator checks and 200 attainer/world checks. Five
single-pair configurations exhaust all invariant partitions; the
two-pair configuration checks its first 500, explicitly not all.
logs/discrete_tv_rigidity_check.json exhausts all 21147 nine-atom
partitions: 20944 split support groups, 151 violate orientation
invariance, and 52 are invariant. Minimum corresponding nonzero TV
diameters are 1/6 and 1/18. A real generator at radius 1/36 has
non-invariant source bins, so the strict endpoint exclusion is needed
for this rigidity proof. The control does not assert that the exact
frontier formula itself fails there. General proof and finite checks
remain distinct; independent audit is still required.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:a044936bdf380d385f31dc00fcb48dd844133579b520e03f5d4f0cce311858b9","revision_digest":"sha256:f5ecdd516afb48d5bc73f821bd8009af1470dbd78318d1492d5ff9a585371209","source_id":"owner:w709:T379-C017:v3","source_revision":"2026-10-20T12:59:13.968160+03:00","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma Patching of arXiv:2509.04155, 'An Approach to Sub-Gaussian Heat Kernel Estimates via Analysis on Metric Spaces'] Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\sigma \geq 1$. Fix any collection $\{x_i\}_{i \in I} \subseteq X$ such that $d(x_i,x_j) \geq \varepsilon$ for all distinct $i,j \in I$, and let
    \[
        G := \bigcup_{i \in I} B(x_i,\sigma \varepsilon).
    \]
    Then $I$ is at most countably infinite and there is a constant $C \geq 1$ depending only on $N$ in (equation eq:MD of the paper) and $\sigma$ such that
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{i \in I} \mathds{1}_{B(x_i,\sigma 2^{-m})} \leq C \mathds{1}_G.
    \end{equation*}
    Here $\mathds{1}_A$ denotes the characteristic function of a Borel set $A \subseteq X$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma Patching of arXiv:2509.04155

[Lemma loclem of arXiv:2411.06006, 'Mixing time of the torus shuffle'] Let $N$ and $r$ be positive integers such that $r^2 \leq N \leq 3 r^2$.
Suppose that  $x \in \{-r, \dots, r\}$ and 
let $Y_t$ be a lazy simple random walk on ${\bf Z}$
started at $x$.

Then
there is a universal constant $C >0$ such that
if
  $y   \in \{-r, \dots, r\}$, then 
  \[
    { \mathbb P}( \mbox{$Y_N = y$ and $|Y_t| \leq Kr$ for all $t$ with $0 \leq t \leq N$}) \geq C/r \,.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma loclem of arXiv:2411.06006

[Lemma lem:subcritical of arXiv:2601.20502, 'Optimal matching under size priority'] Define the families of truncated decorated trees $\left(\mathbb{T}_H,o,(i_{-}^{H},Z_{-}^H),(i_{+}^{H},Z_{+}^H)\right)_{H \geq 0}$ as follows:
    Sample $(\mathbb{T},o)$, set $\mathbb{T}_H=B_H(\mathbb{T},o)$ and   $(i_{-}^{H},Z_{-}^H)(u,v)=(0,0)$ for every edge of $\mathbb{T}_H$ pointing towards the $H-$boundary. Then use Recursion~(equation eq:systemrecursionzoombis of the paper) to define $(i_{-}^{H},Z_{-}^H)$ on the remainder of $\mathbb{T}_H$. We proceed similarly for $(i_{+}^{H},Z_{+}^H)$ by setting $(i_{+}^{H},Z_{+}^H)=(1,+\infty)$ on the boundary instead of $(0,0)$.

    Then under condition~(equation eq:subcriticalcond of the paper), both families $((i_{+}^{H},Z_{+}^H)(o,v))_{v \sim o}$ and $((i_{-}^{H},Z_{-}^H)(o,v))_{v \sim o}$ converge almost surely, as $H$ goes to infinity, to the same family $(i_l,Z_l)_{1 \leq l \leq N}$ where $(i_l,Z_l)$ have i.i.d distribution $\zeta'$ and are independent of $N \sim \pi$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:subcritical of arXiv:2601.20502

[Proposition 38 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] Let \(J_{\infty}\) be the Legendre--Fenchel transform of \(\Lambda_{\infty}\),
and write \(\delta:=a-1>0\). Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*)]

\item For every compact \(K\subset(0,\infty)\), as \(\delta\downarrow0\),
\[
        J_a(\delta x)
        =
        \delta J_{\operatorname{Pois}}(x)
        +
        \delta^2\,\frac{16\pi^2x^2+24\pi x-7}{32\pi}
        +
        O_K(\delta^3)
\]
uniformly for \(x\in K\), where \(J_{\operatorname{Pois}}\) is the Cram\'er
transform of the Poisson law with mean \(1/(4\pi)\),
\[
        J_{\operatorname{Pois}}(x)
        =
        x\log(4\pi x)-x+\frac{1}{4\pi},
        \qquad x>0.
\]

\item For every compact \(K\subset(0,\infty)\), if
\(\theta_{\infty}(x)\) is defined by
\(\Lambda_{\infty}'(\theta_{\infty}(x))=x\), then, as \(a\to\infty\),
\[
        J_a(x)
        =
        J_{\infty}(x)
        +
        \frac{1}{4\pi a}
        \operatorname{Li}_2 \bigl(1-e^{-\theta_{\infty}(x)}\bigr)
        +
        O_K(a^{-2})
\]
uniformly for \(x\in K\).
\end{enumerate}

[Thm 4 of arXiv:2609.03185, 'Uniqueness of tangent flows in free boundary flow'] There exist constants $\epsilon=\epsilon(n,r_0)>0$ and $C=C(n,r_0)<\infty$ such that the following holds.

Let \(M=(M_t)_{t\in(-1,0)}\) be a smooth, properly embedded \(n\)-dimensional mean curvature flow in \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) with free boundary on a smooth hypersurface \(S\), with Fermi coordinates defined
on \(B_{r_0}(0)\), and let \(U\subset B_{r_0}(0)\). Let $X_0=(x_0,t_0)\in U\times(-1,0)$ and $0<R\leq c(n)^{-1}r_0$ satisfy \(t_0-R^2>-1\). Suppose that
\[
\Theta_g(M,X,r)<1+\epsilon
\]
for every \(X\in U\times(-1,0)\) and \(0<r<R\). Then
\[
|A|\leq \frac{C}{R}
\]
on \(M_t\cap B_R(x_0)\) for all $t_0-R^2<t<t_0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 4 of arXiv:2609.03185

[Prop thm:essential-boundedness of arXiv:2411.18155, 'Besov regularity of random wavelet series'] Let $d\in\mathds{N}$, $s,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\theta\in\mathds{R}$, $p=\infty$, and $q\in (0,\infty]$.
Assume that $a$ follows a Besov sequence prior with parameters $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\theta)$ and template random variable $X$.
Suppose that $X$ is such that $a\in b^s_{\infty,q}(\mathds{R}^d)$ almost surely.
If $\beta=0$ or $\gamma=0$, then there exists $R>0$ such that $\left\lvertX\right\rvert\leq R$ almost surely.

[Defn 15 (Sub/Super-harmonicity in the weak sense) of arXiv:2506.17979, '\large\bf A remark on subharmonicity for symmetric Dirichlet forms'] {\rm Let $D$ be an open set in $E$. We say that a nearly Borel
$\overline{\R}$-valued function $u$ defined on $E$ is \emph{subharmonic {\rm(}resp.~superharmonic{\rm)} in $D$ in the weak sense} if $u$ is q.e.~finely continuous on $D$ and for any relatively compact open subset $U$ with $U\Subset D$, $\mathbb{E}_x[|{u}|(X_{\tau_U})]<\infty$ for q.e.~$x\in E$ and ${u}(x)\leq\mathbb{E}_x[{u}(X_{\tau_U})]$ (resp.~${u}(x)\geq\mathbb{E}_x[{u}(X_{\tau_U})]$) holds for q.e.~$x\in E$.
A nearly Borel measurable $\overline{\R}$-valued function $u$ on $E$ is said to be \emph{harmonic in $D$ in the weak sense} if $u$ is both superharmonic and subharmonic in $D$ in the weak sense.
If $u$ is finely continuous (nearly) Borel $\overline{\R}$-valued function on $D$ and for any relatively compact open subset $U$ with $U\Subset D$, $\mathbb{E}_x[|{u}|(X_{\tau_U})]<\infty$ for all $x\in E$, and ${u}(x)\leq\mathbb{E}_x[{u}(X_{\tau_U})]$ holds  for all $x\in E$, then $u$ is called \emph{subharmonic in $D$ in the weak sense without exceptional set}.
The \emph{subharmonicity/harmonicity in $D$ in the weak sense without exceptional set} is analogously defined.
}
title: Sub/Super-harmonicity in the weak sense

Own work, proof (unaudited), W719-T295-C012 v1. Conditional method record; no specialist novelty asserted. For fixed real symmetric H_minus>mu I, mu>=0, beta>=0, H=H_minus+beta aa^T, 0<eta<=1/lambda_max(H), M=I-eta H and rho=1-eta mu, the nonnegative kernel K_k=(eta beta/rho)a^T(M/rho)^k a has total mass beta a^T(H-mu I)^(-1)a<=1. Equal-start full/omitted-row quadratic trajectories with |a^T z_s|<=U rho^s therefore satisfy |a^T(h_t-z_t)|<=U rho^t and |a^T h_t|<=2U rho^t. An exact rational 2D example shows positivity does not extend to arbitrary time-varying products even when each matrix has the required rank-one split and uniform spectral bounds. Here a is a real vector, h_(t+1)=(I-eta H)h_t, z_(t+1)=(I-eta H_minus)z_t, and h_0=z_0. For the phase-retrieval Hessian at a fixed unit signal, H=(2/m)sum_j g_j^2 a_j a_j^T, g_j=a_j^T x_*, take beta=2g_i^2/m and a=a_i, whenever the matrix assumptions hold. The gain follows from the positive matrix geometric series and H-mu I>=beta aa^T; it avoids taking the maximum of g_i^2 separately. This is a frozen quadratic calculation, not a nonlinear local theorem. Actual GD introduces the changing secant error and nonlinear omitted-row forcing, whose projected cumulative contributions remain unpaid. The time-varying example uses eta=1, beta=1/100, mu=1/20, a=(1,0), M1=[[13/50,8/25],[8/25,37/50]], M2=[[13/50,-8/25],[-8/25,37/50]], H_j=I-M_j. Both H_j-beta aa^T>=9I/100 but a^T M2 M1 a=-87/2500. Thus positivity of products cannot be assumed from the one-step spectral hypotheses. This example does not disprove an absolute gain estimate by some other method. No relative-incoherence invariant or actual random-start convergence result is established.

step makes I-eta H positive semidefinite; error-envelope input bound assumed for the quadratic trajectory
nonlinear full/omitted-row secant and row-force remainders are displayed but not controlled

\frac{2\textup{g}_{Y_i}-2\textup{g}_{Y_{i-1}}}{p^i-p^{i-1}}\quad\,\;\;\;\, {\rm if}\quad i\ge 1.\end{cases}$$

[Corollary 54 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] We use the above notation.
If $V$ is quasi-$F$-split, then the Casagrande--Druel variety
\[
X=\operatorname{Bl}_{S_+\cap F}Y
\]
is HT-split.

In particular, if \(V\) is a Fano threefold, then \(X\) is HT-split. Consequently, Akizuki--Nakano-type vanishing holds on \(X\), and the Hodge-to-de Rham spectral sequence degenerates at the \(E_1\)-page.

Own-work draft, independently checked proof, urn:mb-agent:d6ca7a10ae76247b PASS on exact version. For scalar corrected or uncorrected deterministic Adam with standard m0=v0=0, epsilon outside sqrt, positive eta,epsilon,lambda and 0<beta1<sqrt(beta2)<1, if eta lambda/epsilon<=2(1+beta1)/(1-beta1), every finite initial x0 converges to zero together with its raw moments; strict inequality gives geometric decay of x,m. Coordinatewise this holds for diagonal quadratics. At p=1,beta1=.9,beta2=.999,H=38 I_2, scaled top and every defined active curvature tend to38 for arbitrary standard initial positions.
